modules.standfirst: Year 9 content that every paper still tests. The whole topic is one idea — shape decides function — and almost every lost mark is a wording slip: "the enzyme dies", "it changes shape", forgetting kinetic energy.

subsections.html: An enzyme is a protein that speeds up a reaction without being used up. Everything else in this topic follows from one fact: an enzyme works because of its shape. Change the shape and it stops working.

subsections.heading: What an enzyme is
subsections.html:
Spec 2.10

An enzyme is a biological catalyst. "Biological" because it is a protein made by living cells. "Catalyst" because it speeds up a reaction and is not used up.

Every chemical reaction in a living organism — building molecules, breaking them down, respiration — is controlled by enzymes. These are called metabolic reactions. Without enzymes they would happen far too slowly at body temperature to keep you alive.

The two-mark definition of a catalyst

1. A substance that increases the rate of a reaction 1

2. and is not used up / is unchanged at the end 1

"Makes reactions happen" is not enough. The reaction would happen anyway — just slowly.

subsections.heading: The active site and the lock-and-key model
subsections.html:
Spec 2.10

Each enzyme has an active site with a specific shape, and only one substrate fits it.

The substrate is the molecule the enzyme acts on. Its shape is complementary to the active site — it fits the way a key fits a lock. The reaction happens in four steps:

  1. The substrate collides with the enzyme and fits into the active site.
  2. They form an enzyme–substrate complex.
  3. The reaction takes place — the substrate is broken down, or joined to something.
  4. The products are released, and the enzyme is unchanged and ready to be used again.

Because the fit is so exact, each enzyme works on one substrate only. That is called specificity. Amylase cannot digest protein for the same reason a house key will not open a car.

subsections.heading: Temperature, below the optimum — the half everyone forgets
subsections.html:
Spec 2.11 · Y10 2023 Q7 · Y10 2024 Q4

Warming an enzyme up to its optimum makes the reaction faster, because molecules collide more often. Nothing about the enzyme's shape is involved yet.

  1. Higher temperature gives the enzyme and substrate molecules more kinetic energy.
  2. They move faster, so they collide more frequently.
  3. More collisions means more enzyme–substrate complexes form per second.
  4. So the rate of reaction increases.

This is exactly what the snail question wanted, and exactly what students missed. The scheme's marking points were "enzymes · more kinetic energy · more frequent collisions / enzyme substrate complexes form faster · faster respiration".

✗ "The snails at 23 °C are nearer the optimum temperature."
✓ "At higher temperature the enzymes and substrates have more kinetic energy, so they collide more often and more enzyme–substrate complexes form, so respiration and growth are faster."

subsections.heading: Temperature, above the optimum — denaturing
subsections.html:
Spec 2.11

Past the optimum, heat breaks the enzyme's shape, so the substrate no longer fits.

Human enzymes have an optimum of about 37 °C. Above it:

  1. The heat breaks the bonds that hold the protein in its folded shape.
  2. The active site changes shape.
  3. The substrate is no longer complementary to it, so it cannot fit.
  4. No enzyme–substrate complexes form — the enzyme is denatured and the rate falls to zero.

Denaturing is permanent. Cooling a denatured enzyme back down does not fix it, in the same way you cannot un-boil an egg.

✗ "The enzyme dies." — An enzyme is a protein, not a living thing. It cannot die.
✗ "The enzyme changes shape." — Too vague. Say the active site changes shape.
✓ "The active site changes shape, so the substrate no longer fits and the enzyme is denatured."

subsections.heading: Reading a temperature graph
subsections.html:
A rate–temperature graph rises gradually, peaks at the optimum, then falls steeply.

The two sides are not symmetrical, and the difference is worth a mark. The rise is gradual because kinetic energy increases steadily. The fall is steep because once the shape starts breaking, activity collapses quickly.

A question that shows only the rising half — like the snail data, 8 °C to 23 °C — is a kinetic energy question. A question that goes past the peak needs both explanations, one for each side.

subsections.heading: pH — the same ending by a different route
subsections.html:
Spec 2.13

Every enzyme has an optimum pH, and moving away from it in either direction denatures the enzyme.

EnzymeWhere it worksOptimum pH
Salivary amylaseMouthAbout 7
Pepsin (a protease)Stomach — hydrochloric acidAbout 2
Pancreatic enzymesSmall intestine — bile neutralises the acidAbout 8

Too acidic or too alkaline, the charges holding the protein's folds together are disrupted, the active site changes shape, and the substrate no longer fits. Same result as heat, different cause.

Note the direction does not matter. Students often assume only acid is damaging — but putting pepsin into pH 7 denatures it just as surely as putting amylase into pH 2.

subsections.heading: The digestive enzymes
subsections.html:
Spec 2.29 · Y10 2024 Q1(c) · Y11 Jan 2024 Q8(a)

Big food molecules are too large to absorb, so enzymes break them into small soluble ones. The exam wants the named enzyme and the named products.

FoodEnzymeProducts
StarchAmylaseMaltose
MaltoseMaltaseGlucose
ProteinProtease (e.g. pepsin)Amino acids
Lipid (fat)LipaseFatty acids and glycerol

The January 2024 mock gave this table with four gaps: amylase, glucose, proteins, fatty acids and glycerol. Every one was a single word worth a mark.

✗ "Amylase breaks starch into glucose." — It skips a stage. Amylase makes maltose; maltase makes glucose.
✗ "Lipase makes fatty acids." — Both products are needed: fatty acids and glycerol.
✗ "Carbohydrase" when the question wants the named enzyme — give amylase.

subsections.heading: Why herbivores need cellulase
subsections.html:
Y11 Jan 2023 Q1(b)

Plant cell walls are made of cellulose, and only an enzyme called cellulase can break it down.

The three-mark chain from the mock scheme:

  1. Plants contain cellulose 1
  2. It is digested by cellulase 1
  3. into glucose, which releases energy in respiration 1

Humans do not make cellulase, so cellulose passes through us undigested as fibre. Specificity again: no enzyme with the right active site, no digestion.

subsections.heading: The iodine test — how every enzyme practical is measured
subsections.html:
Spec 2.12, 2.14B

Iodine turns blue-black when starch is present and stays orange-brown when it is gone. So it tells you when amylase has finished.

  1. Put single drops of iodine in the wells of a spotting tile.
  2. Mix amylase and starch solution in a test tube, in a water bath at a set temperature, and start a stopwatch.
  3. Every 10 seconds, move one drop of the mixture into a new well of iodine.
  4. While starch is present, the iodine turns blue-black.
  5. Record the time when the iodine stays orange-brown — all the starch has been digested.
  6. Repeat at other temperatures, or with buffer solutions of different pH.

A shorter time means a faster reaction. Rate and time go in opposite directions: rate ∝ 1 ÷ time. That is why a graph of time against pH is a valley, while a graph of rate against pH is a peak. Check which is on the axis before describing the shape.

subsections.heading: Designing an enzyme investigation — six marks
subsections.html:
Y11 Jan 2024 Q8(b) — effect of vinegar on starch digestion

Six-mark "design an investigation" questions are marked against a fixed checklist, so write to the checklist. This school uses CORMMSS:

CORMMSS — one mark each

C — Change: what you vary, with a range. "Use different concentrations of vinegar, and no vinegar." 1

O — Organism / object: same material each time. "Same mass of starch." 1

R — Repeat: "Repeat three times at each concentration and calculate a mean." 1

M1 — Measure what: "Test samples with iodine to see if starch remains." 1

M2 — Measure how: "Record the time until the iodine stays orange-brown." 1

S — Same: two controlled variables. "Same temperature using a water bath; same volume and concentration of amylase." 1

"Keep everything else the same" scores nothing. Every control variable must be named.

subsections.heading: When the rate levels off without denaturing
subsections.html:
A reaction can slow and stop even at the perfect temperature and pH. Two reasons, neither of which is denaturing:

  • The substrate is used up — nothing left to bind.
  • All the active sites are occupied — the enzyme is working flat out. Adding more substrate does nothing; adding more enzyme would speed it up.

If the question says conditions did not change, do not reach for "denatured".

The chain behind every mark

Below the optimum: more kinetic energy → more frequent collisions → more enzyme–substrate complexes → faster.

Above the optimum, or wrong pH: active site changes shape → substrate no longer fits → denatured → stops.

subsections.html:

EnzymeA biological catalyst — a protein that speeds up a reaction without being used up
CatalystA substance that increases the rate of a reaction and is not used up
Active siteThe part of the enzyme the substrate binds to
SubstrateThe molecule an enzyme acts on
ComplementaryThe substrate's shape fits the active site
Enzyme–substrate complexThe enzyme and substrate bound together in the active site
DenaturedThe active site has changed shape, so the substrate no longer fits
OptimumThe temperature or pH at which the enzyme works fastest
SpecificityEach enzyme acts on only one substrate, because only it fits the active site

questions.promptHtml: Snails grow faster at 23 °C than at 8 °C. A student writes "because 23 °C is closer to the enzymes' optimum." The teacher gives 1 of 3. What was missing?
questions.answerHtml:
The student described where 23 °C sits, not why that speeds things up.

The explanation below the optimum is about kinetic energy. At 23 °C the enzyme and substrate molecules move faster, so they collide more frequently, more enzyme–substrate complexes form, and reactions such as respiration run faster — so the snails grow more.

The test question: would the student's answer have scored better at 45 °C? No — there the snails would grow less, because the enzymes denature. "Closer to the optimum" never explains anything by itself.

questions.promptHtml: An enzyme is heated to 70 °C for five minutes, then cooled back to 37 °C. Does it start working again? Explain.
questions.answerHtml:
No. At 70 °C the bonds holding the protein's shape broke, so the active site changed shape and the enzyme was denatured.

Denaturing is permanent. Cooling does not re-fold the protein into its original shape, so the substrate still does not fit.

The contrast worth knowing: an enzyme cooled to 5 °C does recover when warmed. Cold only slows the molecules down — it never changes the shape.

questions.promptHtml: Pepsin works in the stomach at pH 2. When food moves into the small intestine, pepsin stops working. Why, and why does that not matter?
questions.answerHtml:
Why it stops: bile neutralises the stomach acid, so the pH rises to about 8. That is far from pepsin's optimum, so its active site changes shape and it is denatured.

Why it does not matter: the pancreas releases its own proteases into the small intestine, and their optimum is alkaline. Protein digestion simply carries on with a different enzyme suited to the new pH.

questions.promptHtml: In a pH practical the iodine stays orange-brown after 40 s at pH 6, 20 s at pH 7 and 55 s at pH 8. Which pH is fastest, and why is the shortest time the fastest rate?
questions.answerHtml:
pH 7 — the shortest time.

The iodine stops going blue-black at the moment all the starch has been digested. Getting there in 20 s means the amylase worked twice as fast as at pH 6. Time and rate are inversely related.

Plot time on the y-axis and you get a valley with its lowest point at the optimum. Plot rate and you get a peak. Always read the axis label before describing the shape.

questions.promptHtml: Why can one enzyme not digest starch, protein and fat?
questions.answerHtml:
Because of specificity. The active site has one particular shape, and only a substrate with a complementary shape can fit and form an enzyme–substrate complex.

Starch, protein and lipid molecules all have different shapes, so each needs its own enzyme — amylase, protease and lipase.

questions.promptHtml: A reaction slows and stops, although the temperature and pH have not changed. Give two possible reasons — neither of them denaturing.
questions.answerHtml:
1. The substrate has run out. Nothing is left to bind, so no more product forms.

2. Every active site is occupied. The enzyme is saturated. More substrate would change nothing; more enzyme would speed it up.

How to tell them apart: add more substrate. If the reaction restarts, it had run out. If nothing happens, the enzyme was the limit.

questions.promptHtml: Humans eat plenty of plants but cannot release energy from the cellulose in them. Cows can. Explain the difference.
questions.answerHtml:
Cellulose can only be broken down by the enzyme cellulase, because only cellulase has an active site complementary to it.

Humans do not produce cellulase, so cellulose passes through undigested. Cows have microorganisms in their gut that make cellulase, which digests the cellulose into glucose. The glucose is absorbed and used in respiration to release energy.

questions.promptHtml: Why is the enzyme–temperature graph steeper on the right of the peak than on the left?
questions.answerHtml:
The two sides have different causes.

Left side: kinetic energy increases steadily with temperature, so collision frequency rises gradually and so does the rate.

Right side: once the temperature passes the optimum, bonds holding the protein's shape start breaking and more and more enzyme molecules denature at once. Activity collapses quickly — hence the steep drop.

subsections.html: Photosynthesis is how a plant makes its own food. It uses light energy to turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose, and gives off oxygen. Everything else in this topic — the graphs, the leaf, the practicals — is about what speeds that up, and how you prove it happened.

subsections.heading: The equations
subsections.html:
Spec 2.18, 2.19 · 2023 Edexcel 1B Q9

Photosynthesis turns carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen, using light energy absorbed by chlorophyll.

Photosynthesis — word equationcarbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygenlight and chlorophyll go above the arrow, not on the left
Photosynthesis — balanced symbol equation6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂correct formulae one mark, balancing numbers the second

It is an endothermic reaction: light energy is taken in and stored as chemical energy in the glucose. That conversion — light energy to chemical energy — is what "importance" questions want.

✗ "light + carbon dioxide + water → glucose" — light is not a reactant.
✗ "6CO₂ + H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + O₂" — correct formulae, unbalanced: one mark of two.
✓ "6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂", with light and chlorophyll written above the arrow.

subsections.heading: Where it happens — the plant cell
subsections.html:
Spec 2.4 · 2024 Y10 Q1(a) · 2023 Edexcel 1B Q3

Photosynthesis happens in chloroplasts, which contain the green pigment chlorophyll that absorbs the light.

StructurePlantAnimalJob
Nucleus✓✓Contains DNA; controls the cell
Cytoplasm✓✓Where most reactions happen
Cell membrane✓✓Controls what enters and leaves
Mitochondria✓✓Aerobic respiration
Chloroplasts✓✗Photosynthesis — contain chlorophyll
Cell wall✓✗Made of cellulose; gives strength
Permanent vacuole✓✗Holds cell sap; keeps the cell rigid

Chlorophyll absorbs the light; the chloroplast is the container it sits in. Questions that ask "which part contains chlorophyll" want the chloroplast. Questions about "what absorbs light" want chlorophyll.

subsections.heading: What the plant does with the glucose
subsections.html:
Glucose is the raw material for almost everything a plant makes.

  • Respiration — to release energy
  • Starch — insoluble storage, so it does not affect osmosis
  • Cellulose — for cell walls
  • Sucrose — the form transported in the phloem
  • Amino acids and proteins — combined with nitrate ions from the soil
  • Lipids — stored in seeds

That list is why the starch test works as proof of photosynthesis: no photosynthesis, no glucose, no starch.

subsections.heading: Limiting factors — the graph that always comes up
subsections.html:
Spec 2.20 · 2022 Edexcel 1B Q8

A limiting factor is whichever condition is in shortest supply, holding the rate back. There are three: light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature.

The classic graph rises and then flattens. Every answer about it has the same two parts:

  1. Where the line rises, the factor on the x-axis is limiting. More of it gives a faster rate.
  2. Where the line is flat, that factor is no longer limiting. Another factor now is — and you must name one.

The plateau answer — two marks

1. Light intensity is no longer the limiting factor 1

2. Another factor, such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature, is now limiting 1

"Something else is limiting" does not score. Name it.

If a graph shows two lines — one at high CO₂, one at low — the higher plateau proves CO₂ was the limiting factor on the lower line.

subsections.heading: Temperature — different from light and CO₂
subsections.html:
Spec 2.20

Photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes, so temperature has a peak and then a collapse.

Below the optimum, more kinetic energy means more frequent collisions and a faster rate — exactly as in module 1. Above it, the enzymes denature, their active sites change shape, and the rate falls.

Light and carbon dioxide never cause a fall. More of them simply stops helping once something else limits the rate. Temperature is the only one of the three that can make things worse.

subsections.heading: Light intensity and the inverse square law
subsections.html:
2024 Edexcel 1B Q6 · 2023 Edexcel 1B Q9

Light intensity falls with the square of the distance from the lamp.

Light intensity and distancelight intensity ∝ 1 ÷ distance²double the distance → a quarter of the light · treble it → a ninth

Moving a lamp from 10 cm to 20 cm does not halve the light — it cuts it to a quarter. If the question gives a table of distances, the rate should fall faster than the distance grows, at least while light is limiting.

subsections.heading: How the leaf is built for photosynthesis
subsections.html:
Spec 2.21, 2.42B · 2023 Edexcel 2B Q4 · 2022 Edexcel 2B Q3

Every layer of a leaf exists to get light, carbon dioxide or water to the chloroplasts. Link each structure to its job — a bare label rarely scores.

StructureAdaptation
Broad, flat shapeLarge surface area to absorb light
ThinShort diffusion distance for gases
Waxy cuticleWaterproof — reduces water loss; transparent so light passes
Upper epidermisThin and transparent, so light reaches the palisade layer
Palisade mesophyllPacked with chloroplasts, near the top where light is brightest
Spongy mesophyllAir spaces give a large surface area for gas exchange
StomataPores in the lower epidermis that let CO₂ in and O₂ out
Guard cellsOpen the stomata in light, close them in the dark to save water
Veins — xylem and phloemXylem brings water; phloem carries sugars away

subsections.heading: Stomata and the trade-off with water
subsections.html:
Spec 2.43B · 2024 Y11 mock Q4

Stomata must open to let carbon dioxide in, but open stomata also let water vapour out.

That is why closing them has a cost. The mock scheme's two marks: stomata closed or smaller 1, so less carbon dioxide absorbed, so less photosynthesis 1.

Water leaving through the stomata is transpiration. It pulls water up the xylem from the roots:

  1. Root hair cells absorb water from the soil by osmosis.
  2. Water moves up the xylem to the leaves.
  3. It evaporates from the leaf cells and diffuses out of the stomata.
  4. That loss pulls more water up behind it — the transpiration stream.

Transpiration is faster when it is warmer, windier, drier or brighter — bright light opens the stomata.

subsections.heading: Gas exchange — day, night and the word "net"
subsections.html:
Spec 2.40B, 2.41B, 2.44B

Plants respire all the time, but only photosynthesise in light — so what changes through the day is the net gas exchange.

LightWhat happensNet result
DarkRespiration onlyNet O₂ in, net CO₂ out
Dim (compensation point)Photosynthesis = respirationNo net exchange
BrightPhotosynthesis faster than respirationNet CO₂ in, net O₂ out

✗ "Plants photosynthesise in the day and respire at night."
✓ "Plants respire all the time. In bright light photosynthesis is faster than respiration, so there is a net uptake of carbon dioxide."

The word net is where the mark lives. Leave it out and the answer implies respiration stopped.

subsections.heading: Hydrogencarbonate indicator
subsections.html:
Spec 2.45B

Hydrogencarbonate indicator changes colour with the carbon dioxide level, so it shows net gas exchange.

Carbon dioxideColourMeaning
Higher than airYellowRespiration winning — dark
Same as airOrange / redBalanced — compensation point
Lower than airPurplePhotosynthesis winning — bright light

Set up tubes with a leaf in each, one in the dark, one in dim light, one in bright light, plus a tube with no leaf as the control. The control shows the colour change is caused by the leaf.

subsections.heading: The pondweed practical
subsections.html:
Spec 2.23 · 2024 Edexcel 1B Q6

Counting oxygen bubbles from pondweed measures the rate of photosynthesis.

  1. Put pondweed (Elodea) in a test tube of water with sodium hydrogencarbonate to supply CO₂.
  2. Place a lamp a measured distance away and leave it a few minutes to adjust.
  3. Count the bubbles of oxygen in one minute — or collect the gas in a syringe and measure its volume.
  4. Move the lamp to new distances and repeat, three times each, and take a mean.

Control the temperature — use an LED, or a beaker of water between the lamp and the pondweed as a heat shield — and keep the CO₂ concentration and the same piece of pondweed. Counting bubbles is inaccurate because bubbles differ in size; collecting the gas volume is better.

subsections.heading: Proving photosynthesis made starch
subsections.html:
Spec 2.23

A leaf that turns blue-black with iodine has made starch, so it has photosynthesised.

  1. Destarch the plant — 48 hours in the dark — so any starch found was made during the experiment.
  2. Expose it to the condition being tested.
  3. Boil the leaf in water to kill it and break the membranes.
  4. Boil it in ethanol, in a water bath, to remove the chlorophyll so the colour is visible.
  5. Rinse in warm water to soften it, then add iodine. Blue-black = starch.

Three versions test the three needs. Light: cover part of the leaf with foil — the covered part stays orange-brown. Chlorophyll: use a variegated leaf — only the green parts go blue-black. Carbon dioxide: seal the plant in a bag with soda lime, which absorbs CO₂ — no starch.

subsections.heading: Mineral ions
subsections.html:
Spec 2.22 · 2024 Edexcel 1B Q9 · 2024 Y11 mock Q4(e)

Plants make most of what they need from glucose, but two ions from the soil are essential.

IonNeeded forWithout it
MagnesiumMaking chlorophyllYellow leaves
NitrateMaking amino acids, and so proteinsStunted growth, yellow older leaves

The practical grows identical seedlings in solutions each missing one ion, with a complete solution as the control. Measure growth by mass or height, and note leaf colour.

The sentences behind most of the marks

Rising line: this factor is limiting. Flat line: another factor, named, is limiting.

Gas exchange: respiration never stops; in bright light there is a net uptake of CO₂.

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording
PhotosynthesisUsing light energy absorbed by chlorophyll to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water
Limiting factorThe factor in shortest supply, which limits the rate
ChlorophyllThe green pigment that absorbs light, inside chloroplasts
ChloroplastThe organelle where photosynthesis happens
StomaA pore in the leaf for gas exchange, opened and closed by guard cells
TranspirationThe loss of water vapour from the leaves, through the stomata
Compensation pointThe light level where photosynthesis and respiration are equal, so no net gas exchange
DestarchingKeeping a plant in the dark so it uses up its stored starch

questions.promptHtml: A graph of rate of photosynthesis against light intensity rises steeply, then flattens. Explain both parts.
questions.answerHtml:
Rising: light intensity is the limiting factor. More light means more energy absorbed by chlorophyll, so the rate increases.

Flat: light is no longer limiting — adding more has no effect. Another factor is now limiting, such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature.

The test question: how would you prove which one? Repeat at a higher CO₂ concentration. If the plateau rises, CO₂ was the limiting factor.

questions.promptHtml: A lamp is moved from 10 cm to 30 cm. Bubbles fall from 45 to 5 per minute. Is that what you would expect?
questions.answerHtml:
Yes. Treble the distance gives 1 ÷ 3² = 1/9 of the light. A ninth of 45 is 5.

That also tells you light was the limiting factor across the whole range. If the count had only fallen to 30, something else would have been limiting at the start.

questions.promptHtml: Hydrogencarbonate indicator around a leaf is purple in bright light and yellow in the dark. Explain, using the word "net".
questions.answerHtml:
Purple: photosynthesis is faster than respiration, so there is a net uptake of carbon dioxide. CO₂ falls.

Yellow: no photosynthesis, but respiration continues, so there is a net release of carbon dioxide. CO₂ rises.

The plant was respiring in the light too — photosynthesis was simply using CO₂ faster than respiration produced it.

questions.promptHtml: Why is a variegated leaf a fair test of whether chlorophyll is needed?
questions.answerHtml:
The green and white parts are on the same leaf, so they get the same light, carbon dioxide, water and temperature. The only difference is chlorophyll.

After the iodine test, only the green parts turn blue-black. The white parts, with no chlorophyll, made no starch.

questions.promptHtml: An antitranspirant spray partly closes the stomata. Why does it reduce water loss but also slow growth?
questions.answerHtml:
Smaller stomatal pores let less water vapour diffuse out, so transpiration falls.

But the same pores let carbon dioxide in. With less CO₂ absorbed, there is less photosynthesis, less glucose, and less growth. The plant cannot save water without also cutting its CO₂ supply.

questions.promptHtml: A plant grown without magnesium has yellow leaves and grows poorly. A plant without nitrate is green but small. Explain each.
questions.answerHtml:
No magnesium: it cannot make chlorophyll, so the leaves are yellow and absorb less light. Less photosynthesis means less glucose and poor growth.

No nitrate: it can still make chlorophyll and glucose, but cannot turn the glucose into amino acids and proteins, so growth is stunted.

questions.promptHtml: Why must a plant be destarched before a starch-test experiment, and why is the ethanol heated in a water bath?
questions.answerHtml:
Destarching removes starch made before the experiment. Otherwise a blue-black result could come from old starch and would prove nothing.

Water bath: ethanol is flammable, so it must never be heated over a naked flame. The Bunsen is turned off and the ethanol sits in hot water.

questions.promptHtml: Why does a very high temperature reduce the rate of photosynthesis, when a high light intensity never does?
questions.answerHtml:
Photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes. Too hot, and their active sites change shape — they denature — so the rate falls.

Light is not an enzyme. Once another factor limits the rate, extra light simply has no effect. It never damages the process in the way heat does.

questions.promptHtml: Give the balanced chemical symbol equation for photosynthesis. (2)
questions.answerHtml: Correct formulae — CO₂, H₂O, C₆H₁₂O₆, O₂ 1; balanced: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ 1

modules.title: Respiration
modules.standfirst: Four equations and one distinction that decides most of the marks: respiration releases energy, it does not make it. Every year someone writes "produces energy" and loses the mark for it. Real papers then test it through practicals — the respirometer, yeast, respiring seeds.

subsections.html: Respiration is the release of energy from glucose, in every living cell, all the time. The energy is used to make ATP, which cells then use for movement, growth, keeping warm and building large molecules. Respiration is not breathing: breathing is ventilation, covered in module 4.

subsections.heading: What respiration is — and what ATP does
subsections.html:
Spec 2.34, 2.35 · 2022 Y10 Q2(d)

Respiration is a chemical reaction in cells that releases energy from glucose and uses it to make ATP.

Energy cannot be created. It was stored in the glucose all along, and respiration releases it. That is why mark schemes reject "produces energy" outright.

ATP is the molecule that provides energy for cells. The energy released by respiration is used to make ATP, and ATP then carries it to whatever process needs it:

  • Muscle contraction — movement
  • Active transport — moving substances against a concentration gradient
  • Building large molecules — proteins from amino acids, for growth and repair
  • Cell division
  • Keeping warm — in mammals and birds some of the energy is released as heat

✗ "Respiration produces energy."
✗ "Respiration happens in the lungs."
✓ "Respiration releases energy from glucose, in every living cell, and the energy is used to make ATP."

subsections.heading: Aerobic respiration — the equations
subsections.html:
Spec 2.37 · 2024 Edexcel 1B Q4(a)

Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to break glucose down completely into carbon dioxide and water. It happens in the mitochondria.

Aerobic respiration — word equationglucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + waterenergy released and used to make ATP · in the mitochondria
Aerobic respiration — balanced symbol equationC₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂Ocorrect formulae one mark, balancing numbers the second

It is photosynthesis run backwards. Learn one and you have both.

✗ "C₆H₁₂O₆ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O" — correct formulae, unbalanced: one mark of two.
✗ "glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy" — energy is not a substance. Write it under the arrow, or leave it out.
✓ "C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O"

subsections.heading: Anaerobic respiration in animals
subsections.html:
Spec 2.38 · 2023 Y11 mock Q3

Without oxygen, animal cells break glucose down incompletely into lactic acid only.

Anaerobic respiration in animalsglucose → lactic acidone product · no carbon dioxide, no water

This happens in muscle during hard exercise, when oxygen cannot reach the cells fast enough. Some bacteria do the same thing: the bacteria in yoghurt respire anaerobically and make lactic acid, which is what makes the milk go sour and thick.

The animal equation has one product only. Adding carbon dioxide to it is one of the most common errors in the topic.

subsections.heading: Anaerobic respiration in plants and yeast
subsections.html:
Spec 2.38 · 2022 Edexcel 1B Q2 · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1B Q8

Without oxygen, plant and yeast cells break glucose down into ethanol and carbon dioxide.

Anaerobic respiration in plants and yeastglucose → ethanol + carbon dioxidein yeast this is called fermentation

Yeast is a single-celled fungus. People use its anaerobic respiration in two ways:

  • Bread — the carbon dioxide makes the dough rise. The ethanol evaporates when it is baked.
  • Beer and wine — the ethanol is the product wanted.

Plant roots in waterlogged soil respire this way too, because the water pushes the air out of the soil.

equations.name: Anaerobic respiration in plants and yeast

subsections.heading: Comparing aerobic and anaerobic
subsections.html:
Spec 2.36

Anaerobic respiration releases much less energy per glucose, because the glucose is only partly broken down.

FeatureAerobicAnaerobic
OxygenNeededNot needed
Glucose broken downCompletelyIncompletely
Energy releasedA lotMuch less
Products (animals)Carbon dioxide + waterLactic acid
Products (plants and yeast)Carbon dioxide + waterEthanol + carbon dioxide
WhereMitochondriaCytoplasm

The proof that energy is left behind: ethanol burns. If anaerobic respiration had released all the energy, there would be none left in the product.

subsections.heading: Oxygen debt — why you keep panting
subsections.html:
Spec 2.36 · 2022 Y10 Q4(b)

After hard exercise, extra oxygen is needed to break down the lactic acid that built up. That extra oxygen is the oxygen debt.

  1. During hard exercise the muscles need more energy than aerobic respiration alone can supply.
  2. They respire anaerobically as well, making lactic acid.
  3. Lactic acid builds up, causing fatigue and cramp.
  4. After exercise, breathing stays fast and deep to take in extra oxygen.
  5. The oxygen is used to break down the lactic acid. When it is gone, breathing returns to normal.

subsections.heading: Less oxygen, less energy — the chain answer
subsections.html:
2022 Y10 Q2(d) · 2022 Y10 Q4(b) · 2022 Edexcel 2B Q6(a)

Anything that cuts the oxygen supply to cells cuts aerobic respiration, so less energy is released.

This chain turns up inside questions on other topics — emphysema, a hole in the heart, low-oxygen water, anaemia. The marks are for each link:

The low-oxygen chain — three marks

1. Less oxygen diffuses into the blood / reaches the cells 1

2. So less aerobic respiration 1

3. So less energy released — for movement, keeping warm, building molecules — or more anaerobic respiration and lactic acid 1

"No respiration" is wrong. So is "less energy produced".

subsections.heading: Temperature and the rate of respiration
subsections.html:
2024 Edexcel 1B Q4(c) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1B Q8(c) · 2022 Edexcel 1B Q2(b)

Respiration is controlled by enzymes, so temperature affects it exactly as it affects any enzyme. This is module 1 again, and it came up in three real papers.

  1. Below the optimum: warmer means the molecules have more kinetic energy.
  2. They collide more often, forming more enzyme–substrate complexes.
  3. So the rate of respiration increases — more oxygen is used, or more carbon dioxide made, per minute.
  4. Above the optimum: the enzymes denature. The active site changes shape, the substrate no longer fits, and the rate falls.

✗ "The yeast works harder when it is warm."
✓ "More kinetic energy, so more frequent collisions between enzyme and substrate, so a faster rate of respiration."

subsections.heading: Practical — heat from respiring seeds
subsections.html:
Spec 2.39

Germinating seeds release heat as they respire, so a flask of them warms up.

  1. Soak peas so they start to germinate. Boil a second batch to kill them.
  2. Rinse both batches in disinfectant to kill microorganisms on their surface.
  3. Put each batch in a vacuum flask with a thermometer, plugged with cotton wool.
  4. Record the temperature at the start and every few hours for two or three days.
  5. The living seeds' flask gets warmer. The dead seeds' flask — the control — does not.

The vacuum flask insulates, so the heat is not lost. The disinfectant stops microbes on the seeds respiring and warming the flask, which would ruin the comparison. Cotton wool, not a bung, lets oxygen in so the seeds keep respiring aerobically.

subsections.heading: Practical — detecting carbon dioxide
subsections.html:
Spec 2.39 · 2023 Edexcel 1B Q8(b)

Limewater turns milky, and hydrogencarbonate indicator turns yellow, when carbon dioxide is added.

IndicatorNormal airMore carbon dioxide
LimewaterClearTurns milky / cloudy
Hydrogencarbonate indicatorOrange / redTurns yellow

Put small organisms — germinating seeds, woodlice, maggots — on gauze above the indicator in a sealed tube. Set up an identical tube with glass beads instead of organisms as the control. Only the tube with living things changes colour.

Or draw air through limewater, then past the organisms, then through a second limewater. The first stays clear, proving the carbon dioxide came from the organisms.

subsections.heading: The respirometer
subsections.html:
2024 Edexcel 1B Q4

A respirometer measures the rate of respiration by how fast the organisms use up oxygen.

  1. Small organisms sit on gauze in a sealed tube. Below them is soda lime, which absorbs carbon dioxide.
  2. The organisms take in oxygen. The carbon dioxide they give out is absorbed.
  3. So the volume of gas in the tube falls, and the pressure falls.
  4. A drop of coloured liquid in a capillary tube is pulled towards the organisms.
  5. The distance it moves in a set time measures the rate of oxygen use.

Why the soda lime is needed — two marks

1. Respiration releases carbon dioxide, which would replace the oxygen used 1

2. So the bubble would not move; with it absorbed, only the oxygen taken in is measured 1

Keep the tube in a water bath to control the temperature. A tube with glass beads of the same volume is the control.

subsections.heading: Practical — yeast and anaerobic respiration
subsections.html:
2023 Edexcel 1B Q8 · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1B Q8 · 2022 Edexcel 1B Q2

The rate of anaerobic respiration in yeast is measured by the carbon dioxide it gives off.

  1. Boil the glucose solution, then cool it — boiling drives out dissolved oxygen.
  2. Add yeast, then pour a layer of oil on top to stop oxygen getting in, so the yeast must respire anaerobically.
  3. Put the tube in a water bath at a set temperature, checked with a thermometer.
  4. Lead the gas into a gas syringe or an upside-down measuring cylinder of water, or count the bubbles.
  5. Measure the volume in a set time with a timer. Repeat and take a mean.

Change one thing — temperature, or glucose concentration — and keep everything else the same: mass of yeast, volume of solution, time.

In one real paper an oxygen indicator started blue and turned pink. The mark scheme's reading: blue while oxygen was present and the yeast respired aerobically; pink once the oxygen was used up, so the yeast was now respiring anaerobically.

The sentences behind most of the marks

Respiration releases energy from glucose. It does not produce, create or make energy.

Less oxygen → less aerobic respiration → less energy released. Never "no respiration".

Warmer (below the optimum) → more kinetic energy → more collisions → faster respiration.

subsections.html:
ProcessEquation

Aerobic (symbols)C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O

questions.promptHtml: A student writes: "Respiration happens in the lungs and produces energy for the body." Give three corrections.
questions.answerHtml:
1. Location. Respiration happens in every living cell (aerobic respiration in the mitochondria), not in the lungs. The lungs do gas exchange.

2. "Produces". Respiration releases energy that was already stored in glucose. Energy cannot be created.

3. What the energy does. It is used to make ATP, which supplies energy for cell processes — movement, growth, keeping warm, building molecules.

questions.promptHtml: A sprinter's muscles ache after a 200 m race, and they keep breathing heavily for several minutes. Explain both, naming the substance responsible.
questions.answerHtml:
During the race the muscles could not get oxygen fast enough, so they respired anaerobically as well as aerobically. This produced lactic acid, which builds up and causes the ache and fatigue.

Afterwards the sprinter continues to breathe heavily to take in extra oxygen — the oxygen debt — which is used to break down the lactic acid. Once it is cleared, breathing returns to normal.

questions.promptHtml: Why does anaerobic respiration release so much less energy than aerobic respiration from the same amount of glucose?
questions.answerHtml:
Because the glucose is broken down incompletely. Without oxygen the molecule is only partly broken apart, so most of the chemical energy is still locked in the products — lactic acid in animals, ethanol in plants and yeast.

Aerobic respiration breaks glucose down completely to carbon dioxide and water, releasing far more of the stored energy.

Evidence for this: ethanol burns. If anaerobic respiration had released all the energy, there would be none left in the product to burn.

questions.promptHtml: In the respiring seeds practical, why must the dead seeds be rinsed in disinfectant, and why is a vacuum flask used?
questions.answerHtml:
Disinfectant: it kills microorganisms on the seeds. Those microbes would respire and release heat, so the "dead" flask would warm up too and the control would prove nothing.

Vacuum flask: it insulates, so heat released by respiration is not lost to the surroundings. Without it the temperature rise would be too small to measure.

questions.promptHtml: Yeast is used to make both bread and beer. Explain, using one equation, why the same organism does two apparently different jobs.
questions.answerHtml:
Both rely on anaerobic respiration in yeast: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide.

In bread, the useful product is the carbon dioxide — the bubbles make the dough rise. The ethanol evaporates during baking.

In beer, the useful product is the ethanol, and the carbon dioxide provides the fizz.

One reaction, two different products being harvested.

questions.promptHtml: In a respirometer, the coloured drop moves towards the maggots. Why towards them, and why would it hardly move if the soda lime were left out?
questions.answerHtml:
The maggots take in oxygen from the air in the tube. The carbon dioxide they give out is absorbed by the soda lime. So the amount of gas in the tube falls, the pressure falls, and the drop is pulled in towards the maggots.

Without soda lime, each molecule of oxygen used is replaced by a molecule of carbon dioxide — look at the equation: 6O₂ in, 6CO₂ out. The volume of gas barely changes, so the drop barely moves. Absorbing the carbon dioxide means the drop measures oxygen uptake only.

questions.promptHtml: Yeast gives off carbon dioxide faster at 30 °C than at 20 °C, but almost none at 60 °C. Explain both results.
questions.answerHtml:
20 → 30 °C: respiration is controlled by enzymes. More heat gives the molecules more kinetic energy, so enzyme and substrate collide more often and more enzyme–substrate complexes form. Respiration speeds up, so more carbon dioxide is released per minute.

60 °C: this is above the optimum. The enzymes denature — the active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits. Respiration almost stops, and the yeast is killed.

Same two halves as the enzyme graph in module 1. Check which side of the optimum the data is on before you write.

questions.promptHtml: If anaerobic respiration releases so little energy, why do muscles use it at all?
questions.answerHtml:
Because during hard exercise the heart and lungs cannot deliver oxygen fast enough for aerobic respiration to meet the demand.

Anaerobic respiration does not need oxygen, so it tops up the energy supply in the short term. The price is lactic acid, which causes fatigue and has to be broken down later using extra oxygen — the oxygen debt.

It is a short-term emergency supply, not a replacement. That is why you cannot sprint for long.

subsections.html: Air travels trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli. The alveoli are where gas exchange happens: oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out. Everything above the alveoli is plumbing, and the muscles around it are the pump.

subsections.heading: The thorax — the parts
subsections.html:
Spec 2.46 · 2023 Y10 Q4(a) · 2024 Y10 Q3(a) · 2024 Y11 mock Q7(a)

Air passes down a branching system of tubes to millions of tiny air sacs, the alveoli. Label questions on this diagram come up almost every year.

StructureWhat it does
TracheaCarries air to the lungs; held open by rings of cartilage
BronchiOne to each lung, branching from the trachea — also held open by cartilage
BronchiolesNarrow branches ending at the alveoli
AlveoliTiny air sacs — the site of gas exchange
RibsProtect the lungs and move during ventilation
Intercostal musclesBetween the ribs; move the ribcage up and out, or down and in
DiaphragmDome-shaped sheet of muscle below the lungs; flattens when it contracts
Pleural membranesLine the lungs and chest wall; the fluid between them reduces friction

Bronchus is one; bronchi is two. The labelling questions give you letters on a diagram: the thick tube with rings is the trachea, the two tubes it splits into are bronchi, and the fine branches are bronchioles.

subsections.heading: Keeping the airways clean
subsections.html:
Spec 2.46, 2.49

Mucus traps dirt and bacteria, and cilia sweep it up and out of the lungs.

  1. Cells in the lining of the trachea and bronchi make mucus.
  2. Dust and bacteria in the air stick to it.
  3. Cilia — tiny hairs on the lining cells — beat and sweep the mucus up to the throat.
  4. It is swallowed, and stomach acid kills the bacteria.

This matters because smoking breaks it. It is the link between tar and chest infections.

subsections.heading: Breathing in
subsections.html:
Spec 2.47 · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1B Q1(b) · 2023 Y10 Q4(a)(ii)

Muscles contract, the chest gets bigger, the pressure inside drops, and air is pushed in from outside. Volume changes first, pressure follows, air moves last.

  1. The intercostal muscles contract, moving the ribcage up and out.
  2. The diaphragm contracts and flattens, moving down.
  3. The volume of the thorax increases.
  4. The pressure inside decreases, below atmospheric pressure.
  5. Air moves in, down the pressure gradient.

The breathing-in answer — four marks

1. Diaphragm contracts and flattens / moves down 1

2. Intercostal muscles contract, ribcage moves up and out 1

3. Volume of the thorax increases 1

4. Pressure decreases, so air is drawn in 1

✗ "The diaphragm moves up." ✗ "The diaphragm collapses." ✗ "The lungs expand and suck air in."
✓ "The diaphragm contracts and flattens, so the volume increases and the pressure decreases."

The lungs cannot pull. They are passive — they follow the chest wall.

subsections.heading: Breathing out
subsections.html:
Spec 2.47

Breathing out at rest is every step of breathing in, reversed.

FeatureBreathing inBreathing out
Intercostal musclesContractRelax
RibcageMoves up and outMoves down and in
DiaphragmContracts and flattensRelaxes and domes upwards
Volume of thoraxIncreasesDecreases
Pressure in thoraxDecreasesIncreases
AirMoves inMoves out

The diaphragm is domed at rest. Contracting pulls it down into a flatter shape. Relaxing lets it spring back up.

subsections.heading: Gas exchange is diffusion
subsections.html:
Spec 2.48

Oxygen diffuses from the air in the alveoli into the blood, and carbon dioxide diffuses the other way, each down its concentration gradient.

  • Air in the alveolus has a high oxygen concentration. Blood arriving from the body has a low one. So oxygen diffuses into the blood.
  • Blood arriving has a high carbon dioxide concentration. The alveolus air has a low one. So carbon dioxide diffuses into the alveolus and is breathed out.

Diffusion is passive — no energy is used. Anything that makes it faster is an adaptation.

subsections.heading: How the alveoli are adapted — the four-mark answer
subsections.html:
Spec 2.48 · 2022 Y10 Q4(a)

Every adaptation either increases the surface area, shortens the distance, or keeps the concentration gradient steep. Pair each feature with its reason. A bare list scores half marks at best.

AdaptationWhy it helps
Millions of alveoliLarge surface area for diffusion
Wall one cell thickShort diffusion distance between air and blood
Capillary wall one cell thick, pressed against the alveolusShort diffusion distance
Dense network of capillariesBlood flow carries oxygen away and brings carbon dioxide, which maintains the concentration gradient
VentilationFresh air maintains the concentration gradient on the air side
Moist liningGases dissolve before diffusing across

"Maintains the concentration gradient" is the phrase that separates a two-mark answer from a four-mark one.

subsections.heading: Inhaled versus exhaled air
subsections.html:
2024 Y10 Q3(b) · 2024 Y11 mock Q7(b) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1B Q1(a)

Exhaled air has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide, because of gas exchange in the lungs and respiration in the cells.

GasInhaledExhaled
Oxygenabout 21%about 16%
Carbon dioxideabout 0.04%about 4%
Nitrogenabout 78%about 78% — not used
Water vapourVariesMore — saturated

The full answer has three parts: oxygen diffused into the blood and carbon dioxide out; the oxygen is used and the carbon dioxide made by respiration in cells; nitrogen is not used, so it does not change.

Exhaled air still has about 16% oxygen. It is also not the same as alveolar air: it is a mix of air from the alveoli and air that never got past the trachea and bronchi. Gas exchange only happens at the alveoli, so exhaled air has more oxygen than the air deep in the lungs.

The limewater practical: breathe in through one flask and out through the other. The flask you breathe out through turns milky faster, showing exhaled air has more carbon dioxide. The tube you breathe out through must dip into the limewater; the one you breathe in through must not, or you would suck up limewater.

subsections.heading: Smoking — the lungs
subsections.html:
Spec 2.49

Tar destroys the cilia and causes cancer; over time the alveoli break down.

CauseEffect
Tar — on the ciliaParalyses and destroys cilia, so mucus and bacteria are not swept out: smoker's cough, bronchitis, chest infections
Tar — a carcinogenCauses lung cancer: cells divide out of control and form a tumour
Smoke irritating the airwaysMore mucus made, which blocks the bronchioles
EmphysemaAlveolus walls break down into fewer, larger spaces, so surface area falls; less oxygen gets in and the person is breathless

subsections.heading: Smoking — the heart and blood
subsections.html:
Spec 2.49 · 2024 Edexcel 2B Q4(c) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1B Q4

Carbon monoxide reduces how much oxygen the blood can carry; nicotine and smoke damage the heart and blood vessels.

CauseEffect
Carbon monoxideBinds to haemoglobin instead of oxygen, reducing the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood
NicotineAddictive; raises heart rate and narrows blood vessels, raising blood pressure
Coronary heart diseaseSmoking damages artery walls so fatty deposits build up, narrowing the coronary arteries and cutting the oxygen supply to the heart muscle

In pregnancy this is the reason for lower birth mass: carbon monoxide means less oxygen reaches the fetus, so less respiration and less energy released for growth.

✗ "Carbon monoxide poisons the blood."
✓ "Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin, so the blood carries less oxygen."

subsections.heading: Emphysema — why exercise is hard
subsections.html:
2022 Y10 Q4

Less surface area means less oxygen gets into the blood, so the muscles release less energy.

  1. The alveoli have a smaller surface area.
  2. So less oxygen diffuses into the blood and reaches the muscles.
  3. So less aerobic respiration happens in the muscles.
  4. So less energy is released for muscle contraction.

The mark scheme's note: "Energy is produced / made" is not allowed. Use released.

subsections.heading: Practical — exercise and breathing rate
subsections.html:
Spec 2.50 · 2022 Edexcel 1B Q3(b)

Exercise makes muscles respire faster, so breathing gets faster and deeper to supply oxygen and remove carbon dioxide.

  1. Count breaths per minute at rest.
  2. Do a set exercise for a set time — for example step-ups for two minutes.
  3. Count breaths per minute straight after, then every minute until it is back to the resting rate.
  4. Repeat, or use several people, and calculate a mean.

Control: same person or people of the same age, sex and fitness; same type and length of exercise; same counting time.

The explanation: muscles contract more, so they respire faster, needing more oxygen and making more carbon dioxide. Breathing stays high afterwards to repay the oxygen debt — the oxygen needed to break down lactic acid.

subsections.heading: Reading breathing data
subsections.html:
2023 Y10 Q4(b) · 2022 Edexcel 1B Q3(a)

Ventilation rate is breaths per minute multiplied by the volume of each breath.

Ventilation rateventilation rate = breathing rate × volume per breathdm³ per minute · 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³

In the 2023 Year 10 cycling data, ventilation rate rose at low speeds only because each breath got deeper — the breathing rate stayed the same. Only at higher speeds did the rate rise. The teacher's comment: most students just repeated the table instead of commenting on it. Say what changes, where, and which part — rate or depth — is changing.

Vital capacity is the most air you can force out in one breath. It rises until about 20–25 years as the chest and lungs grow, levels off, then falls as the intercostal muscles and diaphragm weaken and the lungs become less elastic. A median is used when a few extreme values would distort the mean.

equations.name: Ventilation rate
equations.formula: ventilation rate = breathing rate × volume per breath

subsections.html:
The sentences behind most of the marks

Breathing in: muscles contract → diaphragm flattens, ribs up and out → volume increases → pressure decreases → air moves in. Never skip the pressure step.

Alveoli: large surface area, short diffusion distance, and blood flow and ventilation maintain the concentration gradient.

VentilationThe movement of air in and out of the lungs — breathing, not respiration
DiffusionNet movement of particles from a high to a low concentration, down a concentration gradient

CiliaTiny hairs on the airway lining that sweep mucus out of the lungs
Oxygen debtThe extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down lactic acid
EmphysemaBreakdown of alveolus walls, reducing surface area for gas exchange
Vital capacityThe maximum volume of air that can be breathed out in one breath

questions.promptHtml: Explain how air is drawn into the lungs, from muscle contraction to air movement.
questions.answerHtml:
The intercostal muscles contract, pulling the ribcage up and out. At the same time the diaphragm contracts and flattens, moving down.

Together these increase the volume of the thorax. Increasing the volume decreases the pressure inside, so it falls below atmospheric pressure. Air therefore moves in, down the pressure gradient.

The lungs are passive throughout. "The lungs suck air in" misses the pressure mark, which is the one the question is really testing.

questions.promptHtml: A patient with emphysema has fewer, larger alveoli. Explain why they become breathless during mild exercise.
questions.answerHtml:
Fewer, larger alveoli means a much smaller total surface area for gas exchange. Less oxygen can diffuse into the blood per breath.

During exercise the muscles respire faster and need more oxygen, but the damaged lungs cannot supply it. The patient breathes faster and deeper to make up for it, and still feels short of breath. More anaerobic respiration occurs, producing lactic acid and fatigue.

questions.promptHtml: Why does blood flowing past the alveoli keep gas exchange going, rather than diffusion simply stopping once the gases even out?
questions.answerHtml:
Because the blood is constantly replaced. Blood arriving from the body has a low oxygen concentration, and blood that has picked up oxygen is carried away. This maintains the concentration gradient.

Breathing does the same job on the other side: fresh air keeps the alveolar oxygen concentration high and carbon dioxide low.

If both stopped, the concentrations would even out and net diffusion would stop — which is what happens if you hold your breath.

questions.promptHtml: A smoker gets repeated chest infections. Explain the link, naming the part of the smoke responsible.
questions.answerHtml:
Tar paralyses and destroys the cilia lining the airways.

Normally the cilia sweep mucus — which traps dust and bacteria — up and out of the lungs. With the cilia damaged, the mucus stays in the airways, along with the bacteria trapped in it.

The bacteria multiply, causing repeated infections such as bronchitis. The build-up of mucus also causes the persistent "smoker's cough".

questions.promptHtml: A student's breathing rate is 14 at rest, 32 straight after exercise, and still 20 two minutes later. Explain the third figure.
questions.answerHtml:
Breathing stays above resting because of the oxygen debt. During exercise some respiration in the muscles was anaerobic, producing lactic acid.

Extra oxygen is needed to break down that lactic acid, so breathing stays high until it has been cleared. Only then does the rate return to 14.

"The body is still recovering" is true but scores nothing. The mark is for naming lactic acid and the oxygen needed to remove it.

questions.promptHtml: Air deep in the alveoli has about 14% oxygen, but the air you breathe out has about 16%. How can exhaled air have more oxygen than the air it came from?
questions.answerHtml:
Because exhaled air is a mixture. Some of it comes from the alveoli, where oxygen has diffused into the blood. The rest was sitting in the trachea, bronchi and bronchioles, which have no gas exchange, so it still has close to 21% oxygen.

Mix the two together and you get something in between. Gas exchange only happens at the alveoli — that is the mark.

questions.promptHtml: A study shows vital capacity rises until about age 22, stays level, then falls with age. Explain the shape, and why the scientists plotted the median for each age.
questions.answerHtml:
Rising: the body is still growing, so the chest and lungs get bigger and hold more air.

Level: growth has stopped, so there is little change.

Falling: the intercostal muscles and diaphragm get weaker and the lungs become less elastic, so less air can be forced out.

Median: each age group had a wide range, with some extreme values — perhaps athletes, or people with lung disease. The median is the middle value, so it is less affected by extreme values than the mean.

questions.promptHtml: A young smoker with healthy alveoli still gets out of breath faster than a non-smoker. Explain why, without mentioning emphysema.
questions.answerHtml:
Carbon monoxide in the smoke binds to haemoglobin in the red blood cells, in the place where oxygen would go.

So the blood carries less oxygen to the muscles, even though the lungs are fine. The muscles respire aerobically less, release less energy, and switch to anaerobic respiration sooner.

The smoker breathes harder to make up for it. Nicotine adds to the problem by raising the heart rate and narrowing blood vessels.

modules.title: Heart, Circulation, Blood and Immunity
modules.standfirst: The joint largest block on the Year 10 checklist, and the most-examined human topic in the real papers. The heart diagram, the ventricle walls, red versus white blood cells and vaccination cover most of what gets asked — and the school has reused a real Edexcel heart question word for word.

subsections.html: Blood carries oxygen, food and waste around the body, pumped by the heart through arteries, capillaries and veins. Humans have a double circulatory system: blood passes through the heart twice for every complete circuit of the body. The blood also carries the white cells that defend the body against disease.

subsections.heading: Why large organisms need a transport system
subsections.html:
Spec 2.52

Large organisms have a small surface area to volume ratio, so diffusion alone is too slow to supply their cells.

A single-celled organism can get all its oxygen by diffusion through its surface — no cell is far from the outside. In a large animal most cells are deep inside, a long way from any surface. Diffusion over that distance would take far too long.

So a transport system — blood pumped through vessels — brings substances close to every cell. Diffusion only has to work over the last tiny gap, from a capillary to the cell.

subsections.heading: The double circulation
subsections.html:
Spec 2.69 · 2022 Y10 Q2

Blood passes through the heart twice per circuit: once to go to the lungs, once to go to the body.

  • The pulmonary circuit: right side of the heart → lungs → back to the heart.
  • The systemic circuit: left side of the heart → body → back to the heart.

The advantage: blood loses pressure passing through the lung capillaries. Returning it to the heart lets it be pumped again at high pressure, so it reaches the body quickly and delivers oxygen and glucose faster. The lungs themselves get blood at lower pressure, which protects their delicate capillaries.

The axolotl in the 2022 Year 10 paper has one ventricle, so oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix and less oxygen reaches its tissues. A hole between the ventricles in a human baby does the same.

subsections.heading: The heart — chambers, valves and vessels
subsections.html:
Spec 2.65 · 2022 Y10 Q3 · 2022 Edexcel 1B Q7(a) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1B Q2(a)

Blood enters the heart into an atrium and leaves from a ventricle; valves stop it flowing backwards. The heart wall is cardiac muscle.

  1. Blood from the veins fills the atria.
  2. The atria contract, pushing blood through valves into the ventricles.
  3. The ventricles contract, pushing blood out into the arteries. The valves between atria and ventricles close so blood cannot flow back.
  4. Valves at the base of the arteries close as the ventricles relax, so blood cannot fall back in.
VesselCarries bloodOxygenated?
Vena cavaBody → right atriumDeoxygenated
Pulmonary arteryRight ventricle → lungsDeoxygenated
Pulmonary veinLungs → left atriumOxygenated
AortaLeft ventricle → bodyOxygenated

The septum is the wall between the left and right sides. It keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood apart.

On a heart diagram the heart's right is on your left — you are looking at someone facing you. Diagrams in the real papers use letters, so find the aorta (the big arch) first and work from there.

subsections.heading: Why the left ventricle wall is thicker
subsections.html:
2023 Y10 Q1(a)(iii) · 2022 Edexcel 1B Q7(a)(iii) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1B Q2(a)(iii)

The left ventricle has more muscle because it must make a higher pressure to push blood all round the body. This has been asked three times.

The ventricle-wall answer — three marks

1. The left ventricle wall is thicker / has more muscle 1

2. So it produces a higher pressure 1

3. Because it pumps blood around the whole body; the right only pumps to the lungs 1

✗ "The right ventricle is thinner because the blood is deoxygenated."
✗ "The left ventricle is bigger."
✓ "The left ventricle has a thicker, more muscular wall to pump blood at higher pressure to the whole body."

subsections.heading: Heart rate — exercise and adrenaline
subsections.html:
Spec 2.66 · 2023 Y11 mock Q5(a)(i)

The heart beats faster when the muscles need more oxygen and glucose, or when adrenaline is released.

During exercise: muscles contract more and respire faster. They need more oxygen and glucose and make more carbon dioxide. The heart beats faster and more strongly, so blood is delivered faster and carbon dioxide removed faster.

Adrenaline: a hormone released by the adrenal glands when you are frightened or excited. It increases heart rate, getting more oxygen and glucose to the muscles, ready for "fight or flight".

The volume pumped per beat is the stroke volume. If a heart condition reduces it, less blood — so less oxygen — reaches the muscles per beat, and there is less respiration.

subsections.heading: Coronary heart disease
subsections.html:
Spec 2.67 · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1B Q2(b) · 2022 Y10 Q3(c)

The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle itself; if fatty deposits narrow them, the muscle is starved of oxygen.

  1. Fatty deposits build up in the wall of a coronary artery.
  2. The lumen narrows, so less blood reaches the heart muscle.
  3. The muscle gets less oxygen and glucose, so less aerobic respiration.
  4. If a clot blocks the artery completely, part of the muscle dies — a heart attack.

The coronary artery carries oxygenated blood to the muscle; the coronary vein carries deoxygenated blood away. A stent is a mesh tube that keeps the coronary artery open, so blood and oxygen can reach the heart muscle.

Risk factorWhy it raises the risk
Diet high in saturated fatRaises blood cholesterol, which forms fatty deposits in the arteries
SmokingRaises blood pressure and makes clots more likely
High blood pressurePuts more strain on the heart and damages artery walls
Lack of exerciseExercise lowers blood pressure and strengthens the heart
ObesityMore strain on the heart; linked to high blood pressure and diabetes
StressRaises blood pressure
GenesSome people inherit a higher risk

When a question gives you data on heart attacks, evaluate the data. The teacher's comment on 2023 Year 10 Q1(c): many explained the causes of heart attacks instead, and missed the age groups. Look for sample size, how long the study ran, where it was done, and whether the pattern holds for every age group.

subsections.heading: Arteries, veins and capillaries
subsections.html:
Spec 2.68 · 2022 Y10 Q3(c)

Every feature of a blood vessel follows from the pressure of the blood inside it.

FeatureArteryVeinCapillary
DirectionAway from the heartTowards the heartThrough tissues
WallThick, muscular and elasticThinOne cell thick
LumenNarrowWideVery narrow
ValvesNoYesNo
PressureHighLowFalling
  • Arteries have thick, elastic walls to withstand the high pressure and stretch and recoil with each beat.
  • Veins have valves to stop backflow, because the pressure is low. The wide lumen makes flow easier.
  • Capillaries are one cell thick for a short diffusion distance — this is where substances are exchanged with the cells.

✗ "Arteries carry oxygenated blood."
✓ "Arteries carry blood away from the heart." Define by direction. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and is still an artery.

subsections.heading: The circulation — main vessels to the organs
subsections.html:
Spec 2.69

Each organ has an artery bringing blood from the aorta and a vein returning it to the vena cava.

OrganBlood inBlood out
LungsPulmonary arteryPulmonary vein
LiverHepatic artery, and the hepatic portal vein from the gutHepatic vein
KidneysRenal arteryRenal vein
Heart muscleCoronary arteriesCoronary veins

The hepatic portal vein is the odd one: it carries blood rich in digested food from the intestines to the liver, not back to the heart. "Hepatic" means liver; "renal" means kidney.

subsections.heading: Blood — the four parts, and what plasma carries
subsections.html:
Spec 2.59, 2.60 · 2023 Edexcel 1B Q5(a) · 2024 Y10 Q5(a)

Blood is plasma carrying red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.

ComponentJob
PlasmaThe liquid part — transports dissolved substances and heat
Red blood cellsCarry oxygen
White blood cellsDefend against pathogens
PlateletsCell fragments that help the blood clot

What plasma carries, and where to — the 2024 Year 10 paper wanted the substance and where it goes:

SubstanceFromTo
Carbon dioxideRespiring cellsLungs
Digested food — glucose, amino acidsSmall intestineLiver and body cells
UreaLiverKidneys
HormonesGlandsTarget organs
Heat energyMuscles and liverAll over the body and the skin

Plasma does not carry the oxygen — red blood cells do.

subsections.heading: Red blood cells
subsections.html:
Spec 2.61 · 2024 Edexcel 1B Q7 · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2B Q1(d) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1B Q5(a)(i)

Red blood cells are built to carry as much oxygen as possible and pass it on quickly.

FeatureWhy it helps
Contain haemoglobinBinds to oxygen in the lungs, forming oxyhaemoglobin
No nucleusMore room for haemoglobin, so more oxygen carried
Biconcave discLarge surface area to volume ratio for fast diffusion of oxygen
Small and flexibleSqueeze through narrow capillaries
Oxygen transporthaemoglobin + oxygen ⇌ oxyhaemoglobinforms in the lungs where oxygen is high · splits in respiring tissues where oxygen is low

No nucleus also means no chromosomes — which is why the 2023 January paper said white blood cells, not red ones, are used to look at chromosomes. And people living at high altitude, where there is less oxygen in the air, make more red blood cells and haemoglobin so they can still carry enough.

Too little haemoglobin — as in anaemia or beta thalassaemia — means less oxygen carried to the muscles, so less respiration, less energy released, and tiredness.

subsections.heading: White blood cells — phagocytes and lymphocytes
subsections.html:
Spec 2.62 · 2023 Edexcel 1B Q5(b) · 2024 Y10 Q5(b) · 2022 Edexcel 1B Q5(c)

Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens; lymphocytes release antibodies specific to one pathogen.

A pathogen is a microorganism that causes disease. On its surface are antigens — molecules the body recognises as foreign.

Phagocytes — phagocytosis:

  1. The phagocyte moves towards the pathogen.
  2. It engulfs it, surrounding it with its cytoplasm.
  3. The pathogen is held inside a vesicle.
  4. Enzymes are released into the vesicle and digest the pathogen.

Lymphocytes make antibodies. Each antibody has a shape complementary to one antigen, so it is specific to one pathogen. Antibodies bind to the antigens and clump the pathogens together, making them easier for phagocytes to destroy.

Red versus white — the three differences the 2024 paper wanted: white cells have a nucleus; red cells are biconcave and white are not; red cells are smaller; red cells contain haemoglobin.

Magnification — asked with a phagocyte twicemagnification = image size ÷ actual sizeput both sizes in the same unit first · 1 mm = 1000 µm

An allergy such as hay fever is the same system reacting to pollen: white blood cells treat its antigens as foreign and produce antibodies.

equations.name: Magnification — asked with a phagocyte twice

subsections.heading: Vaccination and memory cells
subsections.html:
Spec 2.63B · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2B Q6(b)(i)

A vaccine makes the body produce memory cells, so antibodies are made sooner, faster and in greater quantity if the real pathogen arrives.

  1. The vaccine contains a weakened or inactivated form of the pathogen, carrying its antigens.
  2. Lymphocytes recognise the antigens and make specific antibodies.
  3. Memory cells are made, and stay in the blood.
  4. If the real pathogen infects you, the memory cells make antibodies sooner, faster and in greater quantity.
  5. The pathogen is destroyed before you become ill.

The rabies mark scheme ignored "phagocytes" and "a small amount of virus". The marks were for antigens, lymphocytes and memory cells.

subsections.heading: Platelets and clotting
subsections.html:
Spec 2.64B · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2B Q1(e)

Platelets start the clotting process, which stops blood loss and keeps microorganisms out.

  1. At a wound, platelets trigger a series of reactions.
  2. Soluble fibrinogen is turned into insoluble fibrin.
  3. Fibrin forms a mesh that traps red blood cells, making a clot.
  4. The clot dries into a scab.

Two reasons it matters, and the spec names both: it prevents blood loss, and it stops microorganisms entering. Artificial blood with no platelets could not clot — the point one real paper tested.

The sentences behind most of the marks

Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it towards it. Define by direction, never by oxygen.

Left ventricle: thicker, more muscle, higher pressure, pumps to the whole body.

Vaccine: antigens → lymphocytes → antibodies and memory cells → next time antibodies are made sooner, faster, in greater quantity.

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:

VeinA vessel carrying blood towards the heart

AntigenA molecule on a pathogen's surface that the immune system recognises as foreign
AntibodyA protein made by lymphocytes, with a shape specific to one antigen
PhagocyteA white blood cell that engulfs and digests pathogens
Memory cellA lymphocyte that stays in the blood after infection or vaccination and makes antibodies faster next time
Coronary heart diseaseNarrowing of the coronary arteries by fatty deposits, reducing oxygen to the heart muscle

subsections.heading: The second-exposure answer
subsections.html:
StageWhat happens
First exposureLymphocytes take time to make the right antibody, so you get ill
After recoveryMemory cells remain in the blood
Second exposureAntibodies made sooner, faster and in greater quantity, so the pathogen is destroyed before symptoms appear

questions.promptHtml: Explain the advantage of a double circulatory system over a single one, as found in fish.
questions.answerHtml:
In a single circulation, blood goes through the gill capillaries and then straight on to the body. Capillaries are narrow, so blood leaves them at low pressure and travels slowly to the tissues.

In a double circulation the blood returns to the heart after the lungs and is pumped again at high pressure. It reaches the body much faster, so oxygen and glucose are delivered faster and a higher rate of respiration is possible.

That matters for mammals: they keep warm by respiring, so they need a lot of energy released.

questions.promptHtml: A baby is born with a hole between the left and right ventricles. Explain why they tire easily.
questions.answerHtml:
The hole lets oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix in the ventricles.

Blood leaving the left ventricle for the body therefore carries less oxygen than normal. Less oxygen reaches the respiring tissues, so less aerobic respiration occurs and less energy is released.

More anaerobic respiration takes place instead, producing lactic acid, so the baby tires quickly. The axolotl, with its single ventricle, has the same problem.

questions.promptHtml: Explain why veins need valves but arteries do not.
questions.answerHtml:
Blood in arteries is at high pressure, straight from the heart. That pressure keeps it moving forwards.

By the time blood reaches the veins it has passed through the capillaries, and the pressure is low. It could flow backwards, especially going up from the legs against gravity. The valves close if blood starts to move the wrong way.

Veins also rely on nearby muscles contracting to squeeze blood along.

questions.promptHtml: Why does someone who has had measles usually show no symptoms if they catch it a second time?
questions.answerHtml:
After the first infection, memory cells specific to the measles antigen stay in the blood.

On the second infection these memory cells recognise the antigen at once and the specific antibodies are made sooner, faster and in far greater quantity.

The pathogen is destroyed before it can multiply enough to cause symptoms. That is immunity. A vaccine produces the same memory cells on purpose, using a weakened or inactivated pathogen.

questions.promptHtml: A red blood cell has no nucleus and a biconcave shape. Explain how each suits its job.
questions.answerHtml:
No nucleus: more room for haemoglobin, so each cell carries more oxygen.

Biconcave disc: a large surface area to volume ratio, so oxygen diffuses in and out quickly. It also makes the cell flexible enough to squeeze through capillaries.

The cost: with no nucleus the cell cannot divide or repair itself, so red blood cells last only about four months. The body keeps making new ones.

questions.promptHtml: Explain how a blood clot forms, and give two reasons clotting is important.
questions.answerHtml:
Platelets at the wound trigger reactions that turn soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin. The fibrin forms a mesh across the wound, trapping red blood cells to form a clot, which dries into a scab.

Why it matters: it prevents blood loss, and it seals the wound so microorganisms cannot enter.

questions.promptHtml: Your heart pounds when you get a fright, even though you are standing still. Explain why this is useful.
questions.answerHtml:
A fright makes the adrenal glands release adrenaline into the blood. Adrenaline increases the heart rate.

Blood is pumped faster, so more oxygen and glucose reach the muscles. The muscles can respire faster and release more energy the moment you need to run or fight.

It prepares the body before the exercise starts. During exercise itself, the heart rate rises because the muscles are already respiring faster.

questions.promptHtml: People who live high in the mountains have more red blood cells than people at sea level. Explain why.
questions.answerHtml:
At high altitude the air has less oxygen in each breath. Less oxygen diffuses into the blood.

Making more red blood cells, with more haemoglobin, lets the blood pick up and carry enough oxygen anyway. So the tissues still get enough for aerobic respiration.

The real 2024 paper gave data like this. Say what the data shows first — the trend with altitude, and any difference between men and women — before explaining it.

questions.promptHtml: Explain what is meant by a double circulatory system. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
Blood is pumped to the lungs by one side of the heart — the right 1; and to the body by the other side — the left 1

"Blood passes through the heart twice for every circuit of the body" also scores.

markScheme.point: Blood is pumped to the lungs by one side of the heart — the right ; and to the body by the other side — the left

questions.promptHtml: Explain why the left ventricle has a thicker wall than the right ventricle. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
More muscle in the wall 1; to produce a higher pressure 1; because it pumps blood around the whole body, while the right only pumps to the lungs 1

"Because the blood is deoxygenated" scores nothing.

markScheme.point: More muscle in the wall ; to produce a higher pressure ; because it pumps blood around the whole body, while the right only pumps to the lungs

questions.answerHtml: No nucleus, so more room for haemoglobin 1; biconcave disc, giving a large surface area for diffusion 1

questions.promptHtml: Describe how lymphocytes defend the body against a pathogen. (3)
questions.answerHtml: They produce antibodies 1; each antibody is specific / complementary to an antigen on the pathogen 1; antibodies bind to the antigens, clumping the pathogens so phagocytes can destroy them 1

questions.promptHtml: Name the blood vessel that carries deoxygenated blood away from the heart, and state where it goes. (2)
questions.answerHtml: Pulmonary artery 1; from the right ventricle to the lungs 1

markScheme.point: Pulmonary artery ; from the right ventricle to the lungs

questions.answerHtml: They supply the heart muscle with oxygen and glucose 1; a blockage means the heart muscle gets less oxygen, so less aerobic respiration 1; the muscle cells are damaged or die — a heart attack 1

The reflex arc must be written in the right order with the right words, and the two eye reflexes work by opposite pairs of muscles — getting a pair the wrong way round, or letting ligaments "relax", is where most marks are lost.
