subsections.html: The nervous system detects stimuli and produces responses, using electrical impulses that travel fast. It has two parts: the central nervous system — the brain and spinal cord — and the nerves that connect it to the rest of the body. The eye is the receptor this module looks at in detail.

subsections.heading: Stimulus, receptor, effector
subsections.html:
Spec 2.80, 2.82

Every coordinated response needs a stimulus, a receptor to detect it, and an effector to respond.

PartWhat it isExample
StimulusA change in the environmentA hot object touching the hand
ReceptorCells that detect the stimulusTemperature or pain receptors in the skin
EffectorA muscle or gland that carries out the responseThe biceps muscle
ResponseWhat the effector doesThe hand pulls away

Organisms respond to changes so they can find food, avoid danger and keep conditions inside the body steady. Keeping the inside of the body constant — its water content and temperature — is called homeostasis, and it is module 8.

subsections.heading: Nervous and hormonal communication
subsections.html:
Spec 2.83, 2.86

Nerves carry fast, short-lived electrical impulses to one place; hormones travel slowly in the blood and last longer.

FeatureNervousHormonal
SignalElectrical impulsesChemicals — hormones
Carried byNeuronesThe blood
SpeedVery fastSlower
How long the effect lastsShortLonger
Where it actsA precise place — one muscle or glandTarget organs, often spread around the body

subsections.heading: The central nervous system and nerves
subsections.html:
Spec 2.87, 2.88

The brain and spinal cord form the CNS; nerves link it to the sense organs and the effectors.

  1. A receptor in a sense organ is stimulated.
  2. It sends electrical impulses along nerves into the CNS.
  3. The CNS coordinates the response.
  4. Impulses travel out of the CNS along nerves to an effector.

A nerve is a bundle of many neurones. A neurone is a single nerve cell. Use the neurone names in reflex answers.

subsections.heading: The three neurones
subsections.html:
Spec 2.88 · 2023 Edexcel 1B Q4(a)

Sensory neurones carry impulses into the CNS, relay neurones pass them on inside it, and motor neurones carry them out to effectors.

NeuroneCarries impulsesFeature
SensoryReceptor → CNSCell body part-way along
RelayWithin the CNSShort; links sensory to motor
MotorCNS → effectorLong axon; cell body inside the CNS

The long fibres are wrapped in a fatty myelin sheath, which insulates them and speeds up the impulse.

subsections.heading: The reflex arc, in order
subsections.html:
Spec 2.90 · 2023 Edexcel 1B Q4

A reflex is a rapid, automatic response that does not involve conscious thought. The brain is not part of the pathway, which is why it is fast.

The reflex arc — learn this orderstimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (spinal cord) → motor neurone → effector → responseeffector = muscle or gland · impulses cross a synapse between each neurone

The spec example is pulling a finger away from a hot object:

StageHot object example
StimulusThe heat
ReceptorTemperature / pain receptors in the skin of the finger
Sensory neuroneCarries the impulse to the spinal cord
Relay neuroneIn the spinal cord; passes the impulse to the motor neurone
Motor neuroneCarries the impulse to the muscle
EffectorThe biceps muscle
ResponseThe muscle contracts and the hand is pulled away
Time for an impulsetime = distance ÷ speedmetres ÷ metres per second = seconds · the 2023 paper's answer was about 0.0092 s

The two words most often left out are relay and effector. Each stage in a long answer carries its own mark.

equations.name: The reflex arc — learn this order
equations.formula: stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (spinal cord) → motor neurone → effector → response

subsections.heading: Why reflexes are useful
subsections.html:
2023 Y11 mock Q2(c) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1B Q7(c) · 2023 Edexcel 1B Q4(c)(i)

A reflex is fast because the impulse takes a short route through the spinal cord, so it limits harm.

Pulling away from heat, blinking at dust, a woodlouse rolling up when touched — each protects the body before you could think about it. For the woodlouse, rolling up shows only its hard shell and protects it from predators.

A reflex is automatic — you cannot choose not to do it. That is the one-mark answer to "why is this a reflex".

Pain itself is useful too: it stops you using an injured part, so it can heal, and teaches you to avoid what hurt you.

subsections.heading: The synapse
subsections.html:
Spec 2.89 · 2023 Edexcel 1B Q4(b)(ii) · 2024 Y10 Q1(c)

A synapse is a tiny gap between two neurones, crossed by a chemical, not by electricity.

  1. An impulse arrives at the end of the first neurone.
  2. It causes a neurotransmitter to be released into the gap.
  3. The neurotransmitter diffuses across the synapse.
  4. It binds to receptors on the next neurone.
  5. This starts a new electrical impulse.

The neurotransmitter is only released on one side, and the receptors are only on the other. So synapses make impulses travel in one direction only.

Drugs such as painkillers can work by stopping receptors detecting the stimulus, stopping impulses in the sensory or relay neurones, or blocking transmission at synapses — the four-mark ideas in the 2023 paper.

✗ "The impulse jumps across the gap."
✓ "A neurotransmitter is released, diffuses across the synapse and binds to receptors on the next neurone."

subsections.heading: The eye — structure and function
subsections.html:
Spec 2.91 · 2023 Y10 Q8(a) · 2024 Y10 Q8(a)(i) · 2024 Y11 mock Q10(a) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2B Q2(a)(i)

The eye is a receptor: it focuses light onto the retina, where receptor cells turn it into impulses. "Label the cornea" has been asked in three papers.

PartFunction
CorneaTransparent front of the eye; does most of the refraction
IrisColoured ring of muscle; controls the size of the pupil
PupilThe hole light passes through
LensChanges shape to focus light on the retina
Ciliary musclesRing of muscle that changes the lens shape
Suspensory ligamentsAttach the lens to the ciliary muscles
RetinaContains the receptor cells — rods and cones
Optic nerveCarries impulses from the retina to the brain
ScleraTough white outer coat that protects the eye

On a diagram, the cornea is the clear bulge at the very front. The lens sits behind the iris. Do not label the cornea as the lens.

subsections.heading: Rods and cones
subsections.html:
Spec 2.91

Rods work in dim light but see no colour; cones see colour but need bright light.

ReceptorWorks inDetects
RodsDim lightBlack and white only
ConesBright lightColour

That is why everything looks grey at night: there is not enough light to stimulate the cones.

subsections.heading: The pupil reflex — bright and dim light
subsections.html:
Spec 2.92 · 2023 Y10 Q8(a)(iii) · 2024 Y11 mock Q10(a)(ii) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2B Q2(a)(ii)

In bright light the pupil constricts to protect the retina; in dim light it dilates to let more light in. The iris has two sets of muscle that work in opposite directions — they are antagonistic.

FeatureBright lightDim light
Circular musclesContractRelax
Radial musclesRelaxContract
PupilConstricts — smallerDilates — wider
Light enteringLess — protects the retinaMore — enough to see

Memory hook: circular muscles make a circle smaller, like pulling a drawstring. Radial muscles run outwards like spokes and pull the pupil wide.

The albino rats in the 2022 paper have an iris with no pigment, so it does not block light. Changing the pupil size then has little effect: too much light reaches the retina, which can damage it and gives poor vision.

subsections.heading: Focusing — near and distant objects
subsections.html:
Spec 2.92 · 2022 Y10 Q5(a) · 2024 Y10 Q8(a)(ii) · 2023 Y10 Q8(a)(ii)

A near object needs more refraction, so the lens becomes fatter; a distant object needs less, so the lens becomes thinner. This is called accommodation.

FeatureNear objectDistant object
Ciliary musclesContract — the ring gets smallerRelax — the ring gets bigger
Suspensory ligamentsSlackenPulled tight
LensThicker, more curvedThinner
RefractionMoreLess

The near-object answer — the school's six marks

1. Ciliary muscles contract 1

2. The ring gets smaller in diameter 1

3. Suspensory ligaments slacken 1

4. Lens becomes thicker / more curved 1

5. So light is refracted more 1

6. And focused on the retina 1

The part that feels backwards: contracting the ciliary muscle loosens the ligaments. The ciliary muscle is a ring. When it contracts, the ring gets smaller and moves closer to the lens, so the ligaments stop pulling. The lens then springs into a fatter shape.

subsections.heading: When focusing goes wrong
subsections.html:
2022 Y10 Q5(b) · 2024 Y10 Q8(b)

If the lens cannot bend light enough, or light cannot get through it, the image on the retina is blurred or dim. The school has asked about both.

Long sight: the eyeball is too short, or the lens cannot become thick enough. Light from a near object is focused behind the retina, so near things look blurred.

Cataract: the lens goes cloudy. Less light passes through to the retina, so fewer impulses are sent to the brain and vision is dim and blurred.

subsections.heading: Two eyes — judging distance
subsections.html:
2024 Y11 mock Q10(b) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2B Q2(b)

Two eyes facing forward see the same area from slightly different angles, which lets the brain judge distance.

In the practical, a student tries to touch pins on a board using one eye, then both. The independent variable is the number of eyes used. Keep the lighting, the distance from the board and the pins the same.

More pins hit with two eyes shows better distance judgement. Predators such as owls and cats have forward-facing eyes with a large overlapping field of view, which helps them catch prey. "A bigger field of view" on its own is ignored — it is the overlap that matters.

Three chains worth memorising exactly

Reflex: stimulus → receptor → sensory → relay → motor → effector → response.

Near focus: ciliary contract → ligaments slacken → lens thicker → more refraction → focused on the retina.

Bright light: circular contract, radial relax → pupil constricts.

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording
StimulusA change in the environment that is detected
ReceptorA cell that detects a stimulus
EffectorA muscle or gland that carries out the response
Reflex actionA rapid, automatic response that does not involve conscious thought
CNSThe brain and spinal cord
Relay neuroneA neurone in the CNS that links the sensory neurone to the motor neurone
SynapseThe gap between two neurones
NeurotransmitterThe chemical that diffuses across a synapse to the next neurone
Antagonistic musclesA pair working in opposition — one contracts as the other relaxes
AccommodationChanging the shape of the lens to focus on near or distant objects

questions.promptHtml: Describe the pathway of a reflex when someone treads on a drawing pin, naming every stage.
questions.answerHtml:
The pin is the stimulus. Pain receptors in the skin of the foot detect it and start an electrical impulse.

The impulse travels along a sensory neurone to the spinal cord, crosses a synapse to a relay neurone, then another synapse to a motor neurone.

The motor neurone carries the impulse to the effector — a leg muscle — which contracts. The response is that the foot is lifted away.

The pathway goes through the spinal cord, not the conscious part of the brain, so it is very quick and limits the damage.

questions.promptHtml: You walk from bright sunshine into a dark room and cannot see for a moment. Explain what your iris does, and why.
questions.answerHtml:
In the dark the radial muscles contract and the circular muscles relax. This dilates the pupil.

A wider pupil lets more light reach the retina, so enough light falls on the rods to form an image.

The moment of blindness is because the change is not instant — the muscles take a moment to respond, and the rods need time to adjust to dim light.

questions.promptHtml: Explain how the eye changes focus from a distant hill to a book held close.
questions.answerHtml:
Looking at the hill, the ciliary muscles are relaxed, the suspensory ligaments are tight and the lens is thin — little refraction is needed.

Light from the book needs bending more. The ciliary muscles contract, which slackens the suspensory ligaments. With the pull removed, the lens becomes thicker and more curved, so it refracts light more and focuses it on the retina.

The ciliary muscle is a ring: contracting makes the ring smaller, so the ligaments attached around it go slack.

questions.promptHtml: Why can a nerve impulse cross a synapse in only one direction?
questions.answerHtml:
Because the neurotransmitter is only released from one side — the end of the first neurone — and the receptors it binds to are only on the other side, on the next neurone.

There is nothing to release transmitter going backwards, and no receptor to receive it. So the signal can only cross one way.

questions.promptHtml: Someone loses colour vision in dim light but can still see shapes. Which receptor cells are involved, and why?
questions.answerHtml:
Cones detect colour but need bright light. Rods work in dim light but give only black and white.

In dim light there is not enough light to stimulate the cones, so only the rods respond. Shapes and movement are still visible, but with no cone stimulation there is no colour.

questions.promptHtml: A painkiller stops a person feeling pain from an injured knee. Suggest three places in the nervous system where it could be working.
questions.answerHtml:
At the receptor: it stops the pain receptors detecting the stimulus, so no impulses start.

In the neurones: it stops impulses being sent along the sensory or relay neurones.

At the synapses: it blocks the neurotransmitter being released, or binding to receptors, so the impulse does not cross to the next neurone.

Any of these means fewer impulses reach the brain, so the pain is not felt. This was a four-mark question in the 2023 real paper.

questions.promptHtml: Albino rats have an iris with no coloured pigment. Explain why they have poor vision in bright light.
questions.answerHtml:
A normal iris is pigmented, so it blocks light everywhere except the pupil. That is how changing the pupil size controls how much light gets in.

An iris with no pigment lets light straight through it. So even when the circular muscles contract and the pupil constricts, too much light still reaches the retina.

The retina is over-stimulated and can be damaged, so vision is poor in bright light.

questions.promptHtml: Students touched pins on a board. With one eye the median was 2 pins; with both eyes it was 6. What does this show, and why does it matter to an owl?
questions.answerHtml:
Using both eyes gives much better distance judgement — you can tell how far away something is.

Two forward-facing eyes see the same area from slightly different angles. That overlapping field of view is what lets the brain judge distance.

An owl is a predator. It needs to judge exactly how far away its prey is to catch it. It does not need to see behind itself, because few animals hunt it.

subsections.html: Animals coordinate responses two ways: nervously, using electrical impulses, and hormonally, using chemicals carried in the blood. Plants use chemicals only. Both systems are used to keep conditions inside the body steady — that is homeostasis.

subsections.heading: Responding to change
subsections.html:
Spec 2.79, 2.80

Organisms survive by detecting changes in their surroundings and responding to them.

A change is a stimulus. It is picked up by a receptor, and the response is carried out by an effector — a muscle or a gland. In animals, nerves or hormones carry the message from one to the other.

  1. Stimulus — a change, such as a rise in temperature or a bright light.
  2. Receptor — detects the change.
  3. Coordination — by the nervous system or by hormones.
  4. Effector — a muscle contracts or a gland secretes.
  5. Response — the action that follows.

Plants respond too, but more slowly. They have no nerves, so they respond by growing — towards light, or down with gravity. That is a tropism.

subsections.heading: Hormones — the definition that earns marks
subsections.html:
Spec 2.89 · 2022 Edexcel 1B Q1

A hormone is a chemical messenger made in an endocrine gland, carried in the blood, that acts on target organs.

All four elements matter. Students routinely lose a mark by saying hormones travel "around the body" rather than in the blood, or by leaving out that they act on specific target organs rather than everything.

The three-mark definition

1. A chemical messenger 1

2. Made by an endocrine gland and carried in the blood 1

3. Acts on a target organ 1

subsections.heading: Nervous versus hormonal
subsections.html:
Spec 2.80 · 2022 Edexcel 1B Q1(b)

Nerves are fast, short-lived and precise; hormones are slower, longer-lasting and widespread.

FeatureNervousHormonal
SignalElectrical impulseChemical in the blood
Carried byNeuronesThe bloodstream
SpeedVery fastSlower
DurationShort-livedLong-lasting
TargetPrecise — one muscle or glandWidespread — any organ with the right receptors

Speed and duration are the two comparisons worth having ready, and they must be phrased as comparisons: "nervous is faster than hormonal", not "nervous is fast".

The 2022 real paper turned this into a calculation. Hormones travel at 420 cm per minute; nerve impulses at 55 m per second. Get both into the same units first:

Comparing two speeds as a ratioratio = faster speed ÷ slower speed, written as n : 1420 cm/min = 4.2 m/min = 0.07 m/s · 55 ÷ 0.07 = 786 : 1

equations.name: Comparing two speeds as a ratio
equations.formula: ratio = faster speed ÷ slower speed, written as n : 1

subsections.heading: The hormones to know
subsections.html:
Spec 2.89 · 2024 Y10 Q2 · 2022 Edexcel 1B Q1(a)

For each hormone, know the gland it comes from and what it does.

HormoneGlandEffect
AdrenalineAdrenal gland (on top of the kidneys)Prepares the body for action — raises heart rate and breathing rate, dilates pupils, sends more blood to muscles, raises blood glucose
InsulinPancreasLowers blood glucose
GlucagonPancreasRaises blood glucose
ADHPituitary glandMore water reabsorbed in the kidney — see module 8
TestosteroneTestesMale secondary sexual characteristics
OestrogenOvariesFemale secondary sexual characteristics; builds the uterus lining
ProgesteroneOvariesMaintains the uterus lining

The adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys. The pancreas sits just below the stomach. Diagram questions ask you to pick them out, so know where they are.

subsections.heading: Adrenaline, explained rather than listed
subsections.html:
Spec 2.89 · 2024 Y10 Q2(c)

Every effect of adrenaline gets more oxygen and glucose to the muscles, so more respiration releases more energy for "fight or flight".

Adrenaline is released when you are frightened or stressed. Increased heart rate and increased breathing rate deliver more oxygen and glucose to the muscles, so more respiration can occur and more energy is released for movement. Blood glucose rises to supply that respiration. Pupils dilate to let more light into the eye, so you can see the danger.

The school's five marks for adrenaline's advantages

More light into the eye 1; to see danger 1; more blood to the leg muscles 1; more oxygen and glucose to the muscles 1; more respiration, more energy released, run away faster 1

A list of effects with no reason attached scores far less.

subsections.heading: Homeostasis and negative feedback
subsections.html:
Spec 2.81

Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant internal environment. The spec's two examples are body water content and body temperature. Blood glucose is controlled the same way.

All three work by negative feedback:

  1. A change away from the normal level is detected.
  2. A response is triggered that opposes the change.
  3. The level returns towards normal.
  4. Once it is back to normal, the response is switched off.

Why bother? Enzymes work best at about 37 °C, and cells need the right amount of water to avoid shrinking or bursting by osmosis. Keep conditions steady and the enzymes and cells keep working.

subsections.heading: Blood glucose — insulin and glucagon
subsections.html:
Spec 2.89 · 2022 Y10 Q6(b) · 2023 Edexcel 1B Q9(b)

The pancreas detects blood glucose and releases insulin to lower it or glucagon to raise it.

Blood glucosePancreas releasesWhat the liver doesResult
Too high — after a mealInsulinConverts glucose into glycogen and stores it; cells take up more glucoseBlood glucose falls
Too low — after exercise or fastingGlucagonConverts glycogen back into glucose and releases itBlood glucose rises

✗ "The liver releases glucagon."
✗ "Insulin turns glucose into glucagon."
✓ "The pancreas releases glucagon. Glucagon makes the liver convert glycogen into glucose."

Glucagon is the hormone. Glycogen is the stored carbohydrate. One letter apart — check which one you wrote.

In type 1 diabetes the pancreas makes too little insulin, so blood glucose rises too high. It is treated with insulin injections. Insulin cannot be swallowed: it is a protein, so it would be digested by proteases in the stomach and small intestine. Diabetics also limit carbohydrates in their diet and monitor exercise, because exercise uses up glucose and could make it fall too low.

subsections.heading: Body temperature — what the skin does
subsections.html:
Spec 2.93 · 2022 Y10 Q6(a) · 2023 Y10 Q5(b)

The skin controls heat loss by sweating and by changing how much blood flows near its surface. A temperature centre in the brain (the hypothalamus) monitors blood temperature and sends the signals.

MechanismToo hotToo cold
Sweat glandsProduce more sweat. It evaporates, taking heat from the skinLittle or no sweat
Arterioles to the skinVasodilation — they widen, more blood flows near the surface, more heat lost by radiationVasoconstriction — they narrow, less blood near the surface, less heat lost
Muscles—Shivering — muscles contract, and the extra respiration releases heat

The vasodilation answer — three marks

1. The arterioles supplying the skin widen — vasodilation 1

2. So more blood flows near the skin surface 1

3. So more heat is lost by radiation 1

✗ "The capillaries dilate." ✗ "The blood vessels move closer to the skin."
✓ "The arterioles widen, so more blood flows through the capillaries near the surface."

subsections.heading: Reading temperature data — the cyclist
subsections.html:
2022 Y10 Q6(a)

During exercise core temperature rises because respiration releases heat; skin temperature can fall because sweat evaporates.

The 2022 paper gave a graph of a cyclist's core and skin temperatures. The six marks were a chain for each line:

  1. Core temperature rises — the muscles contract more, so there is more respiration, which releases energy as heat.
  2. Skin temperature falls — the cyclist sweats, and the sweat evaporates, cooling the skin.

Describe the pattern, then give the reason for it. Quote a value from the graph if you can.

subsections.heading: Plant tropisms
subsections.html:
Spec 2.79 · 2024 Y10 Q1(b)

A tropism is a growth response towards or away from a stimulus. "Positive" means towards; "negative" means away. Two to know:

TropismStimulusShootsRoots
PhototropismLightPositive — grow towardsNegative
Gravitropism (geotropism)GravityNegative — grow awayPositive — grow down

The advantages: shoots growing towards light get more light for photosynthesis; roots growing down reach water and mineral ions, and anchor the plant.

subsections.heading: Auxin — the mechanism in shoots
subsections.html:
Spec 2.79

Auxin is a plant hormone made at the shoot tip that makes cells elongate.

  1. Auxin is made at the tip of the shoot.
  2. Light comes from one side, and auxin moves to the shaded side.
  3. That gives an unequal distribution: more auxin on the shaded side than the lit side.
  4. The cells on the shaded side elongate more.
  5. The shaded side grows longer, so the shoot bends towards the light.

Answers saying the plant "grows towards the light because it wants light" score nothing — plants have no intent, and the mark is for the mechanism.

subsections.heading: Auxin in roots, and the tip experiments
subsections.html:
Spec 2.79

In roots, auxin inhibits elongation, so the side with more auxin grows less.

Gravity makes auxin collect on the lower side of a root. The lower side elongates less than the upper side, so the root bends downwards. Same hormone, same kind of unequal distribution, opposite effect.

Classic experiments on shoots show where the action is:

What was done to the shootResultWhat it shows
Tip cut offNo bendingAuxin is made in the tip
Tip covered with an opaque capNo bendingThe tip detects the light
Shoot covered below the tip, tip exposedBends towards lightOnly the tip needs light
Light from all sidesGrows straight upAuxin is spread evenly

The sentences behind most of the marks

Auxin: made at the tip → moves to the shaded side → unequal distribution → cells there elongate more → the shoot bends towards the light.

Too hot: sweat evaporates; arterioles widen, more blood near the surface, more heat lost by radiation.

Glucose: high → insulin → glucose to glycogen. Low → glucagon → glycogen to glucose. Both from the pancreas.

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording
HormoneA chemical messenger made by an endocrine gland and carried in the blood to a target organ
Endocrine glandA gland that secretes hormones into the blood
Target organThe organ a hormone acts on, because its cells have the right receptors
HomeostasisThe maintenance of a constant internal environment
Negative feedbackA change triggers a response that opposes it, returning the level to normal
VasodilationWidening of arterioles supplying the skin, so more blood flows near the surface
VasoconstrictionNarrowing of arterioles supplying the skin, so less blood flows near the surface
TropismA growth response of a plant towards or away from a stimulus
PhototropismA growth response to light
GravitropismA growth response to gravity
AuxinA plant hormone made at the shoot tip that causes cell elongation

questions.promptHtml: A shoot on a windowsill bends towards the window. Explain fully, in terms of auxin.
questions.answerHtml:
Auxin is produced at the tip of the shoot. Because light is coming from one side, the auxin moves away from the light and accumulates on the shaded side.

This gives an unequal distribution of auxin — a higher concentration on the shaded side than the lit side.

Auxin causes cell elongation, so the cells on the shaded side grow longer than those on the lit side. The shaded side of the shoot therefore becomes longer, and the shoot bends towards the light.

The advantage is that the leaves receive more light, so the plant can photosynthesise more.

questions.promptHtml: Why does a root grow downwards when auxin also collects on its lower side?
questions.answerHtml:
Gravity causes auxin to accumulate on the lower side of the root, just as it collects on the shaded side of a shoot.

The difference is the effect: in roots, auxin inhibits cell elongation rather than promoting it. So the lower side, with more auxin, elongates less than the upper side.

The upper side grows more, so the root bends downwards — positive gravitropism. This takes it towards water and mineral ions, and anchors the plant.

The same hormone, the same distribution, opposite effect. That reversal is the whole point of the question.

questions.promptHtml: A student is startled by a loud bang. Their heart races for several minutes. Explain why the response involves both control systems.
questions.answerHtml:
Nervous: the sound is detected and an impulse travels along neurones to produce the immediate jump or flinch. This is very fast but short-lived.

Hormonal: adrenaline is released from the adrenal glands into the blood. It travels to target organs including the heart, increasing heart rate and breathing rate.

Because the hormone must be carried in the blood, this response is slower to start but lasts much longer — which is why the heart is still racing minutes after the bang, long after the nervous response has finished.

questions.promptHtml: If the tip is cut off a shoot, it stops bending towards light. What does this show?
questions.answerHtml:
It shows that the tip is where auxin is produced. Removing it removes the source of the hormone, so no unequal distribution can build up and no unequal growth occurs — the shoot grows straight.

Covering the tip with an opaque cap gives the same result, showing that the tip is also where the light is detected. Covering the shoot below the tip while leaving the tip exposed still produces bending, which confirms it.

questions.promptHtml: Why does vasodilation cool you down, and why is "the blood vessels move nearer the skin" wrong?
questions.answerHtml:
The arterioles that supply the skin capillaries widen. More blood flows through the capillaries just under the surface. That blood is warm, so more heat is lost by radiation to the air.

The vessels stay exactly where they are. What changes is how much blood goes through them. Examiners reject "vessels move" because it describes something that never happens.

questions.promptHtml: A person with type 1 diabetes must inject insulin. Why can't they just swallow it as a tablet?
questions.answerHtml:
Insulin is a protein. In the stomach and small intestine, proteases would digest it into amino acids — exactly as they do with the protein in food.

The amino acids have no hormone effect. Injecting puts the insulin straight into the blood, where it can travel to its target organs, such as the liver.

questions.promptHtml: During a long ride, a cyclist's core temperature rises but their skin temperature falls. How can both happen at once?
questions.answerHtml:
Core rises: the leg muscles contract much more, so there is much more respiration. Respiration releases energy as heat, faster than the body can lose it.

Skin falls: the body responds by sweating. The sweat evaporates, and evaporation takes heat from the skin surface, cooling it.

The skin is where heat is being lost; the core is where it is being made. So they can move in opposite directions.

questions.promptHtml: After a meal rich in pasta, blood glucose rises, then returns to normal. Explain why this is negative feedback.
questions.answerHtml:
Starch in the pasta is digested to glucose, which is absorbed into the blood. The pancreas detects the rise and releases insulin.

Insulin makes the liver convert glucose into glycogen, and cells take up more glucose. Blood glucose falls back to normal, and less insulin is released.

It is negative feedback because the response opposes the change: a rise causes a fall. If blood glucose dropped too low, glucagon would do the reverse.

modules.title: Homeostasis, Excretion and the Kidney
modules.standfirst: Nine spec points, and the hardest block on the Year 10 checklist. It is in every Year 10 paper and most real Paper 2s. Filtration then selective reabsorption, the nephron named part by part, and the ADH loop that students most often get backwards.

subsections.html: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant internal environment. The kidneys do two homeostatic jobs: they remove urea (excretion) and they control the water content of the blood (osmoregulation). Both depend on the same two steps — filter almost everything out, then take back what is needed.

subsections.heading: Excretion is not egestion
subsections.html:
Spec 2.71 · 2022 Y10 Q1(a)

Excretion is the removal of the waste products of metabolism — substances the body made. Egestion is the removal of undigested food as faeces, which was never absorbed and never part of a reaction.

OrganExcretes
LungsCarbon dioxide (and water vapour)
KidneysUrea, excess water and excess ions
SkinWater, salts and a little urea in sweat

The liver produces urea but does not excrete it, so it is not the excretory organ for urea — a distinction examiners like.

subsections.heading: Where urea comes from
subsections.html:
Spec 2.71

Urea is made in the liver from excess amino acids, and excreted by the kidneys.

  1. Excess amino acids cannot be stored.
  2. In the liver they are deaminated: the amino group is removed, forming ammonia, which is highly toxic.
  3. The ammonia is immediately converted to the less toxic urea.
  4. Urea travels in the blood to the kidneys and leaves in the urine.

subsections.heading: The urinary system
subsections.html:
Spec 2.73B · 2023 Y10 Q6(a) · 2022 Edexcel 2B Q4(a)

Urine is made in the kidneys and flows kidney → ureter → bladder → urethra.

StructureJob
Renal arteryBrings blood, containing urea, to the kidney
KidneyFilters the blood and makes urine
Renal veinTakes cleaned blood away from the kidney
UreterCarries urine from each kidney to the bladder
BladderStores urine
UrethraCarries urine from the bladder out of the body

✗ "kidney → urethra → bladder"
✓ "kidney → ureter → bladder → urethra"

Two ureters (one per kidney), one urethra. The real mark scheme rejects "urethra" for the ureter, and rejects "gall bladder" for the bladder.

subsections.heading: The nephron — the parts in order
subsections.html:
Spec 2.74B · 2023 Edexcel 2B Q3(a) · 2024 Y10 Q6(a)

Each kidney contains about a million nephrons, and each nephron does filtration then reabsorption along its length.

  1. Glomerulus — a knot of capillaries, where blood is filtered under high pressure.
  2. Bowman's capsule — the cup around the glomerulus that collects the filtrate.
  3. Proximal convoluted tubule (first coiled part) — glucose is reabsorbed here.
  4. Loop of Henle — makes the tissue around it salty, so water can later leave the collecting duct.
  5. Distal convoluted tubule (second coiled part) — ions are adjusted.
  6. Collecting duct — water is reabsorbed here, controlled by ADH. What is left is urine.

"Proximal" means near the start; "distal" means further away. On a diagram, the proximal tubule is the coil joined straight onto the capsule.

subsections.heading: Ultrafiltration — stage 1
subsections.html:
Spec 2.75B · 2023 Y10 Q6(b)(i) · 2023 Edexcel 2B Q3(b)

High blood pressure in the glomerulus forces small molecules out of the blood into the Bowman's capsule.

The vessel bringing blood into the glomerulus is wider than the one taking it out. Blood enters faster than it can leave, so the pressure builds up. That high pressure drives the filtering.

SubstanceFiltered?Why
WaterYesSmall molecule
GlucoseYesSmall molecule
Ions (salts)YesSmall
UreaYesSmall molecule
ProteinsNoToo large to pass out of the glomerulus
Blood cellsNoToo large

So the glomerular filtrate is water, glucose, ions and urea — like plasma with the proteins taken out.

subsections.heading: Selective reabsorption of glucose — stage 2
subsections.html:
Spec 2.77B · 2023 Y11 mock Q9(a) · 2022 Edexcel Jan 2B Q5(a)

All the glucose is taken back into the blood in the proximal convoluted tubule, by active transport.

Glucose is useful, so the body cannot afford to lose it in urine. It is reabsorbed against the concentration gradient, which needs active transport and energy from respiration. That is why the tubule cells are packed with mitochondria.

The three-mark glucose answer

1. Selective reabsorption into the blood 1

2. In the proximal convoluted tubule 1

3. By active transport, using energy, against the concentration gradient 1

The word selective is the point: the kidney filters almost everything out, then chooses what to take back. Urea is not reabsorbed — it stays in the filtrate.

subsections.heading: Water reabsorption in the collecting duct
subsections.html:
Spec 2.76B · 2022 Edexcel Jan 2B Q5(b)

Water leaves the collecting duct by osmosis and goes back into the blood.

The loop of Henle makes the tissue around the collecting duct very salty. As filtrate flows down the collecting duct, water moves out by osmosis, from the dilute filtrate into the salty tissue, and then into the blood. How much water can leave depends on how permeable the collecting duct wall is — and that is what ADH controls.

Because water is taken back but urea is not, urea ends up far more concentrated in urine than in the filtrate.

How many times more concentratedconcentration factor = concentration in urine ÷ concentration in filtratesame units top and bottom · the answer has no units · 1700 ÷ 440 = 3.9 times

equations.name: How many times more concentrated
equations.formula: concentration factor = concentration in urine ÷ concentration in filtrate

subsections.heading: ADH and water balance — the loop to get right
subsections.html:
Spec 2.78B · 2023 Y10 Q6(c) · 2022 Edexcel 2B Q4(c) · 2024 Edexcel 2B Q3(b)

More ADH makes the collecting duct more permeable, so more water is reabsorbed and less urine is made.

When you are dehydrated — too little water, so blood is too concentrated:

  1. The hypothalamus in the brain detects the change.
  2. The pituitary gland releases more ADH into the blood.
  3. ADH makes the collecting duct more permeable to water.
  4. More water is reabsorbed into the blood by osmosis.
  5. A small volume of concentrated, dark urine is produced, and blood water content rises back to normal.

When you have drunk a lot — blood too dilute — every step reverses: less ADH, collecting duct less permeable, less water reabsorbed, and a large volume of dilute, pale urine.

✗ "ADH removes water." ✗ "More ADH makes you urinate more."
✓ "More ADH → collecting duct more permeable → more water reabsorbed into the blood → less, more concentrated urine."

Read the name as "anti-diuretic — anti-urine" and the direction is fixed for good.

subsections.heading: Reading urine data
subsections.html:
Spec 2.79B · 2024 Y10 Q6(b) · 2024 Edexcel 2B Q3 · 2022 Y10 Q1(b)

Normal urine contains water, urea and ions — and no glucose and no protein. Anything else points to one stage going wrong.

What the urine showsStage that has failedWhere
Protein presentFiltration — the filter is damaged and lets large molecules throughGlomerulus
Glucose presentSelective reabsorption cannot take it all backProximal convoluted tubule
Huge volume of very dilute urineWater reabsorption — too little ADHCollecting duct

The 2024 real paper compared three athletes. No drink: small, very dark urine — blood concentrated, more ADH, more water reabsorbed. Pure water: large, pale urine — blood diluted, less ADH. Isotonic drink (salt and sugar at blood concentration): in between, because the salt and sugar are absorbed too, so the blood is not diluted as much.

subsections.heading: Testing urine for glucose and protein
subsections.html:
2023 Edexcel 2B Q3(c) · 2024 Y10 Q6(b)(ii) · 2023 Y11 mock Q9(c)

Biuret reagent tests for protein; Benedict's reagent, heated, tests for glucose.

Testing forReagentMethodPositive result
ProteinBiuret (sodium hydroxide + copper sulfate)Add to the sample, no heatingBlue → lilac / purple
GlucoseBenedict'sAdd, then heat in a water bathBlue → green, yellow or brick red

subsections.heading: Dialysis — when the kidneys fail
subsections.html:
2022 Y10 Q7 · 2023 Edexcel Jan 2B Q1(c)

A dialysis machine removes urea by diffusion through a partially permeable membrane.

Blood flows on one side of the membrane and dialysis fluid on the other. The fluid is chosen carefully:

  • No urea in the fluid, so urea diffuses out of the blood down its concentration gradient.
  • Same glucose and ion concentration as normal blood, so there is no net loss of the useful ones.
  • Large proteins such as albumin are too big to pass through the pores, so they stay in the blood.

The dialyser speeds this up with long, coiled tubing (large surface area), a thin membrane (short diffusion distance), and fluid that keeps flowing so the concentration gradient is maintained.

subsections.heading: Negative feedback, stated generally
subsections.html:
Spec 2.72B

Every homeostatic mechanism detects a change and triggers a response that opposes it.

Water balance by ADH is the kidney example. Temperature control by the skin, and blood glucose by insulin and glucagon, work the same way — both are taught in module 7. Because the response opposes the change, the system is self-correcting.

The sentences this topic turns on

Filtration is not selective; reabsorption is. Everything small is forced out at the glomerulus, then the useful things are taken back.

Glucose: all reabsorbed, in the proximal convoluted tubule, by active transport.

Water: hypothalamus detects → pituitary releases more ADH → collecting duct more permeable → more water back into the blood → less urine.

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording
HomeostasisThe maintenance of a constant internal environment
ExcretionThe removal of the waste products of metabolism
EgestionThe removal of undigested food as faeces
OsmoregulationControlling the water content of the blood
DeaminationRemoval of the amino group from excess amino acids in the liver, forming ammonia then urea
UltrafiltrationFiltering small molecules out of the blood at the glomerulus into the Bowman's capsule, under high pressure
Selective reabsorptionTaking useful substances back into the blood from the filtrate
ADHA hormone from the pituitary that makes the collecting duct more permeable to water
Negative feedbackA response that opposes the change that triggered it, restoring the normal level
UreaThe waste product formed from excess amino acids in the liver

questions.promptHtml: A person runs a marathon on a hot day and drinks very little. Describe what happens to their urine and explain the hormonal control.
questions.answerHtml:
They lose a lot of water in sweat, so the water content of the blood falls and the blood becomes more concentrated.

The hypothalamus detects this, and the pituitary gland releases more ADH into the blood. ADH makes the collecting duct more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed back into the blood by osmosis.

The result is a small volume of concentrated urine, darker in colour. Blood water content returns towards normal — negative feedback.

questions.promptHtml: Protein is found in a patient's urine. Explain what this suggests about their kidneys.
questions.answerHtml:
Normally protein molecules are too large to be filtered at the glomerulus, so they stay in the blood and never enter the filtrate at all.

Protein in the urine therefore suggests the filter in the glomerulus is damaged, letting large molecules through. High blood pressure is one cause.

Note the reasoning: this cannot be a reabsorption problem, because protein is never in the filtrate to be reabsorbed. That distinction is what the question is testing.

questions.promptHtml: Why does an untreated diabetic have glucose in their urine, when a healthy person has none?
questions.answerHtml:
In a healthy person, glucose is filtered out at the glomerulus but all of it is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule by active transport, so none reaches the urine.

In an untreated diabetic, blood glucose is very high because there is too little insulin to lower it. So much glucose is filtered that the active transport system cannot keep up — it cannot reabsorb it all.

The excess glucose stays in the filtrate and appears in the urine.

questions.promptHtml: Explain why the cells of the proximal convoluted tubule contain a large number of mitochondria.
questions.answerHtml:
Glucose is reabsorbed there by active transport, which moves substances against the concentration gradient.

Active transport requires energy, which is released by aerobic respiration. That happens in the mitochondria, so cells doing a lot of active transport need many of them.

The same reasoning explains why root hair cells in plants are also packed with mitochondria.

questions.promptHtml: Explain why urea must be removed from the body, and where it is made.
questions.answerHtml:
The body cannot store excess amino acids. In the liver they are deaminated — the amino group is removed — producing ammonia, which is highly toxic.

The liver immediately converts ammonia into the less toxic urea. Even so, urea is still a waste product and would be harmful if it built up, so it is carried in the blood to the kidneys and excreted in the urine.

A point worth keeping straight: urea is made in the liver but excreted by the kidneys.

questions.promptHtml: Someone drinks two litres of water quickly. Describe the changes in ADH and in their urine.
questions.answerHtml:
The water content of the blood rises, so the blood becomes too dilute.

The pituitary releases less ADH. The collecting duct becomes less permeable to water, so less water is reabsorbed.

More water stays in the filtrate, producing a large volume of dilute, pale urine. Blood water content falls back to normal.

If they kept drinking and made very little urine, the blood would become too dilute and water would enter their cells by osmosis, making them swell — the 2022 Year 10 question.

questions.promptHtml: The blood vessel entering the glomerulus is wider than the one leaving it. Why does that matter?
questions.answerHtml:
Blood can get in more easily than it can get out, so it backs up in the glomerulus and the pressure rises.

That high pressure is what forces water, glucose, ions and urea out of the capillaries into the Bowman's capsule — ultrafiltration. Without it, much less would be filtered and much less urea would be removed.

questions.promptHtml: Dialysis fluid contains glucose and salts at the normal blood concentration, but no urea. Why is it made that way?
questions.answerHtml:
No urea: urea is more concentrated in the blood than in the fluid, so it diffuses out of the blood through the partially permeable membrane. That is the whole purpose.

Normal glucose and salts: the concentration is the same on both sides, so there is no net diffusion. The patient keeps the useful substances, and any excess salt still diffuses out.

The fluid is kept flowing so fresh, urea-free fluid is always next to the membrane, keeping the gradient steep.

modules.title: Ecology and the Environment
modules.standfirst: Nine spec points, and the topic with the most calculations on the Year 10 list. A food web opens almost every real Paper 1. The quadrat method, the percentage-transfer sum and the reasons energy is lost are where the marks concentrate — and the reasons must be tied to trophic levels.

"You get only two marks for listing causes of energy loss — the other marks need the idea that energy is lost between trophic levels."

And from 2024: "Most got the energy-loss marks but not the first: say the food chain from the oak is shorter. Very few used the term trophic level."

A list of losses is worth two marks at most. Say that energy is lost at each transfer between trophic levels, so less is available to the next level — then name the losses.

subsections.html: Ecology is about how living things depend on each other and on their surroundings. Two ideas carry most of the marks: how you measure a population fairly, and why energy runs out as it passes along a food chain.

subsections.heading: The four terms, in order of size
subsections.html:
Spec 4.1 · 2024 Y10 Q9(a)

A population is one species; a community is every species; an ecosystem adds the non-living surroundings.

LevelWhat it covers
HabitatThe place where an organism lives
PopulationAll the organisms of one species in a habitat
CommunityAll the populations of different species in a habitat
EcosystemThe community plus the non-living environment it interacts with

The ecosystem definition needs the non-living part — water, soil, temperature, light. "All the living things in an area" defines a community, not an ecosystem, and that is the most common mix-up.

subsections.heading: Biodiversity
subsections.html:
Spec 4.3B · 2024 Y10 Q7(b)

Biodiversity is the number of different species in an area — and, more fully, how evenly the organisms are spread among them.

The 2024 Year 10 question gave counts of three plant species in two fields. The marks went to:

  • Field X has all three species; field Y does not.
  • Field X has an even spread; field Y is dominated by one species.
  • So field X has the greater biodiversity — but three counts is a small sample.

Two fields can have the same number of species, yet one is more diverse because no single species dominates it.

subsections.heading: Quadrats — estimating a population
subsections.html:
Spec 4.2 · 2022 Edexcel 1B Q4(a)(ii) · 2024 Y11 mock Q1(b)(ii)

You count organisms in a few random squares, take a mean, and scale up to the whole area.

  1. Mark out the area with two tape measures at right angles, like the axes of a graph.
  2. Use a random number generator to pick coordinates, and place a quadrat there.
  3. Count the organisms of the species inside the quadrat.
  4. Repeat for many quadrats — ten or more — and calculate the mean per quadrat.
  5. Scale up to the total area.
Estimating population size from quadratspopulation = mean number per quadrat × (total area ÷ area of one quadrat)mean of several quadrats first · place them randomly · the answer is an estimate

To compare two areas, do exactly the same in each: same quadrat size, same number of quadrats, same time of year. Then compare the means.

✗ "Put the quadrat where the plants are." — biased.
✗ "Use a quadrat and repeat." — the school rejected "repeat" without "count the producers".
✓ "Place quadrats at random coordinates, count the plants in each, take a mean and scale up to the area."

equations.name: Estimating population size from quadrats
equations.formula: population = mean number per quadrat × (total area ÷ area of one quadrat)

subsections.heading: Transects — how distribution changes
subsections.html:
Spec 4.4B

A transect is a line across a habitat, with quadrats placed at regular intervals along it.

Use one when conditions change across an area — from a hedge into a field, or up a beach. At each point along the line, record which species are present and how many, and measure an abiotic factor such as light intensity or soil moisture. You can then link the change in distribution to the change in conditions.

Random quadrats are for estimating how many. A transect is for showing where, and why.

subsections.heading: Abiotic and biotic factors
subsections.html:
Spec 4.5

Abiotic factors are the non-living conditions; biotic factors are the effects of other living things. Both change the size and distribution of a population.

Abiotic — non-livingBiotic — living
Light intensityAvailability of food
TemperaturePredators
Water availabilityCompetition for food, space or light
Soil pH and mineral ionsPathogens — disease
Oxygen or carbon dioxide levelsPollinators

Always link the factor to the organism. "Less light under the trees, so less photosynthesis, so fewer grass plants" scores; "light affects plants" does not.

subsections.heading: Trophic levels and food chains
subsections.html:
Spec 4.6 · 2024 Edexcel 1B Q1(a) · 2023 Edexcel Jan 1B Q7(a)

A food chain starts with a producer, and each arrow shows the direction of energy transfer. The arrows point from the eaten to the eater. Drawing them backwards is a standard lost mark.

Trophic levelRoleExample
1 — ProducerMakes its own food by photosynthesisOak tree, grass
2 — Primary consumerEats the producer — a herbivoreCaterpillar, zebra
3 — Secondary consumerEats the primary consumerBlue tit, cheetah
4 — Tertiary consumerEats the secondary consumerSparrowhawk
DecomposersBreak down dead material and waste from every levelBacteria and fungi

A trophic level is the position an organism feeds at. In a food web, one animal can sit at two levels — a blackbird eating earthworms is a secondary consumer, and eating centipedes that eat woodlice makes it a tertiary consumer too.

subsections.heading: Food webs and interdependence
subsections.html:
Spec 4.7 · 2023 Edexcel 1B Q2(b) · 2023 Edexcel Jan 1B Q7(a)(iii)

Change one population in a food web and the populations that eat it, and that it eats, change too.

Work outwards along each arrow, one step at a time:

  1. What did the removed organism eat? That population increases — fewer are eaten.
  2. What ate it? That population decreases — less food. Unless it has another food source in the web.
  3. Follow the knock-on effect one more step.

An animal with many food sources is least affected when one prey species falls — it just eats more of the others. Real papers test this as a multiple-choice question on a food web.

subsections.heading: Decomposers — how they get energy
subsections.html:
Spec 4.6 · 2023 Edexcel 1B Q2(a)(ii) · 2022 Edexcel Jan 2B Q2(a)

Decomposers release enzymes onto dead material, absorb the small molecules, and respire them.

  1. Bacteria and fungi feed on dead organisms and waste — they are saprotrophic.
  2. They secrete enzymes onto the material — digestion happens outside their cells.
  3. They absorb the soluble products.
  4. They use them in respiration to release energy, and to grow.

Decomposers recycle the elements locked in dead bodies back into the soil — see module 11.

subsections.heading: Pyramids of number, biomass and energy
subsections.html:
Spec 4.7 · 2022 Y10 Q8(a) · 2022 Edexcel 1B Q4(a)(i)

A pyramid shows the size of each trophic level, producers at the bottom.

PyramidWhat each bar showsAlways a true pyramid?
NumbersHow many organismsNo — one oak tree feeds thousands of caterpillars
BiomassTotal dry mass of organismsAlmost always
EnergyEnergy passed on per m² per yearAlways — energy is lost at every level

When you draw one, put the producer at the bottom, make each bar the right relative width, and label every level. The school scheme gave a mark just for the labels, and some students forgot them.

subsections.heading: Why only about 10% passes on
subsections.html:
Spec 4.9 · 2023 Edexcel Jan 1B Q7(b)(i) · 2024 Y11 mock Q1(b)(i)

At each transfer between trophic levels most of the energy is lost, so only about 10% is available to the next level. The named routes:

  • Respiration — energy released and lost as heat, and used in movement
  • Not all of the organism is eaten — roots, bones, fur
  • Not all is digested — lost in faeces (egestion)
  • Excretion — energy lost in urea and urine
  • Some organisms die and are not eaten — decomposers get that energy

This is why food chains are short, rarely more than four or five levels, and why a shorter chain delivers more energy to the top. Mammals and birds lose more than snails or insects, because they respire more to keep warm.

Producers are worse still. They capture only a few per cent of the light that falls on them: some is reflected, some misses the chlorophyll, and some is the wrong wavelength.

subsections.heading: Energy transfer calculations
subsections.html:
2023 Y10 Q3(b) · 2024 Y10 Q4(b) · 2022 Edexcel Jan 1B Q7(b)

Efficiency is the energy (or biomass) passed on, divided by what was there, times 100.

Percentage transfer between trophic levelsefficiency (%) = (energy or biomass at the higher level ÷ energy or biomass at the lower level) × 1002.40 ÷ 10.60 × 100 = 22.6% · 1.4 ÷ 87 × 100 = 1.6%

A variation: assimilation efficiency — how much of what was eaten was actually absorbed. A snail eats 1.2 g and egests 0.3 g, so it absorbs 0.9 g: 0.9 ÷ 1.2 × 100 = 75%. Herbivores score low on this because plant material is hard to digest, so much is egested.

equations.name: Percentage transfer between trophic levels
equations.formula: efficiency (%) = (energy or biomass at the higher level ÷ energy or biomass at the lower level) × 100

subsections.heading: Transfer of substances, and predator–prey cycles
subsections.html:
Spec 4.8

Substances pass up a food chain along with energy — carbon compounds, and also poisons.

When an animal eats, it takes in the proteins, carbohydrates and fats of its food, and builds them into its own body. Anything that is not broken down or excreted — such as some pesticides — builds up. Each animal eats many from the level below, so the concentration increases at each trophic level, and top predators get the highest dose.

Predator and prey numbers rise and fall in cycles. More prey means more food, so the predator population rises. More predators eat more prey, so the prey population falls. With less food the predators fall, and the prey recover. The predator peak always comes after the prey peak.

The sentences behind most of the marks

Quadrats: random coordinates → count → repeat and take a mean → × (total area ÷ quadrat area). It is an estimate.

Energy: energy is lost at each transfer between trophic levels — as heat from respiration, in faeces, in excretion, and in parts not eaten — so only about 10% passes on.

Efficiency: higher level ÷ lower level × 100.

EcosystemA community and the non-living environment it interacts with
BiodiversityThe number of different species in an area
ProducerAn organism that makes its own food by photosynthesis
Trophic levelThe position of an organism in a food chain
DecomposerAn organism that breaks down dead material — bacteria and fungi
QuadratA square frame of known area used to sample a population
TransectA line across a habitat along which quadrats are placed at regular intervals
Abiotic factorA non-living condition, such as light or temperature

questions.promptHtml: A student counts daisies in ten 0.25 m² quadrats in a 200 m² field, finding a mean of 6 per quadrat. Estimate the population and state one assumption.
questions.answerHtml:
Number of quadrat-sized areas in the field = 200 ÷ 0.25 = 800.

Estimated population = 6 × 800 = 4800 daisies.

Assumption: that the quadrats were placed randomly, so the sample is representative of the whole field. If the daisies were clustered in one damp corner and the quadrats missed it, the estimate could be badly wrong.

questions.promptHtml: Explain why a food chain rarely has more than four or five trophic levels.
questions.answerHtml:
Only about 10% of the energy at each trophic level is transferred to the next. The remaining 90% is lost through respiration as heat, in egestion as faeces, in excretion, and in parts not eaten.

After four or five levels so little energy remains that it could not support a population of another organism — there would not be enough food energy to sustain their numbers.

questions.promptHtml: In the chain grass → rabbit → fox, all the foxes are removed. Predict what happens to the rabbits and the grass, and explain.
questions.answerHtml:
Rabbits increase. Their predator has gone, so fewer are eaten and more survive to reproduce.

Grass decreases. The larger rabbit population eats far more grass.

Then rabbits fall again. With the grass depleted there is not enough food, so rabbits starve and their numbers drop — the population is now limited by food rather than by predation.

Working the chain through in both directions, and then following the knock-on effect, is what separates a 3-mark answer from a 1-mark one.

questions.promptHtml: A pyramid of numbers for oak tree → caterpillar → bird is inverted at the base. Explain why, and why a pyramid of biomass would not be.
questions.answerHtml:
A pyramid of numbers counts individuals regardless of size. A single oak tree can feed thousands of caterpillars, so the producer bar is narrower than the level above it.

A pyramid of biomass measures the total dry mass at each level. One oak tree has an enormous mass — far more than all the caterpillars feeding on it — so the pyramid is the normal shape.

Biomass pyramids are almost always true pyramids because each level can only build its mass from the level below, and most of that is lost on the way.

questions.promptHtml: On a predator–prey graph, the predator peak always comes slightly after the prey peak. Explain why.
questions.answerHtml:
The predators depend on the prey for food. When prey numbers rise there is more food available, so more predators survive and reproduce — but that takes time, because the young must be born and grow.

By the time the predator population has risen, the increased predation has already begun to reduce the prey numbers, which is why the prey peak has passed.

The lag is the cause-and-effect made visible: the predator population is responding to the prey population, so it must follow it.

questions.promptHtml: In a forest web, a fox gets its food through acorns → mouse → fox and through grass → grasshopper → shrew → fox. Why does the fox get more of the energy from the oak chain?
questions.answerHtml:
The oak chain is shorter: there is only one trophic level between the producer and the fox, instead of two.

Energy is lost at every transfer between trophic levels — as heat from respiration, in faeces, in excretion, and in parts not eaten. Fewer transfers means fewer losses, so a bigger share of the producer's energy reaches the fox.

The school noted that most students named the losses but missed the first mark — saying the chain is shorter.

questions.promptHtml: A mouse and a snail eat the same mass of plant material. The snail turns more of it into new body mass. Why?
questions.answerHtml:
A mouse is a mammal. It keeps its body temperature constant, so it respires much more to keep warm, and it moves around a lot. That energy is released as heat and lost.

A snail's body temperature just follows its surroundings, and it moves slowly. It uses less of its food energy for respiration, so more is left to build new tissue.

questions.promptHtml: Only about 1–2% of the light falling on a field of grass ends up in new grass tissue. Where does the rest go?
questions.answerHtml:
Much of the light never gets used: some is reflected from the leaves, some passes through or misses the chlorophyll, and some is a wavelength chlorophyll does not absorb.

Of the energy that is captured in glucose, the grass uses a lot in its own respiration, which releases it as heat. Only what is left is built into new tissue — the biomass a herbivore can eat.

subsections.html: Every technique here increases yield by removing something that was limiting growth — or, with microorganisms, by giving them ideal conditions to grow. Name the limiting factor or the condition, follow it through, and the mark follows.

subsections.heading: Glasshouses and polytunnels
subsections.html:
Spec 5.5

A glasshouse raises yield by controlling the conditions that limit photosynthesis.

What is controlledWhy yield rises
TemperatureWarmer conditions increase the rate of photosynthesis (and of the enzymes controlling it), so more glucose is made — until the optimum
Carbon dioxideBurning paraffin heaters or adding CO₂ removes it as a limiting factor
LightArtificial lighting extends the growing day, and light is no longer limiting
Pests and diseaseEnclosure keeps pests out, so less of the crop is damaged or eaten
WaterIrrigation gives a reliable supply, needed as a raw material for photosynthesis

A polytunnel — polythene over hoops — does the same job more cheaply, trapping heat and keeping off wind and some pests. Crops can be grown out of season and earlier in the year.

subsections.heading: Carbon dioxide and temperature
subsections.html:
Spec 5.6

More carbon dioxide and a higher temperature both increase yield — but only up to a point.

  1. More CO₂ or a higher temperature removes a limiting factor.
  2. So the rate of photosynthesis increases.
  3. More glucose is made.
  4. It is converted to starch, cellulose and proteins for growth.
  5. The plants grow larger and faster, so the yield is higher.

The limits: once CO₂ is high enough, another factor such as light or temperature limits the rate, and adding more CO₂ is wasted money. Raising temperature only helps up to the optimum; beyond it the enzymes controlling photosynthesis denature and the rate falls. Heating also costs money, so growers stop where the extra crop no longer pays for the fuel.

A paraffin heater removes two limiting factors at once: it releases heat and carbon dioxide as it burns.

subsections.heading: Designing a glasshouse investigation
subsections.html:
2024 Edexcel 1B Q10

Change one factor, keep everything else the same, measure the crop, and repeat. The real mark scheme follows a pattern you can learn:

StepWhat to write, for "best CO₂ concentration"
C — changeUse at least three different CO₂ concentrations, one per glasshouse
O — organismSame species and variety of crop plant, same age
R — repeatRepeat each concentration
M — measureMeasure the mass of crop (fruit or seeds) after a stated time
S — sameKeep temperature and light the same; same soil, water and fertiliser

Six marks, six points. Name the variables — "keep everything else the same" scores nothing.

subsections.heading: Fertilisers
subsections.html:
Spec 5.7

Fertilisers supply the mineral ions that harvested crops remove from the soil.

IonNeeded for
NitrateMaking amino acids, and so proteins for growth
MagnesiumMaking chlorophyll
PhosphateDNA and cell membranes
PotassiumEnzymes for photosynthesis and respiration

The chain to state: fertiliser supplies nitrate → more amino acids → more protein → more growth → higher yield. Say nitrate ions, not "nitrogen", and do not say fertiliser "feeds" the plant — plants make their own food.

subsections.heading: Why crops need pest control
subsections.html:
Spec 5.8 · 2022 Edexcel Jan 1B Q10(b)

Pests eat or damage crops, so less of the crop can be harvested.

The damage can be indirect. Aphids push their mouthparts into the phloem and take sucrose and amino acids. The plant then has:

  • less sugar for respiration, so less energy for growth and for active transport of mineral ions
  • less sugar to store as starch in grain, fruit or tubers
  • fewer amino acids to make proteins

Pests can also spread disease from plant to plant, and eaten leaves mean less photosynthesis.

subsections.heading: Pesticides versus biological control
subsections.html:
Spec 5.8 · 2022 Edexcel Jan 1B Q10(a) · 2024 Y11 mock Q2

Pesticides are fast but unselective; biological control is specific and self-sustaining but slow.

FeaturePesticidesBiological control
What it isChemicals that kill the pestIntroducing a natural predator of the pest
SpeedFast, kills most of the pest quicklySlow to take effect
Effect on other speciesMay kill harmless or useful species too, such as beesSpecific — targets the pest
PersistenceCan accumulate along food chains, poisoning predatorsDoes not accumulate
RepetitionMust be reappliedPredator population is self-sustaining
ResistancePests can become resistantResistance does not develop
RiskPollutes soil and waterThe predator may become a pest itself, or eat other species

Biological control reduces the pest population rather than eliminating it — some pests must remain or the predator would have no food. That point is worth a mark on its own and is often missed.

subsections.heading: Pesticides in food chains, and resistance
subsections.html:
Spec 5.8 · 2023 Edexcel 1B Q2(b) · 2024 Y11 mock Q2(d)

A persistent pesticide builds up along a food chain, and pests that survive it pass on their resistance.

Build-up: the pesticide is not broken down or excreted. Each animal eats many from the level below, so the concentration increases at each trophic level. Top predators get the highest dose. Even if they survive, killing one population changes the rest of the web — fewer prey for the animals above, less predation on the ones below.

Resistance is natural selection:

  1. A mutation makes a few pests resistant.
  2. The pesticide kills the others; the resistant ones survive.
  3. They reproduce and pass on the allele for resistance.
  4. Over generations, most of the population is resistant, and the pesticide stops working.

subsections.heading: Reading a pest-control graph
subsections.html:
2024 Y11 mock Q2 · 2022 Edexcel Jan 1B Q10(c)

Compare each treatment with the untreated control, then describe what happens over time.

In the fire-ant question, three plots were followed for a year: untreated, pesticide, and phorid flies (a parasite of the ants). The scheme's marks:

  • The untreated plot is the control — ant numbers increase.
  • Both treatments cut numbers at first.
  • With pesticide, numbers recover after about six months; with phorid flies they level off low.
  • So biological control is long-term; the pesticide wears off, or the ants became resistant by natural selection.

When judging a study, also ask how valid it is: one larva tested, no repeats, or a lab instead of a field all weaken the conclusion.

subsections.heading: Yoghurt
subsections.html:
Spec 5.3 · 2024 Edexcel 1B Q3 · 2023 Y11 mock Q3 · 2022 Edexcel Jan 1B Q5

Lactobacillus respires anaerobically, turning lactose in milk into lactic acid, which thickens and preserves it.

  1. Equipment is sterilised.
  2. Milk is pasteurised — heated to about 85–95 °C — to kill unwanted microorganisms.
  3. It is cooled to about 40–45 °C, the optimum for the bacteria.
  4. It is inoculated with Lactobacillus bacteria and kept warm for several hours.
  5. The bacteria respire anaerobically, converting the sugar lactose into lactic acid.
  6. The acid lowers the pH, so the milk proteins coagulate — the milk thickens into yoghurt.

The acid also preserves the yoghurt by stopping other microorganisms growing. Two real papers asked what happens with less oxygen: there is more anaerobic respiration, so acid is made and the acidity rises faster.

subsections.heading: The industrial fermenter — why each condition
subsections.html:
Spec 5.4

A fermenter grows microorganisms on a large scale, and every feature keeps them growing as fast as possible.

FeatureWhy
Aseptic precautionsSterilising the vessel prevents contamination by unwanted microbes that would compete for nutrients or spoil the product
NutrientsSupply the raw materials for growth and respiration
Optimum temperatureFast enzyme activity without denaturing the enzymes
Water jacket / coolingRespiration releases heat; without cooling the temperature would rise and denature the enzymes
Optimum pHEnzymes work fastest and do not denature
OxygenationAir is bubbled in for aerobic respiration, which releases more energy for growth
AgitationA paddle stirs the mixture so microorganisms stay in contact with nutrients and oxygen, and heat is spread evenly

The cooling jacket is the one to understand rather than memorise: the microorganisms are respiring, respiration releases heat, and that heat would build up and denature their own enzymes. It is there to remove heat, not to add it.

subsections.heading: The fermenter — how each condition is controlled
subsections.html:
2023 Edexcel 1B Q8(d)(i)

For "how is it controlled", pair each condition with the part that controls it.

ConditionControlled by
TemperatureA temperature probe and a cold-water jacket
pHA pH probe, with acid or alkali added through an inlet
OxygenSterile air bubbled in through an air inlet (sparger)
MixingA motor-driven stirrer with paddles
No contaminationVessel steam-cleaned before use; incoming air passed through a filter

The 2023 question gave four marks for two conditions: one mark for the part, one for why it matters.

subsections.heading: Fish farming
subsections.html:
2022 Edexcel Jan 2B Q4

Fish farms produce protein-rich food by controlling what the fish eat, where they live and how they breed.

  • Water quality — waste food and faeces are removed, so decomposers do not use up the oxygen.
  • Predation — nets keep out predators, and different sizes or species are kept apart so they do not eat each other.
  • Disease — fish are kept at a sensible density and treated, as disease spreads fast in crowded tanks.
  • Feeding — the right food, in the right amount, at the right times, so little is wasted.
  • Selective breeding — choose fish that grow quickly, breed them, choose the fastest-growing offspring, and repeat over many generations, so the alleles for fast growth are passed on.

The real scheme wanted "grow quickly", not just "large" or "with the desired characteristics".

The sentences behind most of the marks

Yield: name the limiting factor removed → more photosynthesis → more glucose → more growth → higher yield. "The plants grow better" earns nothing on its own.

Yoghurt: Lactobacillus → anaerobic respiration → lactose to lactic acid → pH falls → proteins coagulate.

Fermenter: the cooling jacket removes heat from respiration so the enzymes do not denature.

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording
YieldThe amount of crop produced from a given area
FertiliserA substance supplying mineral ions needed for plant growth
PestAn organism that damages or eats a crop, reducing yield
PesticideA chemical used to kill pests
Biological controlControlling a pest by introducing a natural predator (or parasite) of it
Aseptic precautionsSteps taken to prevent contamination by unwanted microorganisms
PasteurisationHeating milk to kill microorganisms before the culture is added
LactobacillusThe bacterium that converts lactose to lactic acid in yoghurt-making
Selective breedingChoosing organisms with a desired characteristic to breed, over many generations

questions.promptHtml: A grower burns a paraffin heater in a glasshouse. Give two ways this increases the tomato yield.
questions.answerHtml:
Heat: it raises the temperature, increasing the rate of photosynthesis and of the enzymes controlling it, up to the optimum.

Carbon dioxide: burning paraffin releases CO₂, which is a raw material for photosynthesis and is often the limiting factor in a sealed glasshouse.

Both increase the rate of photosynthesis, so more glucose is made, more is converted to starch and cellulose for growth, and the yield rises.

The elegance of the paraffin heater is that one device removes two limiting factors at once.

questions.promptHtml: A farmer uses a pesticide and finds that bird populations nearby fall sharply, even though birds are not pests. Explain.
questions.answerHtml:
The pesticide is persistent — it does not break down quickly, so it stays in the bodies of the organisms that absorb it.

It passes along the food chain as each organism eats many of the level below, so the concentration accumulates and increases at each trophic level.

Birds are near the top of the chain, so they receive the highest dose, which poisons them. Their food supply may also have been reduced if the pesticide killed the insects they eat.

questions.promptHtml: Why does biological control never completely remove a pest, and why is that acceptable to a farmer?
questions.answerHtml:
The predator depends on the pest as its food source. If it ate every pest it would starve and its own population would collapse, allowing the pest to return.

Instead the two populations settle into a predator–prey cycle, with the pest held at a low level.

That is acceptable because the farmer only needs the pest population low enough that crop damage is small. The advantage over pesticides is that the control is self-sustaining — no repeated application, no resistance, and no harm to other species.

questions.promptHtml: Explain why an industrial fermenter needs a cooling jacket rather than a heater.
questions.answerHtml:
The microorganisms inside are respiring, and respiration releases heat to the surroundings. In a large vessel with billions of organisms, that heat builds up quickly.

If the temperature rose above the optimum, the microorganisms' enzymes would denature — their active sites would change shape — and growth would stop.

The cooling jacket removes the excess heat to hold the temperature at the optimum. The vessel may be warmed at the start, but once the culture is growing the problem is always too much heat, not too little.

questions.promptHtml: Describe how milk is turned into yoghurt, and explain why the yoghurt keeps longer than the milk did.
questions.answerHtml:
The equipment is sterilised and the milk is pasteurised to kill unwanted microorganisms, then cooled. Lactobacillus bacteria are added.

They respire anaerobically, converting the lactose in the milk into lactic acid. The acid lowers the pH, causing the milk proteins to coagulate and thicken the mixture into yoghurt.

Why it keeps: the low pH prevents the growth of other microorganisms, including the bacteria that would spoil the milk. The acid acts as a preservative.

questions.promptHtml: Scientists make yoghurt with normal oxygen and with reduced oxygen. The acidity rises faster with reduced oxygen. Why?
questions.answerHtml:
Lactic acid is only made by anaerobic respiration. With plenty of oxygen, the bacteria do more aerobic respiration, which makes carbon dioxide and water instead — no acid.

With less oxygen, more anaerobic respiration happens, so lactose is turned into lactic acid faster, and the acidity rises sooner.

questions.promptHtml: A pesticide and a parasitic fly both cut fire-ant numbers at first. Six months later, the pesticide plot has as many ants as before, but the fly plot does not. Explain.
questions.answerHtml:
Pesticide: it is applied once and then breaks down or washes away, so its effect wears off. Any ants that survived — possibly because they carry an allele for resistance — reproduce and the population recovers.

Flies: they are living. They reproduce as long as there are ants to use, so the control carries on by itself. The ant population is held low in a steady balance.

That is the "long-term" advantage of biological control that the mark scheme wanted.

questions.promptHtml: A grower doubles the carbon dioxide in a glasshouse and the yield rises. They double it again and the yield barely changes. Why?
questions.answerHtml:
At first, CO₂ was the limiting factor. More of it meant more photosynthesis, more glucose and more growth.

After the first increase, CO₂ is no longer limiting. Another factor — light intensity or temperature — now limits the rate, so extra CO₂ has no effect. It also costs money, so it is wasted.

To get more yield now, the grower must raise the factor that is limiting, such as adding lighting.

questions.promptHtml: Describe how a glasshouse can be used to increase crop yield. (3)
questions.answerHtml: The temperature can be kept higher / at the optimum 1; carbon dioxide concentration or light can be increased so they are no longer limiting 1; so the rate of photosynthesis increases, making more glucose for growth 1.

markScheme.point: The temperature can be kept higher / at the optimum ; carbon dioxide concentration or light can be increased so they are no longer limiting ; so the rate of photosynthesis increases, making more glucose for growth .

questions.promptHtml: Explain why adding nitrate fertiliser increases the yield of a wheat crop. (3)

markScheme.point: Nitrate ions are needed to make amino acids ; amino acids are used to make proteins ; proteins are needed for growth, so the plants grow larger and the yield increases .

questions.answerHtml: Lactobacillus 1; it converts lactose into lactic acid by anaerobic respiration 1; the acid lowers the pH, causing the milk proteins to coagulate and thicken 1.

markScheme.point: For aerobic respiration by the microorganisms ; which releases more energy than anaerobic respiration, so they grow and reproduce faster .
