modules.title: Carbon and Nitrogen Cycles
modules.standfirst: Year 10 content. Two cycles, and nearly every mark is for naming the right process or the right bacteria. Four kinds of microorganism live in the nitrogen cycle, and swapping any two of them loses the mark. Real Edexcel papers ask it as a labelled diagram, or hide it inside a passage about rivers, rainforests or fish farms.

subsections.html: Atoms are never used up. Carbon and nitrogen move between the air, living things and the soil, and the same atoms go round again and again. Microorganisms do most of the returning. Every question in this module is really asking: which process moves the atom from here to there?

subsections.heading: The carbon cycle — the processes
subsections.html:
Spec 4.10 · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1B Q3

Carbon moves between the air and living things by photosynthesis, respiration, feeding, decomposition and combustion. The spec names four of these — respiration, photosynthesis, decomposition and combustion — so learn those first.

ProcessWhat happens to carbon
PhotosynthesisPlants remove CO₂ from the air and make glucose
RespirationPlants, animals and decomposers return CO₂ to the air
FeedingCarbon compounds pass along the food chain as animals eat
DecompositionBacteria and fungi break down dead organisms and waste — and respire, releasing CO₂
CombustionBurning wood and fossil fuels returns CO₂ to the air
FossilisationDead matter that does not decay, under pressure over millions of years, becomes coal, oil and gas

In the air, carbon is in carbon dioxide. Inside living things it is in carbon compounds — carbohydrates, proteins and fats. Keep those two words apart and the arrows make sense.

subsections.heading: Photosynthesis — the only way out of the air
subsections.html:
Spec 4.10, 2.18 · links to module 2

Photosynthesis is the only process in the cycle that takes carbon dioxide out of the air.

Photosynthesis — carbon incarbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygenlight energy absorbed by chlorophyll · the carbon ends up in glucose, then starch, cellulose and proteins

Every other arrow puts carbon dioxide back. That one fact answers most "why does CO₂ rise" questions: less photosynthesis (deforestation) or more combustion.

✗ "Trees absorb carbon dioxide by respiration."
✗ "Plants only take carbon in."
✓ "Plants remove CO₂ by photosynthesis, but they also release CO₂ by respiration."

subsections.heading: Respiration — everyone does it
subsections.html:
Spec 4.10 · links to module 3 · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1B Q3(b)(ii)

Every living organism respires, all the time, and every one of them returns carbon dioxide to the air.

Aerobic respiration — carbon outglucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + waterplants, animals, bacteria and fungi · day and night

On a cycle diagram there is a respiration arrow from plants, from animals and from the decomposers. The one from the decomposers is the one students forget.

subsections.heading: Feeding — carbon along the food chain
subsections.html:
Spec 4.8, 4.10 · links to module 9

When an animal eats, carbon passes to it as carbon compounds, not as carbon dioxide.

  1. A plant makes glucose, then starch, cellulose, proteins and fats.
  2. A herbivore eats the plant and digests these into small molecules.
  3. It absorbs them and builds its own carbon compounds — or respires them, releasing CO₂.
  4. A carnivore eats the herbivore, and the same happens again.

Carbon that is not respired or eaten ends up in dead bodies, faeces and urine — which is where the decomposers come in.

subsections.heading: Decomposition — how decomposers return carbon
subsections.html:
Spec 4.10 · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1B Q3(c) · 2023 Edexcel 2B Q1(b)(ii)

Decomposers — bacteria and fungi — release carbon dioxide because they respire the products of the dead matter they digest.

  1. Decomposers secrete enzymes onto dead organisms and waste.
  2. The enzymes digest large carbon compounds into small soluble molecules.
  3. The decomposers absorb these molecules.
  4. They use the glucose in respiration, which releases carbon dioxide into the air.

Decomposition is fastest when it is warm, moist and has plenty of oxygen, because the decomposers' enzymes work best and they can respire aerobically. pH matters too — enzymes have an optimum pH.

Planning a decomposition investigation — the six marks (2022 Jan 1B Q3(d))

C — change the pH: add acid, alkali or buffers to give different pH values 1

O — same type, age and mass of organic material, e.g. leaves 1

R — repeat at each pH and calculate a mean 1

M1 — measure the loss in mass, or the carbon dioxide released (limewater or hydrogencarbonate indicator) 1

M2 — after a stated time, e.g. two weeks 1

S — keep the temperature, oxygen and water the same, and add the same decomposers 1

subsections.heading: Combustion, fossil fuels and locked-up carbon
subsections.html:
Spec 4.10 · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1B Q3(b)(i) · 2022 Edexcel 2B Q1(b)

When dead matter does not decompose, its carbon is locked away — until it is burned.

Waterlogged, acidic or oxygen-poor conditions stop decomposers. Over millions of years, under heat and pressure, the undecayed matter becomes coal, oil and natural gas. Combustion of these fossil fuels releases, in a few years, carbon that was stored for millions — which is why CO₂ in the air is rising (module 12).

The 2022 paper turned this round: plants that store carbon in a substance that decays slowly keep it out of the air for longer. The marks were:

  1. Plants take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis.
  2. The carbon is stored in a compound that is decomposed slowly.
  3. So less carbon dioxide is released by the respiration of decomposers.

subsections.heading: Reading a carbon-cycle diagram
subsections.html:
2022 Jan Edexcel 1B Q3(a)–(b)

Name each arrow by asking where it starts and where it ends.

Arrow goes from……toProcess
Air (CO₂)PlantsPhotosynthesis
Plants or animalsAir (CO₂)Respiration
PlantsAnimalsFeeding (eating)
Dead matter or wasteDecomposers, then airDecomposition, then respiration
Fossil fuels or a factoryAir (CO₂)Combustion

There is only ever one arrow going into plants from the air. If a question asks which arrow removes CO₂, it is that one.

subsections.heading: The nitrogen cycle — why plants need help
subsections.html:
Spec 4.11B, 2.22

Air is 78% nitrogen, but plants cannot use nitrogen gas — they must absorb nitrate ions from the soil.

N₂ is very unreactive. Plants need nitrogen to make amino acids, and so proteins (and DNA and chlorophyll). They take nitrate in through their root hair cells by active transport, because the concentration in the soil is usually lower than in the root. Animals get their nitrogen by eating proteins.

Organism or processConvertsNotes
Nitrogen-fixing bacteriaN₂ gas → nitrogen compounds (ammonium)In root nodules of legumes (peas, beans, clover) and free in soil
DecomposersProteins in dead matter, and urea → ammoniumBacteria and fungi
Nitrifying bacteriaAmmonium → nitrite → nitrateNeed oxygen — aerobic
Denitrifying bacteriaNitrate → N₂ gasAnaerobic — thrive in waterlogged soil
LightningN₂ → nitrogen oxides → nitrate in rainThe energy splits the N≡N bond. Not a spec point, but it appears on diagrams

subsections.heading: Nitrogen fixation and root nodules
subsections.html:
Spec 4.11B

Nitrogen-fixing bacteria are the only living route from nitrogen gas into the food chain.

Some live free in the soil. Others live in root nodules — swellings on the roots of legumes such as peas, beans and clover. It is a partnership: the bacteria give the plant nitrogen compounds for amino acids, and the plant gives the bacteria sugars from photosynthesis.

That is why legumes grow well in poor soil, and why a field is richer in nitrogen after a crop of clover.

subsections.heading: From dead matter to nitrate — decomposers and nitrifying bacteria
subsections.html:
Spec 4.11B · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2B Q5(b)(i) · 2023 Edexcel 2B Q1(c) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2B Q4(b)

Nitrogen in dead organisms reaches plants in two bacterial steps: decomposers make ammonium, then nitrifying bacteria turn ammonium into nitrate.

  1. A plant or animal dies, or an animal excretes urea or produces faeces.
  2. Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down the proteins and urea into ammonium compounds.
  3. Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium into nitrite, then nitrite into nitrate. This is nitrification, and it needs oxygen.
  4. Plant roots absorb the nitrate by active transport and use it to make amino acids and proteins.

The three-mark chain (2023 Jan 2B Q5(b)(i))

1. Decomposition by bacteria / fungi 1

2. Organic waste → ammonium (ammonification) 1

3. Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium to nitrite and nitrite to nitrate 1

"Ammonium to nitrate" with no bacteria named was ignored. Name the nitrifying bacteria, and mention nitrite if you can.

Fish farms use the same bacteria. Fish excrete ammonium, which is toxic to them; a filter full of nitrifying bacteria turns it into nitrite and then the much less harmful nitrate.

subsections.heading: Denitrifying bacteria and waterlogged soil
subsections.html:
Spec 4.11B

Nitrifying bacteria need oxygen; denitrifying bacteria work without it — so waterlogged soil loses its nitrate.

  1. Water fills the air spaces in the soil, so there is little oxygen.
  2. Nitrifying bacteria cannot respire aerobically, so they stop making nitrate.
  3. Denitrifying bacteria are anaerobic, so they thrive and turn nitrate into nitrogen gas, which escapes to the air.
  4. Less nitrate for the crop → fewer amino acids and proteins → stunted growth and yellow leaves.

✗ "Waterlogged soil drowns the bacteria."
✗ "Nitrifying bacteria turn nitrate into nitrogen."
✓ "No oxygen, so nitrifying bacteria stop, and denitrifying bacteria convert nitrate into nitrogen gas."

Say both halves. One bacterium stopping and the other speeding up are two separate marks.

subsections.heading: Farming with the nitrogen cycle
subsections.html:
Spec 4.11B · links to module 10

Farmers keep soil nitrate high by helping the nitrifying and nitrogen-fixing bacteria and hindering the denitrifying ones.

PracticeWhy it adds nitrate
PloughingLets air into the soil — helps nitrifying bacteria, hinders denitrifying bacteria
Draining waterlogged fieldsSame reason — oxygen back in the air spaces
Crop rotation with a legumeNitrogen-fixing bacteria in the root nodules add nitrogen compounds; the crop is ploughed back in
Manure or compostDecomposers turn its proteins into ammonium, then nitrifying bacteria make nitrate
Nitrate fertiliserAdds nitrate directly — but excess can leach into rivers (eutrophication, module 12)

The sentences behind most of the marks

Carbon: photosynthesis is the only way CO₂ leaves the air. Decomposers release CO₂ by respiration.

The four microbes, in order round the cycle: Fixing: N₂ in. Decomposers: protein → ammonium. Nitrifying: ammonium → nitrite → nitrate, needs oxygen. Denitrifying: nitrate → N₂ out, no oxygen.

questions.promptHtml: A leaf falls to the forest floor. Trace one carbon atom in it back into the atmosphere.
questions.answerHtml:
The carbon is in organic compounds such as cellulose. Decomposers — bacteria and fungi — secrete enzymes that break these down, and absorb the products.

The decomposers use the glucose in respiration, which releases the carbon as carbon dioxide into the air. Decomposition itself does not release CO₂ — the decomposers' respiration does.

questions.promptHtml: A field floods for several weeks. Afterwards the crop grows poorly. Explain, using the nitrogen cycle.
questions.answerHtml:
Waterlogged soil has no air spaces, so it lacks oxygen.

Nitrifying bacteria need oxygen, so they stop turning ammonium into nitrates. Denitrifying bacteria are anaerobic and thrive, converting the nitrates that remain into nitrogen gas.

Both changes mean less nitrate in the soil. The crop cannot make enough amino acids and proteins, so its growth is stunted.

questions.promptHtml: Why might a farmer plant clover in a field one year and wheat the next?
questions.answerHtml:
Clover is a legume with nitrogen-fixing bacteria in its root nodules. They convert nitrogen gas into nitrogen compounds, enriching the soil.

When the clover is ploughed in, decomposers and nitrifying bacteria turn its proteins into nitrates. The wheat then has plenty of nitrate for amino acids and proteins, so less fertiliser is needed.

questions.promptHtml: Name the only process in the carbon cycle that removes CO₂ from the air, and explain why cutting down rainforest raises CO₂ in two ways.
questions.answerHtml:
Photosynthesis is the only process that removes CO₂.

Deforestation raises CO₂ because fewer trees means less photosynthesis, so less is removed; and the trees are usually burned or left to decompose, which releases the carbon stored in them.

questions.promptHtml: Leaves decompose within months on a warm, damp forest floor, but can last thousands of years in a peat bog. Explain the difference.
questions.answerHtml:
Decomposers need oxygen to respire aerobically, water, and a suitable temperature and pH for their enzymes.

A bog is waterlogged, so there is almost no oxygen, and it is acidic. Few decomposers survive and their enzymes work slowly, so the dead matter is not broken down. Its carbon stays locked away instead of returning to the air as CO₂. Over millions of years, that is how fossil fuels formed.

questions.promptHtml: A fish tank filter is full of bacteria. Why do new tanks often kill fish in the first few weeks?
questions.answerHtml:
Fish excrete ammonium, which is toxic. In an established tank, nitrifying bacteria in the filter convert ammonium into nitrite and then into nitrate, which is far less harmful.

In a new tank the population of nitrifying bacteria is still small, so ammonium builds up faster than they can convert it. The filter also needs oxygen flowing through it, because nitrifying bacteria are aerobic.

questions.promptHtml: Why do plants take in nitrate by active transport rather than diffusion, and what would happen to a root with no oxygen?
questions.answerHtml:
The concentration of nitrate in the soil water is usually lower than inside the root hair cells. Diffusion only moves particles down a gradient, so it would carry nitrate out. Active transport moves it against the concentration gradient, using energy from respiration.

Without oxygen the root cells cannot respire aerobically, so there is too little energy for active transport. Nitrate uptake falls — a second reason waterlogged plants struggle.

questions.promptHtml: Follow one nitrogen atom from the air, into a pea plant, into a rabbit, and back to the air.
questions.answerHtml:
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in the pea's root nodules turn N₂ into nitrogen compounds. The pea uses them to make amino acids and proteins.

The rabbit eats the pea, digests the proteins to amino acids and builds its own proteins. Excess is excreted as urea. When the rabbit dies, decomposers turn its proteins into ammonium, and nitrifying bacteria turn that into nitrate.

In waterlogged soil, denitrifying bacteria turn the nitrate into nitrogen gas, which returns to the air.

modules.title: Human Impacts on the Environment
modules.standfirst: Year 10 content. Pollution, the greenhouse effect, eutrophication and deforestation. Edexcel loves this topic as a long data or passage question worth 10 or more marks. Eutrophication is a chain of six steps, and the marks go to people who get the bacteria using up the oxygen — not the algae.

subsections.html: Humans add gases to the air, minerals and sewage to the water, and cut down forests. Every question here wants the same shape of answer: what the pollutant is, what it does, and the biological consequence — which organisms are harmed, and why.

subsections.heading: Sulfur dioxide and acid rain
subsections.html:
Spec 4.12 · 2024 Edexcel 2B Q1(c)(i) · 2023 Y11 mock Q4

Sulfur dioxide from burning fossil fuels dissolves in rain to make acid rain, which kills organisms in lakes and damages trees.

  1. Coal and oil contain sulfur. Burning them releases sulfur dioxide (volcanoes release it naturally).
  2. It dissolves in water in clouds, forming acid rain.
  3. Acid rain falls into lakes and rivers and lowers the pH. Fish, their eggs and invertebrates die — whole food chains collapse.
  4. It falls on forests: it damages leaves and leaches minerals out of the soil, so trees grow poorly and die.

It also corrodes limestone buildings — but that is chemistry. In biology, give the biological consequence.

subsections.heading: Carbon monoxide
subsections.html:
Spec 4.12 · 2023 Y11 mock Q4 · 2024 Edexcel 2B Q4(c)

Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin in red blood cells, so the blood carries less oxygen.

  • Source: incomplete combustion of fuels — not enough oxygen. Car exhausts, faulty gas boilers, and cigarette smoke.
  • Effect: it binds to haemoglobin more strongly than oxygen does, and does not let go.
  • Consequence: less oxygen reaches the cells, so less aerobic respiration and less energy released. Drowsiness, then unconsciousness and death.

The 2024 paper linked it to pregnancy: smoking mothers had smaller babies, because carbon monoxide in the smoke means less oxygen reaches the fetus through the placenta (module 13).

✗ "Carbon monoxide poisons you."
✗ "Carbon monoxide is a greenhouse gas."
✓ "Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin, reducing the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood."

subsections.heading: The greenhouse effect
subsections.html:
Spec 4.15 · 2024 Edexcel 1B Q5(a)(ii)

Greenhouse gases absorb the infrared radiation given off by the warm Earth and re-radiate it, trapping heat in the atmosphere.

  1. Radiation from the Sun passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth's surface.
  2. The warm Earth gives off infrared (long-wave) radiation.
  3. Greenhouse gases absorb some of this infrared and re-radiate it, some back towards Earth.
  4. So heat is trapped and the Earth stays warmer than it would otherwise be.

That is natural and necessary — without it Earth would be too cold for most life. The problem is the enhanced greenhouse effect: extra gases from human activity trap more heat, causing global warming.

"Explain the greenhouse effect" — two marks (2024 1B Q5(a)(ii))

1. Infrared radiation is absorbed by greenhouse gases / heat is trapped 1

2. So the temperature of the Earth increases 1

"It makes a hole in the ozone layer" is a different problem, and scores nothing.

subsections.heading: Greenhouse gases and where they come from
subsections.html:
Spec 4.13, 4.14 · 2024 Edexcel 1B Q5(a)(i) · 2022 Edexcel 2B Q1(a)(i)

The five greenhouse gases on the spec are carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, CFCs and water vapour. Oxygen and carbon monoxide are not greenhouse gases.

GasMain human source
Carbon dioxideBurning fossil fuels; deforestation
MethaneCattle (digestion); rice paddy fields; landfill; decaying waste
Nitrous oxideNitrogen fertilisers broken down by soil bacteria; vehicle engines
CFCsOld refrigerators and aerosols — now banned
Water vapourEvaporation — mostly natural

The 2024 multiple choice listed CFCs, methane, oxygen and water vapour. The answer was all but oxygen — students who forgot water vapour chose wrongly.

subsections.heading: Global warming and its consequences
subsections.html:
Spec 4.15 · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2B Q5(a)(ii) · 2022 Edexcel 2B Q1(a)(iii)

More greenhouse gas traps more heat, raising the Earth's average temperature — and every mark is for a biological consequence of that.

  • Ice caps and glaciers melt → sea levels rise → flooding of low-lying land and habitat loss
  • Climate change — more extreme weather, droughts, storms, desertification
  • Species migrate or change distribution; some become extinct; food chains are disrupted
  • Pests and diseases spread into new areas
  • Crop yields change; some regions can no longer grow the same crops
  • Oceans absorb more CO₂ and become more acidic → coral bleaching

✗ "Global warming makes the Earth hotter." — that is the definition, not a consequence.
✓ "Ice caps melt, so sea levels rise, flooding habitats." · "Species migrate or become extinct."

subsections.heading: Reading emissions and deforestation data
subsections.html:
2024 Edexcel 1B Q5(b) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2B Q5(a)(i)

Data questions on this topic are worth up to eight marks, and the calculations are always one of two types.

Percentage from a graphpercentage = (value for one source ÷ total of all sources) × 1002024: energy 110 of a total 453 million tonnes → 24%
Rate of changerate = change in value ÷ time taken2023 Jan: rainforest fell by 1200 over 25 years → 48 per year · give the units

For a "describe and explain the trend" question, quote numbers with years, then give a reason for each change: less coal burned for energy (more wind and solar), fewer cattle so less methane, more cars then more electric cars.

equations.name: Percentage from a graph
equations.formula: percentage = (value for one source ÷ total of all sources) × 100

equations.name: Rate of change
equations.formula: rate = change in value ÷ time taken

subsections.heading: Water pollution by sewage
subsections.html:
Spec 4.16

Untreated sewage is food for bacteria, and the bacteria's respiration uses up the oxygen in the water.

  1. Raw sewage enters a river. It contains organic matter and minerals such as nitrate and phosphate.
  2. Bacteria feed on the organic matter and multiply rapidly.
  3. They respire aerobically, using up the dissolved oxygen.
  4. Fish and other animals cannot respire and die — or move away.
  5. The minerals also cause eutrophication downstream. Sewage may also carry pathogens that spread disease.

So sewage can strip the oxygen even without an algal bloom: the bacteria have food from day one.

subsections.heading: Eutrophication — the chain
subsections.html:
Spec 4.17 · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2B Q5(b)(iii) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2B Q4(c)

Eutrophication is excess minerals in water causing an algal bloom, whose decay by bacteria uses up the oxygen. Fertiliser or sewage gets into a river or lake. Then:

  1. Excess nitrates and phosphates are leached from the fields into the water.
  2. Algae grow rapidly — an algal bloom covers the surface.
  3. The bloom blocks light, so plants below cannot photosynthesise and die.
  4. The algae also die.
  5. Decomposers (bacteria) feed on the dead plants and algae and multiply.
  6. The bacteria respire aerobically, using up the oxygen in the water — so fish and other animals die.

The four-mark biodiversity answer (2023 Jan 2B Q5(b)(iii))

1. Nitrate leached / run-off into the river 1

2. Algae grow and block light, so plants die 1

3. Dead matter decomposed; bacterial respiration means less oxygen 1

4. Fish and other species die — fewer species, lower biodiversity 1

subsections.heading: Why it is the bacteria, not the algae
subsections.html:
Spec 4.17

The oxygen is used up by the huge population of decomposing bacteria, not by the algae.

While they are alive, algae photosynthesise and give off oxygen at the surface. The crash comes later: dead algae and dead plants are food for bacteria, the bacteria multiply enormously, and their respiration strips the dissolved oxygen.

✗ "The algae use up all the oxygen."
✗ "The fish die because there is no light."
✓ "Bacteria decompose the dead plants and algae; their aerobic respiration uses up the oxygen, so fish cannot respire."

The 2022 fish-farm question turned this round. Crabs and lobsters eat waste food and faeces, so less decomposition, fewer bacteria and less bacterial respiration — more oxygen stays in the water. Seaweed absorbs the nitrate, so there is no algal bloom.

subsections.heading: Deforestation — soil, water and minerals
subsections.html:
Spec 4.18B · 2023 Edexcel 2B Q1(b)(i)

Without trees, nothing holds the soil or takes up its minerals and water.

EffectWhy
Soil erosionNo roots holding the soil, and no canopy breaking the rain, so soil washes away
LeachingMinerals wash out of the soil into rivers instead of being taken up by trees — soil becomes infertile, rivers become eutrophic
Disturbed evapotranspirationLess transpiration, so less water vapour, fewer clouds and less rain locally; more flooding, as water runs straight off
Loss of biodiversityHabitats destroyed; species lose food and shelter

The 2023 dinoflagellate passage wanted this chain: trees removed → soil erosion → minerals such as nitrates and magnesium washed into the sea → the algae get nitrate for amino acids and magnesium for chlorophyll → population explodes. Match each mineral to its use.

subsections.heading: Deforestation — the carbon cycle and the air
subsections.html:
Spec 4.18B, 4.10 · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2B Q5(a)

Deforestation raises carbon dioxide in two ways: less photosynthesis, and the carbon in the trees is released.

  1. Fewer trees → less photosynthesis → less CO₂ removed from the air.
  2. The trees are burned (combustion) or left to decompose (decomposers respire) → their stored carbon is released as CO₂.
  3. More CO₂ → enhanced greenhouse effect → global warming.

It also upsets the balance of atmospheric gases: less oxygen is released by photosynthesis. But the mark schemes want CO₂ up first — "less oxygen to breathe" is not the point.

subsections.heading: Reducing the damage — evaluating a solution
subsections.html:
2023 Y11 mock Q4(b) · 2023 Edexcel 2B Q1(e)

"Evaluate" or "discuss" questions want both sides, each with a named gas and a biological consequence.

SolutionBenefitDrawback
Anaerobic digester, burning biogas instead of coalLess CO₂ and methane → less greenhouse effect; less carbon monoxide → less effect on haemoglobinMay release more sulfur dioxide → acid rain, killing fish and trees
Living (photosynthetic) street lightsThey take in CO₂ by photosynthesis; less electricity, so less fossil fuel burned → less CO₂ and SO₂, so less global warming and acid rainDim light; the organisms must be kept alive
Less fertiliser, or buffer strips of plants by riversLess nitrate leached → no algal bloomLower crop yield
ReforestationMore photosynthesis; roots stop erosionLand not available for farming

The mock scheme gave its five marks for: less CO₂ and methane 1, less carbon monoxide 1, less greenhouse effect with a consequence 1, less damage to haemoglobin 1, but more sulfur dioxide and acid rain 1.

The sentences behind most of the marks

Eutrophication: nitrates → algal bloom → blocks light → plants die → bacteria decompose them → bacteria respire → oxygen used up → fish die.

Greenhouse effect: greenhouse gases absorb infrared from the Earth → heat trapped → temperature rises → ice melts, sea levels rise, habitats lost.

Pollutants: SO₂ → acid rain → fish and trees die. CO → binds haemoglobin → less oxygen carried.

questions.promptHtml: After heavy rain, fish in a lake next to a farm die. Explain the full sequence of events.
questions.answerHtml:
Rain washes fertiliser from the fields into the lake, adding nitrates and phosphates. Algae grow rapidly and form a bloom on the surface.

The bloom blocks light from plants lower down, which cannot photosynthesise and die. Bacteria decompose the dead plants and algae and multiply rapidly.

The bacteria respire aerobically, using up the dissolved oxygen. Without oxygen, fish cannot respire and they die.

questions.promptHtml: A town switches from coal power to an anaerobic digester that burns biogas. Give one environmental benefit and one drawback.
questions.answerHtml:
Benefit: less carbon dioxide and methane released overall, so less contribution to the greenhouse effect and global warming — and less carbon monoxide, so less effect on oxygen transport in the blood.

Drawback: the Year 11 mock accepted that digesters may release more sulfur dioxide, causing acid rain that kills fish and damages trees.

The mark scheme wanted a discussion on both sides with a biological consequence for each — a gas named with no effect scores little.

questions.promptHtml: Why is the greenhouse effect necessary for life, and why is it now a problem?
questions.answerHtml:
Without greenhouse gases, the infrared radiated by Earth would escape to space and the planet would be far too cold for most life.

Human activity has increased the concentration of those gases, so more infrared is trapped. This enhanced greenhouse effect raises the average temperature, causing climate change, rising sea levels and habitat loss.

questions.promptHtml: Oxygen levels in a eutrophic lake are often high in the afternoon while the algae are alive, then crash a few weeks later. Why?
questions.answerHtml:
While alive, the algae photosynthesise and release oxygen, so the surface water is well oxygenated in daylight.

When the algae and the shaded plants die, they become food for bacteria. The bacterial population grows enormously, and their aerobic respiration uses up the dissolved oxygen faster than it can be replaced. That is when the fish die — proof that the bacteria, not the living algae, remove the oxygen.

questions.promptHtml: A pregnant woman smokes. Explain why her baby is likely to have a lower birth mass.
questions.answerHtml:
Cigarette smoke contains carbon monoxide. It binds to haemoglobin in the mother's red blood cells, so her blood carries less oxygen.

Less oxygen diffuses across the placenta to the fetus. The fetus's cells carry out less aerobic respiration, releasing less energy for growth, so it grows more slowly. This was the data in 2024 Edexcel 2B Q4.

questions.promptHtml: Cutting down a rainforest makes the soil infertile within a few years. Explain why.
questions.answerHtml:
In a forest, mineral ions released by decomposers are taken up quickly by tree roots. The canopy also breaks the force of the rain.

Without trees, heavy rain hits bare ground. Soil erosion removes the fertile topsoil, and leaching washes the minerals down and out into rivers. No roots are there to absorb them, and no leaf litter replaces them. The remaining soil has too few minerals for crops.

questions.promptHtml: Both burning fossil fuels and cutting down forests raise atmospheric CO₂. Explain why deforestation counts twice.
questions.answerHtml:
Burning fossil fuels only adds carbon dioxide.

Deforestation adds CO₂ — the trees are burned or decomposed, releasing their stored carbon — and removes a sink: fewer trees means less photosynthesis, so less CO₂ is taken out of the air every year afterwards.

questions.promptHtml: Untreated sewage kills fish in a river even when no algal bloom forms. How?
questions.answerHtml:
Sewage is itself organic matter — food for bacteria. The bacteria multiply rapidly and respire aerobically, using up the dissolved oxygen directly.

So the oxygen falls without the algae-and-light stage. Fish cannot get enough oxygen for respiration and die. The minerals in the sewage may still cause eutrophication further downstream.

modules.title: Cell Division and Human Reproduction
modules.standfirst: Year 11. Mitosis against meiosis is the comparison that always comes up, and the menstrual cycle needs four hormones kept straight. The January 2024 mock used a karyotype with a missing chromosome — and so did a real Edexcel paper a year earlier, almost word for word.

subsections.html: Every human starts as one cell. Two kinds of cell division get us there: meiosis makes the sex cells, and mitosis turns the fertilised egg into a body. The rest of the module is the organs and hormones that bring the sex cells together and look after the embryo.

subsections.heading: Sexual and asexual reproduction
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1 · 2024 Edexcel 1B Q2(d)

Sexual reproduction joins gametes from two parents, so the offspring vary; asexual reproduction uses one parent and mitosis, so the offspring are clones.

SexualAsexual
ParentsTwoOne
GametesYes — made by meiosisNo gametes, no meiosis
FertilisationYes — gametes fuseNo fusion
OffspringGenetically variedGenetically identical (clones)
SpeedSlowerFaster
AdvantageVariation — a species can survive environmental change or diseaseFast; no mate needed; good characteristics kept

For "give three differences", the 2024 scheme accepted any three rows — as long as each compares both types.

subsections.heading: Fertilisation and the zygote
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2

Fertilisation is the fusion of a male and a female gamete nucleus to make a zygote, which divides by mitosis to become an embryo.

  1. A haploid sperm (23 chromosomes) meets a haploid egg (23) in the oviduct.
  2. The nuclei fuse, making a diploid zygote (46).
  3. The zygote divides by mitosis again and again, making a ball of cells — the embryo.
  4. The embryo moves down to the uterus and implants in the thick lining.

subsections.heading: Chromosomes — diploid and haploid
subsections.html:
Spec 3.32

Human body cells are diploid, with 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs; gametes are haploid, with 23 — one from each pair.

One chromosome of each pair came from the mother, one from the father. Each chromosome is a long molecule of DNA carrying many genes (module 15). Pair 23 is the sex chromosomes: XX in a female, XY in a male.

Chromosome numbers in humansgamete (23) + gamete (23) → zygote (46)haploid + haploid → diploid · this is why gametes must have half the number

subsections.heading: Mitosis — two identical cells
subsections.html:
Spec 3.28, 3.29 · 2024 Y11 mock Q6(a)(ii)

Mitosis makes two diploid daughter cells that are genetically identical to the parent cell and to each other.

  1. Each chromosome is copied — which is why chromosomes look like an X just before division.
  2. The copied chromosomes line up across the middle of the cell.
  3. The two copies of each chromosome are pulled apart, one to each end.
  4. Two new nuclei form, and the cell divides into two identical cells.

Mitosis is used for growth, repair, cloning and asexual reproduction. White blood cells, skin cells and a growing embryo are all made by mitosis.

subsections.heading: Meiosis — four different gametes
subsections.html:
Spec 3.30

Meiosis makes four haploid cells, each genetically different — the gametes.

MitosisMeiosis
PurposeGrowth, repair, cloning, asexual reproductionMaking gametes
Where in humansAll body cellsTestes and ovaries only
DivisionsOneTwo
Cells madeTwoFour
Chromosome numberDiploid (46) — same as parentHaploid (23) — half
GeneticallyIdentical to parent and each otherDifferent from each other

✗ "Meiosis makes two cells." · ✗ "Meiosis makes identical cells."
✓ "Meiosis makes four, genetically different, haploid cells."

subsections.heading: Why meiosis and fertilisation give variation
subsections.html:
Spec 3.31

Meiosis shuffles the chromosomes into every gamete differently, and random fertilisation means any sperm can meet any egg.

  1. In meiosis, the pairs of chromosomes separate randomly, so each gamete gets a different mix of maternal and paternal chromosomes.
  2. So every sperm and every egg is genetically different.
  3. Random fertilisation: which sperm fuses with which egg is down to chance.
  4. So every zygote has a new combination of alleles — which is why siblings differ.

subsections.heading: Karyotypes and the sex chromosomes
subsections.html:
Spec 3.25, 3.32 · 2024 Y11 mock Q6 · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1B Q5

A karyotype is a photograph of a cell's chromosomes arranged in pairs — so it needs a cell with a nucleus.

  • Red blood cells cannot be used: they have no nucleus, so no chromosomes.
  • White blood cells are used: they have a nucleus, and they are made by mitosis, so they show the person's full diploid set.
  • A male karyotype has a Y chromosome — pair 23 is one large (X) and one small (Y).

The 45-chromosome karyotype — the mark points (2023 Jan 1B Q5(b), 2024 mock Q6(b))

1. 45 chromosomes instead of 46 — only one in pair 23 1

2. Only one X, no Y — so the person is female 1

3. Ovaries do not develop — less oestrogen, no normal puberty or secondary sexual characteristics 1

4. Cannot produce eggs — infertile 1

Cause: the sex chromosomes failed to separate in meiosis, so one gamete had no sex chromosome 1

This is Turner syndrome. The name is not needed — the reasoning is.

subsections.heading: The male reproductive system
subsections.html:
Spec 3.8

The male system makes sperm, keeps them alive in fluid, and delivers them into the vagina.

StructureJob
TestesMake sperm by meiosis, and the hormone testosterone
ScrotumHolds the testes outside the body, where it is slightly cooler — better for sperm production
Sperm ductCarries sperm from the testes to the urethra
Glands (prostate, seminal vesicles)Add fluid with nutrients, making semen — sperm can swim in it
UrethraCarries semen or urine out through the penis — never both at once
PenisBecomes erect to deliver semen into the vagina

subsections.heading: The female reproductive system
subsections.html:
Spec 3.8

The female system releases eggs, provides the place for fertilisation, and houses the developing baby.

StructureJob
OvariesContain eggs; release one each month; make oestrogen and progesterone
OviductCarries the egg to the uterus (cilia and muscle); site of fertilisation
UterusMuscular wall; thick lining where the embryo implants and develops
CervixRing of muscle at the base of the uterus; holds the baby in until birth
VaginaWhere sperm are deposited; the birth canal

✗ "Fertilisation happens in the uterus."
✓ "Fertilisation happens in the oviduct; the embryo implants in the uterus."

subsections.heading: Puberty — oestrogen and testosterone
subsections.html:
Spec 3.9

At puberty, testosterone from the testes and oestrogen from the ovaries cause the secondary sexual characteristics.

HormoneMade bySecondary sexual characteristics
TestosteroneTestesDeeper voice; facial and body hair; muscles develop; penis and testes grow; sperm production starts
OestrogenOvariesBreasts develop; hips widen; body hair; menstrual cycle starts

Pubic and underarm hair appears in both. For a mark, name a characteristic that belongs to one sex.

subsections.heading: The menstrual cycle — four hormones
subsections.html:
Spec 3.10B · 2023 Edexcel 2B Q5(a) · 2024 Edexcel 2B Q4(a)

Two hormones from the pituitary (FSH, LH) control the ovary; two from the ovary (oestrogen, progesterone) control the uterus lining.

HormoneMade byDoes
FSHPituitary glandCauses an egg (follicle) to mature in the ovary; stimulates oestrogen release
OestrogenOvaryBuilds up (repairs) the uterus lining; stimulates LH release
LHPituitary glandTriggers ovulation — egg release, about day 14; stimulates progesterone release
ProgesteroneOvaryMaintains the lining; inhibits FSH and LH
  1. Days 1–5: the lining breaks down and is lost — menstruation.
  2. FSH makes an egg mature and the ovary release oestrogen.
  3. Oestrogen builds up the lining and triggers a surge of LH.
  4. LH causes ovulation at about day 14. The empty follicle (corpus luteum) makes progesterone.
  5. Progesterone maintains the lining and stops FSH and LH, so no more eggs mature.
  6. No fertilisation → progesterone falls → the lining breaks down → the cycle restarts.

"Describe the roles of FSH and LH" — four marks (2023 2B Q5(a)(iii))

1. FSH makes eggs / follicles mature 1

2. FSH stimulates oestrogen release 1

3. LH causes ovulation / egg release 1

4. LH stimulates progesterone release 1

subsections.heading: Using the hormones — contraception data
subsections.html:
2023 Edexcel 2B Q5(b)

Hormonal contraceptives work because progesterone (often with oestrogen) inhibits FSH and LH, so no egg matures and none is released.

The mechanism links straight back to the cycle. What Edexcel actually asked was to evaluate methods from a data table — so here is the shape of the answer:

MethodAdvantageDisadvantage
Daily tabletNo doctor or needles; easy to stop if she wants childrenEasy to forget; less effective if vomiting
InjectionLasts weeks, so nothing to remember dailyNeeds a doctor; can be painful; slower for the cycle to return
ImplantLasts years; good for people far from a doctorNeeds a minor operation; risk of infection; hard to change your mind

Two overall points also scored: tablets were less effective in the data, and none protect against HIV.

subsections.heading: The placenta and amniotic fluid
subsections.html:
Spec 3.11, 3.12 · 2024 Edexcel 2B Q4(b)

The placenta lets food and oxygen diffuse from mother to fetus and waste diffuse back, without the two bloods mixing; the amniotic fluid cushions the fetus.

  • Into the fetus: glucose, amino acids, oxygen, also minerals, vitamins and antibodies.
  • Out of the fetus: carbon dioxide and urea.
  • Adapted by: a large surface area (villi), a thin barrier, and a good blood supply on both sides to keep the concentration gradients steep.
  • The umbilical cord joins the fetus to the placenta.
  • The amniotic fluid, inside the amnion, protects the fetus from bumps and physical damage.

Harmful substances cross too — carbon monoxide and nicotine from smoking, alcohol, some viruses. That is why the 2024 data showed smokers' babies gaining less mass (module 12).

Mitosis in four words, meiosis in four

Mitosis: two, identical, diploid, growth. Meiosis: four, different, haploid, gametes.

Cycle: FSH matures · oestrogen builds · LH releases · progesterone maintains.

questions.promptHtml: Why must gametes be made by meiosis and not mitosis?
questions.answerHtml:
At fertilisation two gametes fuse. If each had 46 chromosomes the zygote would have 92, doubling every generation.

Meiosis halves the number to 23, so fertilisation restores the diploid number of 46. It also makes every gamete genetically different, producing variation.

questions.promptHtml: A karyotype shows 45 chromosomes with only one sex chromosome, an X. What is the person's sex, and suggest how this happened.
questions.answerHtml:
Female — there is no Y chromosome. This is Turner syndrome.

The likely cause is that the sex chromosomes failed to separate properly during meiosis, so one gamete had no sex chromosome at all. When it fused with a normal gamete carrying an X, the zygote had 45.

From the mock scheme: the ovaries do not develop normally, so there is less oestrogen, puberty and secondary sexual characteristics are delayed, and she is usually infertile.

questions.promptHtml: Explain what happens to progesterone levels if an egg is fertilised, and why that matters.
questions.answerHtml:
Progesterone levels stay high (later the placenta makes it).

Progesterone maintains the uterus lining, so the embryo can stay implanted and develop. It also inhibits FSH and LH, so no more eggs mature or are released during pregnancy.

questions.promptHtml: Every cell in your body came from one zygote, yet they all have the same chromosomes. Which type of division made them, and why does that matter?
questions.answerHtml:
Mitosis. Each division copies every chromosome, then separates the copies so each new cell gets a full, identical set of 46.

That means every body cell carries the same genes as the zygote. Cells become different (muscle, nerve, skin) by using different genes — not by having different ones. It is also why a white blood cell can show your whole karyotype.

questions.promptHtml: Sperm carry either an X or a Y chromosome; eggs always carry an X. Use meiosis to explain why the chance of a boy is 50%.
questions.answerHtml:
A man's cells are XY. In meiosis the pair separates, so half his sperm get the X and half get the Y.

A woman's cells are XX, so every egg gets an X. Fertilisation is random: an X sperm gives XX (girl), a Y sperm gives XY (boy). With equal numbers of each sperm, the chance is 1 in 2 every time — the father's sperm decides.

questions.promptHtml: On a hormone graph, the oestrogen peak comes just before the LH peak, and ovulation follows. Explain the link.
questions.answerHtml:
FSH makes an egg mature, and the ovary releases rising amounts of oestrogen, which builds up the uterus lining.

High oestrogen stimulates the pituitary to release a surge of LH. The LH surge triggers ovulation. So the lining is ready just as the egg is released — timed so an embryo would have somewhere to implant.

questions.promptHtml: A contraceptive tablet contains progesterone. Use the menstrual cycle to explain why it prevents pregnancy.
questions.answerHtml:
Progesterone inhibits FSH and LH from the pituitary.

Without FSH, no egg matures. Without an LH surge, no ovulation happens. No egg is released, so there is nothing for a sperm to fertilise. It is the same reason no new eggs are released during pregnancy, when progesterone stays high.

questions.promptHtml: Why does the placenta need a large surface area and a good blood supply, when the two bloods never mix?
questions.answerHtml:
Everything crosses the placenta by diffusion (and some active transport). The rate of diffusion is faster with a large surface area, a thin barrier and a steep concentration gradient.

The mother's blood keeps bringing glucose and oxygen, and the fetal blood keeps carrying them away, so the gradients stay steep. Because the bloods do not mix, the fetus is protected from the mother's blood pressure and from many pathogens.

modules.title: Reproduction in Plants
modules.standfirst: Year 11. Both mocks had a flower question: label the parts, trace the pollen, compare insect and wind pollination. So do four of the last ten real Edexcel papers — usually as Question 1 or 2, where easy marks are meant to be banked. Pollination and fertilisation are different events, and the germination practical needs the right three conditions.

From the school's January 2023 mock scheme, on the conditions for germination:

"Light for photosynthesis does not score for germination — seeds do not photosynthesise yet."

The three conditions are water, oxygen and a suitable temperature — each with its reason: water activates enzymes, oxygen for respiration, warmth for enzyme action.

subsections.html: A flower is a plant's reproductive organ. Its job is to get pollen from one flower to another, then turn a fertilised ovule into a seed that can grow somewhere new. Plants can also skip all of that and clone themselves.

subsections.heading: Parts of a flower
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3 · 2024 Edexcel 1B Q2(a) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1B Q2(a)

The male parts (stamens) make pollen; the female parts (carpel) receive it and hold the ovules.

PartJob
AntherMakes pollen, which contains the male gamete
FilamentStalk holding the anther (anther + filament = stamen)
StigmaWhere pollen lands — and where the pollen grain germinates
StyleStalk the pollen tube grows down
OvaryContains the ovules; becomes the fruit
OvuleContains the female gamete; becomes the seed
PetalsAttract insects in insect-pollinated flowers
SepalsProtect the flower while it is a bud
NectaryMakes sugary nectar to attract insects

Stigma + style + ovary = the carpel. On a diagram, the stigma is at the top of the central column and the ovary is the swelling at the bottom.

subsections.heading: Insect-pollinated flowers
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3 · 2024 Y11 mock Q9(b) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1B Q1(b)

An insect-pollinated flower is built to attract an insect and make it brush against the anthers and stigma.

  • Large, brightly coloured, scented petals — attract insects
  • Nectary — sugary nectar as a reward
  • Anthers inside the flower, firmly attached — pollen rubs onto the insect as it reaches the nectar
  • Stigma inside the flower and sticky — pollen from the insect sticks to it
  • Pollen grains larger, sticky or spiky — cling to the insect's body

subsections.heading: Wind-pollinated flowers
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3 · 2022 Edexcel 1B Q5(a) · 2024 Edexcel 1B Q2(b)

A wind-pollinated flower is built to release pollen into the wind and catch pollen from it — so everything hangs outside.

FeatureInsect-pollinatedWind-pollinated (e.g. grass)
PetalsLarge, bright, scentedSmall, green or absent
NectarNectary presentNone
AnthersInside the flower, firmly attachedHang outside on long, loose filaments
StigmaInside, stickyOutside, large and feathery to catch pollen
PollenLarger, sticky or spiky, less of itSmall, light, smooth, huge amounts

"How are W, X and Y adapted for wind pollination?" (2022 1B Q5(a)(i))

Stigma: feathery, large surface area, outside the flower — to catch pollen 1

Anther: outside the flower, exposed — so wind can blow the pollen away 1

Filament: long and loose — the anther hangs out and shakes in the wind 1

✗ "Wind-pollinated flowers do not attract insects." — that is the definition, not a structural difference.
✓ Compare the structure: "Petals are small and green; the stigma is outside and feathery."

subsections.heading: Pollination — self and cross
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3 · 2023 Y11 mock Q8(a) · 2024 Y11 mock Q9(a)

Pollination is the transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma.

  • Self-pollination — anther to stigma of the same plant. Less variation.
  • Cross-pollination — anther of one plant to stigma of another plant of the same species. Gametes with different alleles fuse, so the offspring show more variation.

On a diagram, the pollination arrow goes from the anther to the stigma — not to the ovary, and not from the stigma back to the anther.

subsections.heading: From pollen to fertilisation
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2, 3.4 · 2024 Edexcel 1B Q2(a)(iii)

Fertilisation happens after pollination, when the male nucleus travels down a pollen tube and fuses with the female nucleus in the ovule.

  1. Pollen lands on the stigma.
  2. The pollen grain germinates and grows a pollen tube down through the style to the ovary.
  3. The tube enters an ovule (through a tiny hole, the micropyle).
  4. The male nucleus travels down the tube into the ovule.
  5. It fuses with the female nucleus — that fusion is fertilisation. A zygote forms.

✗ "Pollination is when the male and female gametes fuse."
✗ "Pollen grains germinate in the ovary."
✓ "Pollination is the transfer of pollen. The pollen grain germinates on the stigma. Fertilisation is the fusion of nuclei in the ovule."

subsections.heading: Seeds and fruits form
subsections.html:
Spec 3.4 · 2024 Y11 mock Q9(a)(iii)

After fertilisation, the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit.

BeforeAfter fertilisation
ZygoteDivides by mitosis into the embryo (young root and shoot)
OvuleThe seed — embryo, food store and a tough seed coat (testa)
OvaryThe fruit, containing the seeds
Petals, stamens, stigmaWither and fall off

One ovary can hold many ovules, so one fruit can hold many seeds — each from a separate pollen grain.

subsections.heading: Why seeds are spread
subsections.html:
2023 Y11 mock Q8(b), (d)–(g) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1B Q1(c)

Seeds that land far from the parent do not compete with it for light, water and mineral ions. Dispersal is not a named spec point, but both the mock and a real paper asked it.

  • Animals: bright, sweet fruit is eaten; the seeds pass through the gut undigested and are egested somewhere else. Hooked fruits catch on fur.
  • Wind: light seeds with wings or fluffy parachutes fall slowly, so the wind carries them further.

The mock also gave one mark for the downside: a seed that lands near the parent grows in conditions that already suited the parent.

subsections.heading: Conditions for germination
subsections.html:
Spec 3.5 · 2023 Y11 mock Q8(c)

Seeds need water, oxygen and a suitable temperature to germinate — and not light.

ConditionWhy it is needed
WaterMakes the seed swell; activates enzymes that break down the food store
OxygenFor aerobic respiration, releasing energy for growth
WarmthA suitable temperature for the enzymes to work

Light is not needed — seeds live on their stored food until the first leaves appear. The Year 11 mock explicitly refused "light for photosynthesis" as a germination condition.

subsections.heading: The germination practical
subsections.html:
Spec 3.5

Remove one condition from each tube and keep the others; only the tube with all three germinates.

TubeSet-upTestsResult
AMoist cotton wool, 20 °CAll conditions — the controlGerminates
BDry cotton wool, 20 °CNo waterNo germination
CBoiled, cooled water under a layer of oil, 20 °CNo oxygenNo germination
DMoist cotton wool in a fridge, 4 °CToo coldNo or very slow germination

Use the same number and type of seeds in each tube, repeat the set-up, and count the percentage that germinate after a set time, e.g. five days. An alternative for tube C is a sealed flask with pyrogallol or soda lime to absorb oxygen.

subsections.heading: How a germinating seed feeds itself
subsections.html:
Spec 3.6

A germinating seed uses its stored food for respiration and growth until its leaves can photosynthesise.

  1. The seed absorbs water, which activates its enzymes.
  2. Amylase digests stored starch into sugars; proteases digest stored protein into amino acids.
  3. The sugars are used in respiration to release energy, and to build new cells by mitosis.
  4. The root grows down, the shoot grows up towards the light.
  5. Once the first leaves open, the seedling photosynthesises and makes its own food.

So the dry mass of a seedling falls for the first few days — respiration turns stored food into carbon dioxide — then rises once photosynthesis makes more glucose than respiration uses.

subsections.heading: Asexual reproduction — runners
subsections.html:
Spec 3.7 · 2024 Edexcel 1B Q2(c)(i) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1B Q2(c)(i)

A runner is a sideways stem that grows along the ground and roots to form a new, genetically identical plant — a natural method of asexual reproduction.

Strawberries and spider plants do this. The new plant grows from the parent's cells by mitosis, with no gametes and no fertilisation, so it is a clone. Once rooted, the runner can be cut and the new plant lives on its own.

subsections.heading: Asexual reproduction — cuttings
subsections.html:
Spec 3.7 · 2024 Edexcel 1B Q2(c)(ii) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1B Q2(c)

A cutting is a piece of stem that a gardener plants so it grows roots — an artificial method that makes clones.

  1. Cut a short piece of stem with a few leaves from the parent plant.
  2. Remove the lower leaves, to reduce water loss by transpiration.
  3. Dip the cut end in rooting powder (plant hormone) to make roots grow.
  4. Plant it in damp compost and cover with a plastic bag to keep the air humid.
Cloning plants: advantagesDisadvantages
Every plant has the same desired characteristics — colour, flavour, yieldNo genetic variation — one disease or change in conditions can kill them all
Faster than growing from seed; no pollination neededNo new combinations of characteristics
Works for plants whose seeds are not viable, or rare plants

The 2024 scheme accepted cuttings, grafting or layering as artificial methods — but rejected tissue culture for that part. Say cuttings.

subsections.heading: Designing a pollination investigation
subsections.html:
2022 Edexcel 1B Q10

Six-mark "design an investigation" questions are marked on CORMS — one mark for each letter, two for M and two for S.

Does flower colour affect how many insects visit? — the six marks

C — use flowers of different colours (or paper flowers of different colours) 1

O — same species, size and shape of flower 1

R — repeat for several flowers of each colour 1

M1 — count the number of insects landing on each flower 1

M2 — in a stated time, e.g. 30 minutes 1

S — same scent and nectar, same location, time of day and weather 1

What becomes what

Ovule → seed. Ovary → fruit. Pollen lands and germinates on the stigma; the tube grows down the style; the nuclei fuse in the ovule.

Germination: water (enzymes), oxygen (respiration), warmth (enzymes) — not light.

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording
PollinationTransfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma
FertilisationFusion of the male nucleus with the female nucleus in the ovule
GerminationThe start of growth of a seed into a new plant
Self-pollinationPollen transferred to a stigma on the same plant
Cross-pollinationPollen transferred between flowers of different plants of the same species
RunnerA stem growing along the ground that forms clones
CuttingA piece of stem planted to grow roots, producing a clone
CloneAn organism genetically identical to its parent

questions.promptHtml: Explain why wind-pollinated flowers produce far more pollen than insect-pollinated ones.
questions.answerHtml:
Wind carries pollen randomly, so almost all of it lands nowhere useful. Producing huge amounts makes it likely that some reaches a stigma.

Insects carry pollen directly from flower to flower, so much less is wasted and less needs to be made.

questions.promptHtml: In the germination practical, why is the water in one tube boiled, cooled and covered with oil?
questions.answerHtml:
Boiling removes dissolved oxygen from the water. Cooling avoids killing the seeds with heat. The oil layer stops oxygen from the air dissolving back in.

So that tube tests whether oxygen is needed, with water and warmth still present. The seeds do not germinate because they cannot respire aerobically to release energy for growth.

questions.promptHtml: Some fruits are brightly coloured and sweet. Suggest how this helps the plant.
questions.answerHtml:
The colour attracts animals, which eat the fruit for its sugars. The seeds pass through the gut undigested and are egested far from the parent.

That disperses the seeds, so the new plants do not compete with the parent for light, water and minerals.

questions.promptHtml: A bee carries pollen from a rose to an apple flower. The apple flower is pollinated, but no seeds form. Why?
questions.answerHtml:
Pollen landing on a stigma is pollination — the transfer. Fertilisation only happens if the pollen grain germinates and grows a tube down the style to the ovule.

Pollen from a different species does not grow a working pollen tube on the apple's stigma, so no male nucleus reaches an ovule, no nuclei fuse, and no seed forms. Pollination and fertilisation really are two separate events.

questions.promptHtml: A pea pod contains six peas. How many ovules, ovaries and pollen grains were involved, and which part of the plant is the pod?
questions.answerHtml:
The pod is the fruit, so it came from one ovary. Each pea is a seed, so there were six ovules, each fertilised.

Each fertilisation needs its own male nucleus, so at least six pollen grains must have germinated and grown six pollen tubes.

questions.promptHtml: Dry seeds can be stored for years, but once they are soaked their oxygen uptake rises sharply. Explain why.
questions.answerHtml:
In a dry seed, enzymes are inactive and respiration is extremely slow — the seed is dormant.

Water activates the enzymes. Amylase digests the starch store into sugars, and the seed respires them aerobically to release energy for growth. Aerobic respiration uses oxygen, so oxygen uptake rises. That is also why oxygen is one of the three germination conditions.

questions.promptHtml: The dry mass of a batch of seedlings falls for the first five days, then rises. Explain both parts.
questions.answerHtml:
Falling: the seedlings have no leaves yet. They respire their stored starch, and the carbon leaves as carbon dioxide, so mass is lost.

Rising: once the leaves open, the seedlings photosynthesise. When they make glucose faster than they respire it, they build new material and the dry mass increases.

questions.promptHtml: A grower has one apple tree with perfect fruit. Why would she take cuttings rather than plant its seeds, and what is the risk?
questions.answerHtml:
Seeds come from sexual reproduction: meiosis and fertilisation mix alleles, so the new trees would vary and most would not have the perfect fruit. Cuttings grow by mitosis, so they are clones with exactly the same characteristics — and they grow faster.

The risk: every tree is genetically identical, so if one is susceptible to a disease or a change in climate, they all are.

modules.title: DNA and Protein Synthesis
modules.standfirst: Year 11. The January 2024 mock asked for the genome, DNA against RNA, and the roles of RNA in making a protein — eight marks that are almost entirely named words: mRNA, tRNA, codon, anticodon, ribosome. The real Edexcel papers add base-pairing puzzles and one favourite "explain" question: why most mutations change nothing.

subsections.html: DNA is an instruction list. Its only job is to say which proteins to make — and the proteins (enzymes, haemoglobin, hormones like insulin) do everything else. This module is how the list is written, how it is read, and what happens when it is misprinted.

subsections.heading: From genome to gene
subsections.html:
Spec 3.14, 3.15 · 2024 Y11 mock Q3(a) · 2023 Edexcel 2B Q6(b)(ii)

The genome is all the DNA of an organism; a gene is a section of DNA that codes for a specific protein.

LevelWhat it isHow many in a human body cell
GenomeAll the DNA of an organismOne complete set of instructions
ChromosomeOne long, coiled molecule of DNA, in the nucleus46, in 23 pairs
GeneA section of DNA that codes for a specific proteinThousands on each chromosome
AlleleA different version of the same geneTwo of each gene — one on each chromosome of a pair

Read it as a zoom: genome → chromosome → gene → base sequence. Chromosomes are in the nucleus, and the genes are located on them.

✗ "A gene codes for a characteristic, like eye colour."
✓ "A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a specific protein." The protein then affects the characteristic.

subsections.heading: The structure of DNA
subsections.html:
Spec 3.16B · 2024 Edexcel 2B Q5(a)(i)

DNA is two strands coiled into a double helix, held together by pairs of bases.

Each strand is a long chain of units called nucleotides. Every nucleotide has three parts:

  • a sugar (deoxyribose)
  • a phosphate group
  • one of four bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C) or guanine (G)

Sugar and phosphate alternate to form the backbone of each strand. The bases stick inwards and pair up across the middle, like the rungs of a twisted ladder.

subsections.heading: Complementary base pairing
subsections.html:
Spec 3.16B · 2024 Edexcel 2B Q5(a)(i)

A always pairs with T, and C always pairs with G — so one strand fixes the other.

Base pairing — memoriseA – T    C – Gin RNA, U takes the place of T, so A pairs with U

Worked, the way the 2024 paper set it:

  1. Given strand: TAC CGT AAT TAT
  2. Swap each base for its partner: T→A, A→T, C→G, G→C.
  3. Complementary DNA strand: ATG GCA TTA ATA

The wrong options in that question contained U. DNA never contains uracil, so any DNA answer with U in it is out straight away.

✗ "A pairs with G" — both are the larger bases; they never pair.
✓ A–T and C–G in DNA; A–U when one side is RNA.

subsections.heading: DNA versus RNA
subsections.html:
Spec 3.17B · 2024 Y11 mock Q3(b)

RNA is a single-stranded copy that uses uracil instead of thymine.

FeatureDNARNA
StrandsDouble — a double helixSingle
SugarDeoxyriboseRibose
BasesA, T, C, GA, U, C, G — uracil replaces thymine
LengthVery long — a whole chromosomeShort — a copy of one gene
WhereStays in the nucleusmRNA moves out to the ribosomes

The mock gave one mark each for three differences. Each difference must be a comparison: "RNA has uracil" is half a point; "DNA has thymine, RNA has uracil instead" is the whole point.

subsections.heading: Why the code has to be copied
subsections.html:
Spec 3.18B · 2023 Edexcel 1B Q3(a)(iv)

DNA stays in the nucleus, but proteins are made at ribosomes in the cytoplasm — so a mobile copy, mRNA, carries the code out.

Think of DNA as the master copy of a recipe book that is never taken out of the library. You photocopy the one page you need and take the copy to the kitchen. The photocopy is mRNA; the kitchen is the ribosome.

That gives protein synthesis its two stages, and each has a fixed place:

StageWhereWhat goes inWhat comes out
TranscriptionNucleusDNA of one genemRNA
TranslationRibosome, in the cytoplasmmRNA + amino acids carried by tRNAA chain of amino acids — the protein

The 2024 paper tested the order as one line: DNA → transcription → RNA → translation → protein.

subsections.heading: Transcription — DNA to mRNA
subsections.html:
Spec 3.18B · 2022 Edexcel Jan 2B Q6(a) · 2022 Edexcel 2B Q6(b)

In transcription, one strand of a gene is used as a template to build a matching strand of mRNA.

  1. The DNA unzips at the gene — the bonds between the base pairs break and the two strands separate.
  2. Free RNA nucleotides line up against the exposed bases of one strand, by complementary base pairing.
  3. They join into a strand of messenger RNA (mRNA) — with U wherever T would have gone.
  4. The mRNA leaves the nucleus through a pore and travels to a ribosome.
  5. The DNA zips back up, unchanged.

Worked, from the January 2022 paper: DNA strand ATTCCGAGT gives mRNA UAAGGCUCA. Pair as normal, then check: is there any T left in your mRNA? If yes, it is wrong.

subsections.heading: Translation — mRNA to protein
subsections.html:
Spec 3.18B · 2023 Edexcel Jan 2B Q6(b)(iii) · 2024 Y11 mock Q3(c)

In translation, a ribosome reads the mRNA three bases at a time, and tRNA brings the matching amino acid for each triplet.

  1. The mRNA attaches to a ribosome.
  2. The ribosome reads the mRNA one codon — a triplet of three bases — at a time.
  3. Each tRNA (transfer RNA) molecule carries one specific amino acid, and has three bases of its own, the anticodon.
  4. A tRNA whose anticodon is complementary to the codon binds to it.
  5. Its amino acid is added to the chain; the ribosome moves on to the next codon.
  6. The amino acids are joined together into a chain — a polypeptide — which folds into the protein.

Translation — the four marks the 2023 scheme gave

1. Ribosomes bind to the mRNA; this is translation 1

2. Each triplet of bases, a codon, codes for one amino acid 1

3. tRNA brings amino acids; its anticodon binds to the codon 1

4. The amino acids are joined together to form a chain — a polypeptide 1

"To make a protein" on its own was ignored.

✗ "mRNA brings the amino acids to the ribosome."
✓ "tRNA brings the amino acids. mRNA carries the code."

✗ "The codon is on the tRNA."
✓ Codon on mRNA; anticodon on tRNA.

subsections.heading: The triplet code
subsections.html:
Spec 3.18B · 2024 Edexcel 2B Q5(b)(i)

Every three bases code for one amino acid, so the order of bases decides the order of amino acids.

Count your way through it: a gene 300 bases long codes for 300 ÷ 3 = 100 amino acids. Change the order of bases and you change the order of amino acids; change the order of amino acids and the protein folds into a different shape.

The code has more codons than amino acids, so many amino acids have more than one codon. If a paper gives you a codon table, it is usually testing this. For example:

Amino acidmRNA codonsNumber of codons
PhenylalanineUUU, UUC2
GlycineGGU, GGC, GGA, GGG4
MethionineAUG1

To count the codon combinations that give "phenylalanine – glycine – methionine", multiply: 2 × 4 × 1 = 8. If the question asks for the number of other combinations, take away the one you were given: 7.

subsections.heading: Protein synthesis as one answer
subsections.html:
Spec 3.18B · 2022 Edexcel 2B Q6(b)(ii) · 2024 Y11 mock Q3(c)

A full description names both stages, both places and both kinds of RNA.

Describe protein synthesis — the mark points

1. Transcription happens in the nucleus 1

2. mRNA is made from the DNA, by complementary base pairing 1

3. The mRNA leaves the nucleus and binds to a ribosome — translation 1

4. tRNA brings specific amino acids 1

5. The anticodon on tRNA binds to the complementary codon on mRNA 1

6. Amino acids are joined into a chain — a polypeptide 1

A four-mark question takes any four; write all six and you cannot miss.

subsections.heading: From gene to characteristic
subsections.html:
Spec 3.35B · 2022 Edexcel 2B Q6

A gene affects a characteristic because it decides the shape of a protein, and the shape decides what the protein can do.

This is the enzymes idea from module 1 again. An enzyme's active site only fits its substrate because its amino acids fold in one exact way. The same goes for haemoglobin, which carries oxygen: in beta thalassaemia a mutation in a haemoglobin gene means less working haemoglobin is made, so less oxygen reaches the muscles — less respiration, less energy released.

The chain of cause is always the same length:

  1. base sequence of DNA
  2. → codons in mRNA
  3. → sequence of amino acids
  4. → shape of the protein
  5. → how well it works — and so the phenotype

subsections.heading: Mutations and how they change the phenotype
subsections.html:
Spec 3.34, 3.35B · 2022 Edexcel Jan 2B Q6(c)

A mutation is a rare, random change in the base sequence of DNA, and it can be inherited.

A mutation can swap one base for another, add a base, or lose one. If it changes a codon, a different amino acid may go into the chain. That can change how the protein folds — for an enzyme, the active site may no longer fit the substrate.

How a mutation affects the phenotype — three marks

1. A mutation is a rare, random change in the DNA / base sequence 1

2. It changes the sequence of amino acids in the protein 1

3. So a different or non-working protein or enzyme is made, changing the phenotype 1

Mutations are also where new alleles come from. Without them there would be no variation for natural selection to act on — that story is module 17.

subsections.heading: Why most mutations have no effect
subsections.html:
Spec 3.36B · 2024 Edexcel 2B Q5(b)(ii) · 2023 Edexcel 2B Q6(b)(iii)

Most mutations have no effect on the phenotype, some have a small effect, and only rarely is the effect significant.

The 2024 scheme gave marks for any three of these reasons:

  • The new codon may code for the same amino acid — many amino acids have more than one codon.
  • So the protein is unchanged and works exactly as before.
  • Even if one amino acid changes, the protein's shape may not change — an enzyme's active site can still fit its substrate.
  • The new allele may be recessive, so it is not expressed while a dominant allele is present.
  • The change may be in DNA that does not code for a protein.

That is why, in the 2023 snapdragon question, the number of DNA changes rose faster with radiation than the number of new phenotypes: plenty of the mutations were silent.

subsections.heading: What makes mutations more likely
subsections.html:
Spec 3.37B · 2024 Edexcel 2B Q5(b)(iii) · 2022 Edexcel Jan 2B Q6(d)

Mutations happen naturally, but ionising radiation and some chemicals make them more frequent.

CauseExamples
Ionising radiationGamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet rays, radioactive material
Chemical mutagensChemicals in tobacco smoke, such as tar

The butterfly question is the model for evaluating data on this. Abnormal butterflies near a radioactive leak became more common over time, and more of their offspring were abnormal — the mutations were being passed on, and recessive ones appeared when two carriers mated. But good answers also doubt the data: no control population, no data from before the leak, radiation not measured, sample size not given, and some abnormalities might not be genetic at all.

✗ "Radiation causes mutations, so all the abnormal butterflies were caused by the radiation."
✓ "Radiation increases the rate of mutation. Without a control group we cannot be sure the abnormalities were caused by it."

The sentences behind most of the marks

Transcription in the nucleus: DNA → mRNA. Translation at the ribosome: tRNA brings amino acids, anticodon pairs with codon, amino acids joined into a chain.

Mutation → different codon → different amino acid → different shape → protein does not work. Most mutations change nothing, because the amino acid or the shape stays the same.

Pairing: A–T, C–G in DNA; A–U in RNA.

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording
GenomeAll the DNA of an organism
GeneA section of DNA that codes for a specific protein
ChromosomeA long molecule of DNA in the nucleus, carrying many genes
NucleotideA sugar, phosphate and base — the unit DNA and RNA are built from
Double helixTwo strands coiled together, linked by paired bases
Complementary base pairingA pairs with T and C with G (A with U in RNA)
CodonA triplet of bases on mRNA that codes for one amino acid
AnticodonThe three bases on tRNA that are complementary to a codon
TranscriptionMaking mRNA from a DNA template, in the nucleus
TranslationReading mRNA at a ribosome to join amino acids into a protein
MutationA rare, random change in the base sequence of DNA, which can be inherited
MutagenSomething that increases the rate of mutation — ionising radiation or certain chemicals

questions.promptHtml: One strand of DNA reads ATTGCA. Write the complementary DNA strand and the mRNA made from the original.
questions.answerHtml:
Complementary DNA: TAACGT — A pairs with T, C with G.

mRNA from ATTGCA: UAACGU — the same pairing, except U replaces T, because RNA has uracil instead of thymine.

Notice the mRNA is identical to the complementary DNA strand except for U in place of T. That is a quick way to check your answer.

questions.promptHtml: A single base change in a gene makes an enzyme stop working. Explain how.
questions.answerHtml:
The mutation changes one codon, so a different amino acid may be placed in the chain during translation.

The sequence of amino acids decides how the protein folds. A different amino acid can change the folding, and so the shape of the active site. The substrate no longer fits, so the enzyme cannot work.

questions.promptHtml: Why can't the DNA itself go to the ribosome? Why does the cell bother making mRNA?
questions.answerHtml:
DNA is an enormous molecule — a whole chromosome — and it stays in the nucleus, where it is kept safe. Ribosomes are out in the cytoplasm.

mRNA is a short, single-stranded copy of just one gene. It is small enough to leave the nucleus and carry the code to a ribosome. The master copy never leaves, so it is not damaged, and many mRNA copies can be made from one gene when a lot of protein is needed.

questions.promptHtml: A mutation changes the codon GGU to GGC. Both code for glycine. What happens to the protein and the phenotype?
questions.answerHtml:
Nothing changes. The new codon still codes for glycine, so the same amino acid goes into the chain.

Same amino acid sequence → same shape → the protein works as before → no change to the phenotype. This is the commonest reason why most mutations have no effect.

questions.promptHtml: A mutation does change one amino acid in an enzyme, but the enzyme still works. How is that possible?
questions.answerHtml:
The changed amino acid may be in a part of the enzyme that does not affect its shape much, or it may be similar to the one it replaced.

If the active site keeps its shape, the substrate still fits, and the enzyme still catalyses the reaction. What matters is the shape, not the exact list of amino acids.

questions.promptHtml: A person carries a harmful mutation in one allele of a gene but is perfectly healthy. Explain how.
questions.answerHtml:
The mutated allele is recessive. The person is heterozygous: their other allele is normal and dominant, and it still codes for a working protein.

The mutation only shows in the phenotype if the person inherits two copies. It can still be passed on to their children — that is how carriers work (module 16).

questions.promptHtml: A gene is 1200 bases long on one strand. How many amino acids does it code for, and why is that the answer?
questions.answerHtml:
1200 ÷ 3 = 400 amino acids.

The code is read in triplets: each codon of three bases codes for one amino acid. The ribosome moves along the mRNA one codon at a time, adding one amino acid per codon.

questions.promptHtml: Scientists find more abnormal butterflies near a nuclear accident than elsewhere. Why can't they be certain the radiation caused the abnormalities?
questions.answerHtml:
Ionising radiation increases the rate of mutation, so the link is likely — but the study cannot prove it.

There is no control group or data from before the accident, so they do not know the normal level of abnormality. The radiation dose was not measured. Other factors — diet, disease, pollution — could cause abnormalities that are not genetic at all. Larger, repeated samples would make the conclusion stronger.

The table shows the mRNA codons for three amino acids: serine has 6 codons, alanine has 4 and tryptophan has 1.

(a) Calculate how many different mRNA sequences could code for serine – alanine – tryptophan. (1)
(b) Use this to explain why a mutation in a gene for this sequence may have no effect. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) 6 × 4 × 1 = 24 1

(b) A base change may give a different codon for the same amino acid 1; so the amino acid sequence and the protein are unchanged 1

markScheme.point: (b) A base change may give a different codon for the same amino acid ; so the amino acid sequence and the protein are unchanged

questions.promptHtml:
Which row is correct?

A — transcription, in the ribosome
B — translation, codon on tRNA
C — translation, anticodon on tRNA
D — transcription, anticodon on mRNA (1)
questions.answerHtml: C 1 — anticodons are on tRNA, which is used in translation. Transcription happens in the nucleus.

markScheme.point: C — anticodons are on tRNA, which is used in translation. Transcription happens in the nucleus.

questions.promptHtml: Beta thalassaemia is caused by a mutation in a gene for haemoglobin. People with the condition make less haemoglobin. Explain why they get tired easily during exercise. (3)
questions.answerHtml: Less oxygen is carried by the blood 1; to the muscles 1; so less aerobic respiration and less energy released, or more anaerobic respiration and lactic acid 1

questions.promptHtml:
Scientists counted the percentage of abnormal butterflies near a radioactive leak, two months and ten months after it happened. The percentage rose, and was higher still in butterflies bred from them.

(a) Suggest why the percentage of abnormal offspring was higher than in the adults. (2)
(b) Give two reasons why these data do not prove that radiation caused the abnormalities. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Mutations in the adults' DNA are passed on to their offspring 1; recessive mutations carried by heterozygous adults show when two carriers mate 1

(b) No control group, or no data from before the leak 1; radiation level not measured, or other factors could cause the abnormalities 1

modules.title: Inheritance
modules.standfirst: Year 11, and one of the most reliable marks-per-minute topics on the course. The genetic cross is a four-mark routine — parents, gametes, offspring, ratio — and each step is its own mark. Three real papers then asked the same follow-up: the chance of a male child with a given trait. Get the vocabulary exact and learn to multiply.
