subsections.html: You inherit two alleles of each gene — one from each parent. Which ones you have is your genotype; what shows is your phenotype. A genetic diagram is just a tidy way of listing every combination the parents could pass on, so you can read off the chances.

subsections.heading: Genes, alleles and chromosome pairs
subsections.html:
Spec 3.19 · 2023 Edexcel Jan 2B Q3(a)

Genes come in different versions called alleles, and those differences are why inherited characteristics differ.

Chromosomes come in pairs — one of each pair from your mother, one from your father. The same gene sits at the same place on both chromosomes of a pair, so you have two copies of every gene. The two copies may be the same allele or different alleles.

A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a protein (module 15). An allele is one version of that gene. The gene for fur colour is one gene; "black" and "agouti" are two alleles of it.

Gametes — sperm and eggs — are made by meiosis, so they carry only one chromosome from each pair, and so only one allele of each gene. At fertilisation, two gametes combine and the pair is restored.

subsections.heading: The six words
subsections.html:
Spec 3.20 · 2024 Edexcel 1B Q8(a) · 2022 Edexcel Jan 1B Q9(a) · 2023 Y11 mock Q5(a)(ii)

Dominant and recessive describe alleles; homozygous and heterozygous describe genotypes; genotype is the letters and phenotype is what you see.

WordMeaningExample
DominantExpressed in the phenotype with only one copyF
RecessiveOnly expressed with two copies — when no dominant allele is presentf
HomozygousTwo identical allelesFF or ff
HeterozygousTwo different allelesFf
GenotypeThe alleles an organism hasFf
PhenotypeThe observable characteristicunaffected by cystic fibrosis

Convention: the capital letter is the dominant allele, the lower case of the same letter is the recessive one. Choose a letter whose capital and small forms look different — F/f, A/a, B/b — and avoid X and Y.

✗ "Dominant means it is stronger" or "more common in the population".
✓ "Only one copy is needed for it to be expressed in the phenotype." A dominant allele can be rare.

subsections.heading: Working out a genotype from a phenotype
subsections.html:
Spec 3.20, 3.24 · 2022 Edexcel 1B Q8(a)(i)

A recessive phenotype tells you the genotype; a dominant phenotype does not.

You seePossible genotypesWhy
The recessive characteristicff onlyA single F would have been expressed
The dominant characteristicFF or FfBoth look the same — you need more evidence

The evidence usually comes from relatives:

  • A dominant-looking parent who has a recessive child must be Ff — the child's f came from somewhere.
  • A dominant-looking child of a recessive parent must be Ff — the recessive parent could only give f.

Which allele is dominant? In the 2022 rat question, black × agouti gave all agouti offspring. The offspring must carry both alleles, yet only agouti shows — so agouti is dominant. That was the two-mark answer: agouti, because all the offspring were agouti even though they carried the black allele.

subsections.heading: The genetic diagram — four marks
subsections.html:
Spec 3.23 · 2023 Y11 mock Q5(a)(iii) · 2022 Edexcel Jan 1B Q9(b)

Every genetic diagram has four marked lines: parent genotypes, gametes, offspring genotypes, and offspring phenotypes with the ratio.

Worked example — the mock's cross. A heterozygous animal with a condition caused by a dominant allele (Hh) is crossed with an unaffected animal (hh):

  1. Parent phenotypes: affected × unaffected
  2. Parent genotypes: Hh × hh 1
  3. Gametes: H and h from the first parent; h and h from the second 1
  4. Offspring genotypes from the Punnett square 1
  5. Offspring phenotypes and ratio: Hh affected, hh unaffected — 1 : 1 1
Gameteshh
HHh — affectedHh — affected
hhh — unaffectedhh — unaffected

Put each parent's gametes along one edge and fill each box with one gamete from the top and one from the side. The boxes are the four equally likely outcomes.

The four-line checklist

Parents: both genotypes written out, e.g. Hh × hh.

Gametes: shown separately — circled, or along the edges of the Punnett square. One letter each.

Offspring: every box filled.

Phenotypes: each genotype labelled with what it looks like, plus the ratio.

subsections.heading: Two carriers — the 3 : 1 cross
subsections.html:
Spec 3.23, 3.24 · 2024 Edexcel 1B Q8(b) · 2022 Edexcel Jan 1B Q9(b) · 2022 Edexcel 1B Q8(a)(ii)

Two heterozygous parents give a 3 : 1 ratio of dominant to recessive phenotype — a 1 in 4 chance of an affected child for a recessive condition.

Worked example — cystic fibrosis, caused by a recessive allele f. Two unaffected carrier parents:

  1. Parent phenotypes: unaffected × unaffected
  2. Parent genotypes: Ff × Ff
  3. Gametes: F and f from each parent
GametesFf
FFF — unaffectedFf — unaffected (carrier)
fFf — unaffected (carrier)ff — cystic fibrosis
  1. Offspring genotypes: 1 FF : 2 Ff : 1 ff
  2. Offspring phenotypes: 3 unaffected : 1 with cystic fibrosis

The same diagram, with different letters, answered the alkaptonuria question (Aa × Aa) and the second rat cross (Aa × Aa, 3 agouti : 1 black).

✗ Writing the ratio as "1 : 2 : 1" when the question asks for phenotypes.
✓ Genotype ratio 1 FF : 2 Ff : 1 ff; phenotype ratio 3 unaffected : 1 affected. Say which one you are giving.

subsections.heading: Two pure-breeding parents
subsections.html:
Spec 3.23 · 2023 Edexcel 1B Q6(a)

Crossing a homozygous dominant with a homozygous recessive gives offspring that are all heterozygous, all with the dominant phenotype.

Worked example — pea plants. Axial flowers (A) are dominant to terminal flowers (a).

  1. Parent genotypes: AA (axial) × aa (terminal)
  2. Gametes: all A from one parent; all a from the other
  3. Offspring: all Aa — 100% axial
Gametesaa
AAa — axialAa — axial
AAa — axialAa — axial

If those Aa offspring are then crossed with each other, you are back to the 3 : 1 cross: the recessive characteristic reappears in a quarter of the next generation. The allele was hidden, not lost.

subsections.heading: Probability from a cross
subsections.html:
Spec 3.25 · 2023 Y11 mock Q5(a)(iv)

Each box of a Punnett square is one quarter of the chances, so count boxes and divide by four.

CrossChance of recessive phenotypeChance of dominant phenotypeChance of heterozygous
Hh × Hh1/4 = 0.25 = 25%3/4 = 0.752/4 = 0.5
Hh × hh2/4 = 0.5 = 50%0.50.5
HH × hh011
HH × Hh010.5

Give the answer in the form the question asks for — a fraction, a decimal, a percentage or "1 in 4". A ratio like 1 : 3 is not a probability: 1 : 3 means a probability of 1/4, not 1/3.

Every fertilisation is independent. If a couple's first child has cystic fibrosis, the chance for their second child is still 0.25 — the gametes have no memory.

subsections.heading: The "and" rule — boy or girl as well
subsections.html:
Spec 3.25, 3.27 · 2022 Edexcel 1B Q8(a)(iii) · 2022 Edexcel Jan 1B Q9(b)(ii) · 2023 Edexcel Jan 2B Q3(b)(ii)

To find the chance of two separate things both happening, multiply their probabilities.

Sex is decided separately from the gene in the cross, and the chance of a boy is always 1/2. So:

Probability of two independent outcomesP(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)e.g. P(male and unaffected) = P(male) × P(unaffected)
Real questionWorkingAnswer
Rats, Aa × Aa: male and agouti1/2 × 3/43/8 = 0.375
Alkaptonuria, Aa × Aa: male and no condition1/2 × 3/43/8 = 0.375
Roan cattle, CRCW × CRCW: male and roan1/2 × 2/41/4 = 0.25

The same rule works for two children: the chance that two children of Ff × Ff parents both have cystic fibrosis is 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16.

✗ "Male and agouti: 1/2 + 3/4" — adding gives more than 1, which is impossible.
✓ "1/2 × 3/4 = 0.375." "And" means multiply. The answer must be smaller than either chance on its own.

subsections.heading: Why real ratios are never exact
subsections.html:
Spec 3.25 · 2023 Edexcel 1B Q6(b)

Ratios from a cross are probabilities, so real numbers only come close — and the bigger the sample, the closer they get.

Worked, from the 2023 paper: 858 pea plants, 608 axial.

  1. Terminal = 858 − 608 = 250
  2. Ratio = 608 ÷ 250 = 2.43 : 1 — close to, but not, 3 : 1

Why not exactly 3 : 1? The scheme's points: the expected ratio is 3 : 1; which gametes fuse at fertilisation is random, so it is down to chance; and some plants of one type may not have survived or germinated. Four kittens from Hh × hh will not necessarily be two and two.

subsections.heading: Finding an unknown genotype
subsections.html:
Spec 3.23, 3.24

To find out whether a dominant-looking organism is homozygous or heterozygous, cross it with a homozygous recessive and look at the offspring.

If the unknown parent isCrossOffspring
Homozygous — BBBB × bbAll show the dominant characteristic (all Bb)
Heterozygous — BbBb × bbAbout half show the recessive characteristic (1 Bb : 1 bb)

A single recessive offspring proves the parent is Bb. But all-dominant offspring from a small litter only suggest BB — with a 1/2 chance each time, a heterozygous parent could produce a few dominant offspring in a row by chance.

subsections.heading: Codominance — both alleles show
subsections.html:
Spec 3.21B · 2023 Edexcel Jan 2B Q3(b) · 2022 Edexcel Jan 2B Q1(b)

With codominant alleles, both are expressed in the heterozygote, so it has a third phenotype of its own.

Codominant alleles are written as a capital letter for the gene with a superscript for each allele. Cattle hair: CR (red) and CW (white).

GenotypePhenotype
CRCRRed
CWCWWhite
CRCWRoan — red and white hairs both show

Roan × roan — the 2023 question:

GametesCRCW
CRCRCR — redCRCW — roan
CWCRCW — roanCWCW — white

Ratio 1 red : 2 roan : 1 white. With codominance the genotype ratio and the phenotype ratio are the same, because every genotype looks different.

Blood groups use three alleles: IA and IB are codominant, and IO is recessive to both. IAIO (group A) × IBIO (group B):

GametesIBIO
IAIAIB — group ABIAIO — group A
IOIBIO — group BIOIO — group O

All four blood groups are possible, each with a probability of 1/4 — the answer to the 2022 multiple-choice question.

subsections.heading: Sex determination
subsections.html:
Spec 3.26, 3.27 · 2023 Edexcel Jan 1B Q5

Sex is controlled by one pair of chromosomes: XX in a female and XY in a male.

Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes; the 23rd pair are the sex chromosomes. In a karyotype — a photo of the chromosomes arranged in pairs — a male is recognised because his 23rd pair is not matched: one large X and one small Y.

  1. Parent phenotypes: female × male
  2. Parent genotypes: XX × XY
  3. Gametes: all eggs carry X; half the sperm carry X, half carry Y
GametesX (sperm)Y (sperm)
X (egg)XX — femaleXY — male
X (egg)XX — femaleXY — male
  1. Offspring: 1 female : 1 male — a probability of 0.5 for each, at every fertilisation

The sex of the child is decided by which sperm fertilises the egg, so it is the father's gamete that decides.

subsections.heading: Family pedigrees
subsections.html:
Spec 3.24 · 2024 Edexcel 1B Q8(b)(i) · 2023 Y11 mock Q5(b)

In a pedigree, two unaffected parents with an affected child prove the condition is recessive and both parents are carriers.

A pedigree is a family tree. Squares are males, circles are females, and shaded shapes are affected. A horizontal line joins parents; a vertical line drops to their children. Reading one for a recessive condition like cystic fibrosis:

Person in the pedigreeGenotypeHow you know
Anyone affectedffRecessive phenotype — only one possible genotype
Unaffected parent of an affected childFfMust have passed on an f, but shows the dominant phenotype
Unaffected child of an affected parentFfReceived f from the affected parent, but is unaffected
Unaffected, with no affected parents or childrenFF or FfNot enough information — say both

For a dominant condition the clue is the reverse: two affected parents with an unaffected child — both parents must be heterozygous.

This is also why breeders worry about recessive alleles, which the Year 11 mock rewarded. A dominant harmful allele always shows, so affected animals can be spotted and not bred from. A recessive allele hides in heterozygous carriers who look normal, so it is passed on unnoticed.

subsections.heading: Polygenic inheritance
subsections.html:
Spec 3.22 · 2023 Edexcel Jan 2B Q3(c)(i) · 2022 Edexcel 1B Q8(b)(i)

Most characteristics are controlled by many genes, not one — this is polygenic inheritance.

A single-gene characteristic, like roan hair or cystic fibrosis, falls into a few clear categories. A polygenic one, like height or body mass, has a smooth range of values, because each of several genes adds a little, and the environment — nutrition, for example — adds more on top.

Why height varies more than hair colour — two marks

1. Height is polygenic — controlled by many genes 1

2. The environment, such as nutrition, also affects height 1

The scheme ignored "multiple alleles". Polygenic means many genes, not many versions of one gene.

The sentences behind most of the marks

The cross in four lines: parents' genotypes → gametes → Punnett offspring → phenotypes and ratio. Label every line.

Heterozygous × heterozygous: 3 : 1, a 0.25 chance of the recessive phenotype. Heterozygous × recessive: 1 : 1, a 0.5 chance.

"Male and…": multiply by 1/2. Unaffected parents, affected child: recessive, both parents carriers.

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording
GeneA section of DNA that codes for a specific protein
AlleleA different form of the same gene
Dominant alleleOnly one copy is needed for it to be expressed in the phenotype
Recessive alleleOnly expressed when two copies are present — not expressed if a dominant allele is present
HomozygousHaving two identical alleles of a gene
HeterozygousHaving two different alleles of a gene
GenotypeThe combination of alleles an organism has
PhenotypeThe observable characteristics of an organism
CodominanceBoth alleles expressed in the phenotype of a heterozygote
Polygenic inheritanceA characteristic controlled by many genes
CarrierA heterozygous individual with one recessive allele, who does not show the condition
Sex chromosomesThe pair that decides sex — XX female, XY male

questions.promptHtml: Two brown-eyed parents have a blue-eyed child. Brown is dominant (B). Explain, with genotypes, and give the chance their next child has blue eyes.
questions.answerHtml:
A blue-eyed child must be bb, so each parent passed on a b. Both parents show brown, so each must also carry a B: both are Bb.

Bb × Bb gives BB, Bb, Bb, bb — so the chance of blue eyes is 1 in 4, 0.25, for every child.

questions.promptHtml: Why is it easier for breeders to remove a dominant harmful allele than a recessive one?
questions.answerHtml:
A dominant allele is always expressed, so every animal carrying it shows the condition and can be stopped from breeding.

A recessive allele is hidden in heterozygous animals, which look normal. They are bred from without anyone knowing, so the allele keeps being passed on.

questions.promptHtml: Black rats are crossed with agouti rats. Every offspring is agouti. Which allele is dominant, and what are the genotypes of the offspring?
questions.answerHtml:
Agouti is dominant. Every offspring received one allele from the black parent, so each one carries the black allele — yet none of them is black. The black allele is being hidden, so it is recessive.

The offspring are all heterozygous, Aa. (The parents were most likely AA × aa: if the agouti parent had been Aa, about half the offspring would have been black.)

questions.promptHtml: Two carriers of cystic fibrosis have three unaffected children. A friend says their fourth child is "due" to have it. Explain why the friend is wrong.
questions.answerHtml:
Each fertilisation is independent. Which sperm meets which egg is random each time, and the earlier children do not change the gametes.

The chance for the fourth child is exactly what it was for the first: 1/4 = 0.25. The 3 : 1 ratio describes the probability for each child, not a pattern that must be completed.

questions.promptHtml: Two unaffected parents who are both carriers of alkaptonuria (Aa) are expecting a child. Why is the probability that the child is a boy without the condition 0.375, not 0.75?
questions.answerHtml:
0.75 is the chance of being unaffected — three of the four boxes in Aa × Aa. But the question asks for two things at once: unaffected and male.

Sex is decided separately, with a chance of 1/2. Both must happen, so multiply: 3/4 × 1/2 = 3/8 = 0.375. Half of the unaffected children are expected to be girls, so the answer must be smaller than 0.75.

questions.promptHtml: A roan bull is crossed with a white cow. Why can you predict the calves' phenotypes directly from their genotypes, which you cannot do with a dominant and recessive allele?
questions.answerHtml:
The alleles are codominant, so the heterozygote has its own phenotype. CRCW × CWCW gives CRCW (roan) and CWCW (white) in a 1 : 1 ratio.

Every genotype looks different, so the phenotype tells you the genotype. With a dominant allele, FF and Ff look the same, so you cannot tell them apart by looking.

questions.promptHtml: A student crosses two heterozygous pea plants and gets 608 tall and 250 short. She says her result disproves the 3 : 1 rule. Is she right?
questions.answerHtml:
No. 608 ÷ 250 = 2.4 : 1, which is close to 3 : 1. The 3 : 1 ratio is a probability, not a guarantee.

Which gametes fuse at fertilisation is random, so real results vary around the expected ratio. Some seeds may also have failed to germinate. A bigger sample would be expected to come closer to 3 : 1.

questions.promptHtml: Hair colour in cattle comes in three clear types, but height varies smoothly from short to tall. Explain the difference.
questions.answerHtml:
Hair colour is controlled by one gene with two alleles, so there are only three genotypes and three phenotypes.

Height is polygenic — controlled by many genes, each adding a little — so there are many combinations of alleles and a continuous range of heights. The environment also affects height, for example how well the animal is fed, which spreads the values even more.

modules.title: Selection and Evolution
modules.standfirst: Year 11. Natural selection is a five-step story that turns up in unfamiliar clothes — woodlice rolling up, fire ants resisting pesticide, whales outcompeting a giant shark. Selective breeding is the same story with humans choosing. The mark scheme rejects "passes on the mutation". It must be alleles.

subsections.html: Individuals in a species are not identical. Some of those differences are inherited, and some of the inherited ones help an organism survive. Over many generations, the helpful alleles become more common. That is natural selection — and when humans do the choosing instead of the environment, it is selective breeding.

subsections.heading: Variation — genes, environment or both
subsections.html:
Spec 3.33 · 2023 Edexcel Jan 2B Q3(c)(i)

Variation within a species can be genetic, environmental, or a combination of both.

CauseWhat it meansExamples
GeneticDecided by the alleles inheritedBlood group, eye colour, cystic fibrosis
EnvironmentalDecided by conditions during lifeScars, language spoken, a plant growing tall in shade
BothGenes set a range; the environment decides where in it you end upHeight, body mass, crop yield

Identical twins have identical genes, so any difference between them must be environmental. Only genetic variation can be passed on to offspring — and so only genetic variation matters for natural selection.

subsections.heading: Where genetic variation comes from
subsections.html:
Spec 3.30, 3.31, 3.34

Genetic variation comes from mutation, which makes new alleles, and from sexual reproduction, which shuffles existing ones.

  1. Mutation — a rare, random change in DNA. The only source of brand-new alleles (module 15).
  2. Meiosis — each gamete gets a different mix of chromosomes, so gametes are genetically different.
  3. Random fertilisation — any sperm can fuse with any egg, giving new combinations of alleles.

Asexual reproduction uses mitosis only, so the offspring are clones. Apart from rare mutations, there is no variation between them.

subsections.heading: Why some features vary more than others
subsections.html:
Spec 3.22, 3.33 · 2023 Edexcel Jan 2B Q3(c)(i)

A feature controlled by one gene falls into a few clear groups; one controlled by many genes and the environment varies smoothly.

Hair colour in cattle: one gene, two alleles, three colours. Height in cattle: polygenic — many genes each add a little — and nutrition adds more. So a herd has three hair colours but a whole range of heights. The 2023 scheme gave one mark for each idea, and ignored "multiple alleles".

subsections.heading: Darwin's theory — natural selection in five steps
subsections.html:
Spec 3.38 · 2023 Y11 mock Q2(c)(iii)

Individuals with inherited features that suit their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce, so they pass on their alleles and those alleles become more common.

  1. A mutation produces a new allele, so there is variation in the population.
  2. Some individuals have a characteristic that gives a survival advantage in their environment — for example avoiding predators, finding food, resisting disease.
  3. Those individuals are more likely to survive; others die, often through competition or predation.
  4. The survivors reproduce.
  5. They pass on the advantageous allele to their offspring, so over many generations it becomes more common in the population.

Every step is a mark. The one lost most is the last: say alleles or genes are passed on.

✗ "The woodlice learned to roll up to survive."
✗ "The woodlice adapted to roll up because of the predators."
✓ "A mutation gave some woodlice an allele for rolling up. They were more likely to survive predators and reproduce, passing on the allele."

Individuals do not change to suit their environment. The environment decides which of the already-different individuals leave offspring.

subsections.heading: Writing it for an unfamiliar organism
subsections.html:
Spec 3.38 · 2023 Y11 mock Q2(c)(iii)

Every natural selection question is the same five steps with the organism's own advantage dropped in at step 2.

First find the advantage in the question. Rolling up protects the soft underside from predators. Pale fur is camouflage in snow. A long neck reaches higher leaves. Then write the chain.

The woodlouse answer — four marks

1. A mutation produced an allele for rolling up 1

2. There is variation — woodlice that roll up are protected from predators and survive 1

3. They reproduce 1

4. Passing on the alleles to their offspring 1

"Survival of the fittest" on its own scores nothing. Write the steps.

subsections.heading: Competition and extinction
subsections.html:
Spec 3.38 · 2024 Edexcel 2B Q1(b)

When two species compete for the same food, the better-adapted one survives and reproduces more, and the other can be driven to extinction.

The 2024 passage: scientists think the giant shark megalodon was replaced by giant, predatory toothed whales. The marks went to:

  • competition between megalodon and the whales for food
  • the whales were better adapted — faster, or better at hunting — so they ate more of the food
  • the whales survived and reproduced more, having more offspring

Most species that have ever lived are now extinct. A species goes extinct when its environment changes — a new competitor, a new predator, a new disease, a change in climate — and none of its individuals have the alleles to survive it.

subsections.heading: From natural selection to evolution
subsections.html:
Spec 3.38

Evolution is the change in the inherited characteristics of a population over many generations, and natural selection is how it happens.

One generation changes the proportion of an allele a little. Thousands of generations change a population a lot. If two groups of the same species are separated — by a sea, a mountain range — and face different conditions, different alleles are selected in each. Given enough time, they can become so different that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring: they have become separate species.

Darwin's evidence came from observing variation in the wild, from fossils showing gradual change, and from the results of selective breeding.

subsections.heading: Antibiotic resistance
subsections.html:
Spec 3.39

Antibiotic resistance spreads by natural selection: the antibiotic kills the non-resistant bacteria, and the resistant ones survive and reproduce.

  1. A random mutation gives one bacterium an allele for resistance.
  2. The antibiotic is used. It kills the non-resistant bacteria.
  3. The resistant bacterium survives, with less competition.
  4. It reproduces — bacteria divide every 20 minutes or so in good conditions.
  5. Its offspring inherit the resistance allele. Soon most of the population is resistant.

It is fast because bacteria reproduce so quickly: many generations pass in a single day.

✗ "The antibiotic caused the bacteria to become resistant."
✓ "A random mutation had already made some bacteria resistant. The antibiotic selected them by killing the rest."

subsections.heading: Why resistant infections are hard to control
subsections.html:
Spec 3.39

Once bacteria are resistant, the usual antibiotic no longer kills them, so the infection spreads and is difficult to treat.

MRSA is a strain of Staphylococcus aureus resistant to many antibiotics; it spreads in hospitals, where many people are ill and many antibiotics are used. Doctors then have to find a different antibiotic, and bacteria may become resistant to that one too.

To slow the spread of resistance:

  • Do not use antibiotics for viral infections — they do not work on viruses, and every use selects for resistance.
  • Finish the course, so the more resistant bacteria are killed too, rather than surviving to multiply.
  • Avoid overuse — for example, routine use in farm animals.
  • Good hygiene in hospitals, so resistant bacteria are not passed between patients.

subsections.heading: Pesticide resistance
subsections.html:
Spec 3.39 · 2024 Y11 mock Q2(d)

Pesticide resistance works exactly like antibiotic resistance, with insects in place of bacteria.

In the fire ant question, numbers fell sharply after the pesticide, then rose again after about six months. Two explanations scored: the pesticide wore off, or a few ants had an allele for resistance, survived, reproduced and passed it on. Phorid flies — a biological control that breeds and keeps working — held numbers down for longer. That comparison is module 10.

subsections.heading: Selective breeding in plants
subsections.html:
Spec 5.10 · 2022 Edexcel 1B Q9 · 2023 Edexcel 2B Q6(a)(i)

In selective breeding, humans choose the parents with the characteristic they want, breed them, and repeat over many generations.

  1. Choose parent plants with the desired characteristic — for example the highest grain yield.
  2. Cross-pollinate them, or let them self-pollinate.
  3. Grow the seeds and select the offspring that show the characteristic best.
  4. Breed those, and repeat over many generations.

Examples: high-yield wheat, disease-resistant crops, brightly coloured flowers. The 2022 paper added dwarf wheat — a shorter, thicker stem means less energy used for growing tall and so more for grain, and the plants are less likely to be blown over by wind and rain and are easier to harvest.

Describe selective breeding — three marks

1. Select and breed parents with the desired characteristic, e.g. highest yield 1

2. Select the offspring with that characteristic and breed them 1

3. Repeat over many generations 1

subsections.heading: Selective breeding in animals
subsections.html:
Spec 5.11 · 2022 Edexcel Jan 2B Q4(a) · 2023 Edexcel Jan 2B Q3(c)(ii)

The same method works for animals: mate the best, keep the best offspring, repeat — so the alleles for the characteristic are passed on and become more common.

Examples: cows that give more milk, beef cattle that grow faster, sheep with better wool, fish that grow rapidly, docile dogs. For the fish question, the extra mark was the reason: genes or alleles for fast growth are passed on.

It takes a long time, because each round must wait for the animals to grow up and breed.

subsections.heading: Problems with selective breeding — and how it differs from natural selection
subsections.html:
Spec 5.10, 5.11, 3.38

Selective breeding narrows the range of alleles, so the population loses variation.

  • Inbreeding — the best animals are often related, so harmful recessive alleles are more likely to meet, causing genetic disorders.
  • Less variation — if a new disease appears, there may be no individuals with an allele to resist it, so the whole crop or herd can be lost.
  • Features chosen for people's benefit can harm the animal — for example breathing problems in some dog breeds.
FeatureNatural selectionSelective breeding
Who "chooses"The environment — who survivesHumans — who breeds
Characteristics favouredThose that help survivalThose useful to humans
SpeedUsually very slowFaster — only chosen parents breed
Effect on variationVariation kept by mutation and sexual reproductionVariation reduced

The sentences behind most of the marks

Natural selection: mutation → variation → survive → reproduce → pass on alleles → allele more common over generations.

Resistance: the mutation came first; the antibiotic or pesticide only selects it.

Selective breeding: choose parents with the desired characteristic → breed → select the best offspring → repeat over many generations.

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording
VariationDifferences between individuals of a species — genetic, environmental or both
MutationA rare, random change in genetic material that can be inherited
Natural selectionIndividuals with advantageous characteristics survive, reproduce and pass on their alleles
EvolutionA change in the inherited characteristics of a population over many generations
SpeciationFormation of a new species that can no longer interbreed with the original to produce fertile offspring
Antibiotic resistanceBacteria not killed by an antibiotic, because of an allele from a mutation
Selective breedingHumans choosing organisms with desired characteristics to breed, over many generations
InbreedingBreeding closely related individuals, which reduces variation

questions.promptHtml: Some woodlice roll into a ball when touched. Explain how this behaviour could have become common through natural selection.
questions.answerHtml:
A mutation produced an allele causing rolling-up behaviour, giving variation.

Woodlice that roll up expose only their hard shell, so they are less likely to be eaten and more likely to survive. They reproduce and pass on the allele. Over many generations the allele becomes more common, so more of the population rolls up.

questions.promptHtml: Why do doctors tell patients to finish a course of antibiotics?
questions.answerHtml:
Stopping early kills only the most susceptible bacteria, leaving the more resistant ones alive. They reproduce and pass on the alleles for resistance.

Finishing the course kills as many bacteria as possible, so fewer resistant ones survive to multiply.

questions.promptHtml: Why does antibiotic resistance spread through bacteria in months, while a new feature in elephants takes thousands of years?
questions.answerHtml:
Natural selection works one generation at a time. Bacteria can divide every 20 minutes or so, so there are many generations in a single day. Elephants take over ten years to breed.

Bacteria also exist in huge numbers, so a rare resistance mutation is likely to be present somewhere. And the antibiotic is a very strong selection pressure — it kills almost all the non-resistant bacteria at once.

questions.promptHtml: A student writes: "Giraffes stretched their necks to reach high leaves, and their young were born with longer necks." What is wrong with this explanation?
questions.answerHtml:
Stretching during life does not change the alleles in the gametes, so it cannot be inherited. Only genetic variation is passed on.

Darwin's version: giraffes already varied in neck length because of different alleles. Those with longer necks reached more food, so were more likely to survive and reproduce, passing on the alleles for longer necks. Over many generations, the average neck got longer.

questions.promptHtml: Fire ant numbers fall after a pesticide is sprayed, then rise again six months later even though spraying continues. Explain, using natural selection.
questions.answerHtml:
By chance, a few ants had an allele — from a mutation — that made them resistant to the pesticide. The pesticide killed the non-resistant ants, so the resistant ones survived with less competition.

They reproduced and passed on the resistance allele, so each generation had a larger proportion of resistant ants. The pesticide no longer controls the population.

questions.promptHtml: Identical twins are separated at birth. As adults, one is 8 cm taller than the other. What does this tell you about the cause of the difference?
questions.answerHtml:
Identical twins have identical alleles, so the difference cannot be genetic. It must be environmental — for example diet, illness or exercise during childhood.

Height is affected by both genes and environment: the genes set a range, and the environment decides where in that range each twin ends up.

questions.promptHtml: A whole field of a selectively bred, high-yield wheat variety is destroyed by a new fungal disease, while a field of old-fashioned wheat nearby survives. Explain why.
questions.answerHtml:
Selective breeding for yield used only a few parent plants, so the new variety has a small range of alleles — very little variation. If none of the plants has an allele for resistance to the new fungus, all of them are killed.

The old wheat is more varied, so some plants are likely to carry an allele that lets them resist the disease and survive.

questions.promptHtml: How is selective breeding like natural selection, and how is it different?
questions.answerHtml:
Alike: both need variation; in both, only some individuals breed, so their alleles become more common over many generations.

Different: in natural selection the environment decides who survives, favouring features that help survival. In selective breeding humans decide who breeds, favouring features useful to people — which may not help the organism at all. Selective breeding is usually faster and reduces variation.

The real papers wrap them in passages — frozen mammoths, suberin crops, fast-growing fish.

subsections.html: Modules 15 to 17 showed that DNA codes for proteins and that organisms can be changed over generations by breeding. This module is about changing or copying organisms directly: moving a gene from one species to another, and making genetically identical copies.

subsections.heading: What genetic modification is
subsections.html:
Spec 5.16

Genetic modification means cutting a gene out of one organism and inserting it into another, which then makes the protein that gene codes for.

An organism that contains a gene from a different species is transgenic. A bacterium carrying the human insulin gene, a crop carrying a bacterial insecticide gene, and a fish carrying a growth gene are all transgenic.

It works because the genetic code is the same in all organisms: a bacterium's ribosomes read the human codons exactly as a human cell would, and make the human protein.

subsections.heading: Restriction enzymes — the scissors
subsections.html:
Spec 5.12 · 2022 Edexcel 2B Q1(c)

Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific base sequences, leaving short single-stranded "sticky ends".

Each restriction enzyme recognises one particular sequence of bases, so it always cuts in the same place. It cuts the two strands a few bases apart, leaving a few unpaired bases hanging off each end. These unpaired bases are the sticky ends: they will base-pair with any complementary sticky end.

The key rule: cut the gene and the plasmid with the same restriction enzyme. Then their sticky ends are complementary and can pair up.

✗ "Ligase cuts out the gene." — the 2022 multiple choice put ligase in as a wrong answer.
✓ "Restriction enzymes cut; ligase joins."

subsections.heading: Ligase — the glue
subsections.html:
Spec 5.12

DNA ligase joins pieces of DNA together, sealing the gene into the plasmid.

Once the sticky ends of the gene and the cut plasmid have paired up, the backbones of the two pieces still have gaps in them. Ligase joins the sugar–phosphate backbones, so the gene becomes a permanent part of the plasmid. The result — DNA combined from two different organisms — is recombinant DNA.

subsections.heading: Vectors — plasmids and viruses
subsections.html:
Spec 5.13

A vector carries the new gene into the cell being modified; plasmids and viruses can both act as vectors.

VectorWhat it isHow it delivers the gene
PlasmidA small, circular ring of DNA found in bacteria, separate from the main chromosomeTaken up by a bacterium, which copies it every time it divides
VirusA particle that injects its genetic material into a host cellThe gene is inserted into the virus's DNA; the virus carries it into the host cell

subsections.heading: Making human insulin in bacteria
subsections.html:
Spec 5.14 · 2023 Edexcel 1B Q9(a)

The human insulin gene is cut out, sealed into a bacterial plasmid, and put into bacteria, which multiply in a fermenter and make insulin.

  1. A restriction enzyme cuts the insulin gene out of human DNA, leaving sticky ends.
  2. The same restriction enzyme cuts open a bacterial plasmid, giving complementary sticky ends.
  3. The sticky ends pair up, and ligase joins the gene into the plasmid — recombinant DNA.
  4. The plasmid, now a vector, is taken up by a bacterium.
  5. The bacteria are grown in a fermenter with nutrients, at the right temperature and pH. They multiply rapidly; every new bacterium carries the gene.
  6. The bacteria make human insulin, which is extracted and purified for people with diabetes.

The four marks the 2023 scheme gave

1. A restriction enzyme is used to cut out the insulin gene 1

2. The same restriction enzyme cuts the bacterial plasmid 1

3. Producing complementary sticky ends 1

4. Ligase joins the gene into the plasmid 1

A fifth creditworthy point: the plasmid is inserted into a bacterium. Five points for four marks — write all five.

subsections.heading: Why bacteria, and why human insulin
subsections.html:
Spec 5.14

Bacteria make a good factory because they reproduce very fast and read the human gene exactly.

  • Rapid reproduction — one modified bacterium becomes billions in a fermenter within days.
  • Same genetic code — the insulin they make is identical to human insulin, so fewer allergic reactions than insulin taken from pigs or cattle.
  • Large amounts, cheaply and reliably, without depending on animals from slaughterhouses.
  • Plasmids are easy to cut, modify and put back into bacteria.

The same method is used for other human proteins, such as human growth hormone.

subsections.heading: Genetically modified crops
subsections.html:
Spec 5.15 · 2022 Edexcel 2B Q1

Genetically modified plants are given genes that improve food production — more yield, less loss, or more nutrition.

Gene addedWhat it doesWhy yield rises
Pest resistance — a bacterial gene for an insecticide proteinThe plant makes a toxin that kills insects eating itLess crop damage; less insecticide sprayed
Herbicide resistanceThe crop survives a weedkiller that kills the weeds around itLess competition from weeds for light, water and minerals
Extra nutrients — e.g. Golden RiceRice makes a substance the body turns into vitamin ABetter diet where rice is the main food
Tolerance of poor conditionse.g. suberin in roots gives tolerance to salty soilCrops grow where they could not before

The 2022 passage used a gene for suberin, a slow-decaying, carbon-rich substance, so crops would lock up carbon from the air. Carbon dioxide is taken in for photosynthesis and stored in the suberin, which decomposes very slowly — so less carbon dioxide returns to the air.

subsections.heading: Weighing up genetic modification
subsections.html:
Spec 5.15 · 2024 Edexcel 2B Q6(b)(v)

An evaluation needs points on both sides, taken from the data in front of you, plus a comment on how good that data is.

BenefitsConcerns
Higher yields; more food from the same landGenes could spread to wild plants by pollination — e.g. herbicide-resistant weeds
Less pesticide sprayedInsects that are not pests could be harmed; food chains affected
More nutritious foodFewer varieties grown, so less variation — one disease could hit them all
Crops for difficult conditionsLong-term effects on health and ecosystems not fully known; seeds can be expensive

The GM tilapia question is the model. The GM fish grew faster and wasted less food, so there were fewer faeces, less decomposition by bacteria, less oxygen used up, and less eutrophication — points for "better for the environment". Points against: no data on disease, the fish are genetically similar so a disease could spread easily, escaped GM fish could breed with wild fish or outcompete them, and the study was not repeated.

subsections.heading: Clones and micropropagation
subsections.html:
Spec 5.17B · 2023 Edexcel 2B Q6(a)(ii)

A clone is a genetically identical copy; micropropagation makes many plant clones from tiny pieces of one plant.

Clones are made by mitosis, which copies the chromosomes exactly. Micropropagation (tissue culture):

  1. Take small pieces of tissue from the plant — explants, often from the shoot tips.
  2. Sterilise them — e.g. wash in dilute bleach or ethanol — to kill microorganisms.
  3. Place them on sterile agar in a container.
  4. The agar contains nutrients — glucose, mineral ions such as nitrate, amino acids — and plant hormones such as auxin, which make the cells divide and grow roots and shoots.
  5. Keep sterile and warm, in the light. Each explant grows into a small plant.
  6. Transfer the plantlets to compost to grow on.

✗ "Put it on agar with nutrients."
✓ "Agar containing glucose and mineral ions, and plant hormones such as auxin."

The 2023 scheme ignored "nutrient" on its own. Name them.

subsections.heading: Why growers use micropropagation
subsections.html:
Spec 5.18B · 2022 Edexcel 2B Q1(e) · 2023 Edexcel Jan 2B Q4(a)

Micropropagation gives large numbers of genetically identical plants, quickly, from a single valuable plant.

  • Large numbers of plants from one parent — thousands from a few cells.
  • Fast, and can be done at any time of year.
  • All the plants are genetically identical, so all have the desired characteristic — e.g. all make suberin, all have low saturated fat.
  • No need for pollination — useful when only one transgenic plant exists, with nothing to breed it with, and it avoids cross-pollinating wild plants.
  • Can save rare or endangered plant species.

The downside is the same as for any clone: no variation, so a single disease or change in conditions could kill every plant.

The 2022 scheme ignored "faster growth of plants". Micropropagation is a faster way to produce plants; the plants themselves do not grow any faster.

subsections.heading: Cloning a mammal — Dolly the sheep
subsections.html:
Spec 5.19B · 2024 Edexcel 2B Q1(d)(ii)

To clone a mammal, the nucleus of a body cell is put into an egg cell whose own nucleus has been removed, and the embryo is grown in a surrogate mother.

  1. Take an egg cell from a female and remove its nucleus — it is now enucleated.
  2. Take a body cell (for Dolly, an udder cell) from the adult to be cloned, and remove its nucleus. It is diploid — it has a full set of chromosomes.
  3. Insert the body-cell nucleus into the empty egg cell.
  4. Give an electric shock, which stimulates the cell to divide.
  5. It divides by mitosis into an embryo.
  6. Implant the embryo into the uterus of a surrogate mother, where it develops.

The lamb is a clone of the animal that gave the body cell — not the egg donor and not the surrogate. All its chromosomes came from that one nucleus. The 2024 passage applied the same steps to cells stored in a cryozoo: an endangered banteng was cloned using its stored body cells and an egg from another species.

subsections.heading: Cloned transgenic animals
subsections.html:
Spec 5.20B

Genetic modification and cloning can be combined, so one transgenic animal becomes a herd that makes a useful human protein.

  1. A human gene for a useful protein is inserted into an animal — often so that the protein is made in its milk.
  2. That one transgenic animal is cloned, using the method above.
  3. Every clone carries the gene, so the whole herd produces the protein, which is extracted from the milk.

Sheep and goats have been used this way to produce human proteins for treating diseases, such as proteins that control blood clotting.

For cloning animalsAgainst cloning animals
Many identical copies of an animal with a valuable featureNo variation — one disease could wipe out all of them
Faster than breeding; the feature is not diluted by a mate's allelesLow success rate — many embryos fail
Could save endangered — or even extinct — speciesClones may have health problems and shorter lives; ethical concerns

The sentences behind most of the marks

Insulin: restriction enzyme cuts out the gene → same enzyme cuts the plasmid → complementary sticky ends → ligase joins → plasmid into bacterium → grown in a fermenter.

Micropropagation: small pieces → sterilise → agar with glucose, mineral ions and auxin → many identical plants.

Dolly: enucleated egg + body-cell nucleus → electric shock → mitosis → embryo → surrogate's uterus.

questions.promptHtml: Why must the same restriction enzyme cut both the human DNA and the plasmid?
questions.answerHtml:
Each restriction enzyme cuts at one specific base sequence, leaving particular sticky ends. Using the same enzyme gives the gene and the plasmid complementary sticky ends.

The bases pair up, holding the gene in place so ligase can join it into the plasmid. Different enzymes would leave ends that do not match.

questions.promptHtml: A body cell is taken from a black sheep, an egg from a white sheep, and the embryo implanted into a brown sheep. What colour is the lamb, and why?
questions.answerHtml:
Black. The lamb's DNA all comes from the nucleus inserted into the egg — from the black sheep's body cell.

The white sheep's egg had its nucleus removed, so contributes no genes. The brown surrogate only provides the uterus.

questions.promptHtml: How can a bacterium make a human protein when it has never had human genes before?
questions.answerHtml:
The genetic code is the same in all organisms: the same codons code for the same amino acids in bacteria and humans.

Once the human gene is in the bacterium, its ribosomes read the gene's code and join the amino acids in exactly the same order as a human cell would. So the protein made is identical to human insulin.

questions.promptHtml: Why is the nucleus for cloning taken from a body cell and not from a sperm or egg?
questions.answerHtml:
A body cell is diploid — its nucleus holds the full set of chromosomes, the complete genome of the animal being cloned.

Sperm and eggs are made by meiosis, so they are haploid — half the chromosomes, and each gamete a different mix. An embryo from one would have too few chromosomes and would not be identical to the parent.

questions.promptHtml: Scientists have produced one transgenic plant. Why do they copy it by micropropagation instead of letting it reproduce sexually?
questions.answerHtml:
There is only one transgenic plant, so there is nothing of the same kind to breed it with. Sexual reproduction would also mix its alleles with another plant's, so not every offspring would carry the new gene.

Micropropagation uses mitosis, so every new plant is genetically identical — all carry the gene. It is fast, gives large numbers, works at any time of year, and needs no pollination, so the gene is not spread to wild plants.

questions.promptHtml: Why must the explants and agar be kept sterile in micropropagation?
questions.answerHtml:
The agar contains glucose and nutrients, so it is ideal food for bacteria and fungi. Any microorganism that gets in would grow fast and compete with, infect or kill the tiny plant pieces.

Sterilising the explants and working with sterile equipment stops this, so the plant cells get the nutrients.

questions.promptHtml: A farmer grows only one variety of GM, herbicide-resistant maize. Give one way this increases yield and one risk it creates.
questions.answerHtml:
Yield: the farmer can spray weedkiller that kills the weeds but not the maize. With fewer weeds there is less competition for light, water and mineral ions, so the maize grows better.

Risk: the plants are genetically very similar — little variation — so a new disease could affect them all. The resistance gene could also spread to wild relatives by pollination, making herbicide-resistant weeds.

questions.promptHtml: A goat is genetically modified so that its milk contains a human protein, then cloned. Why clone it rather than breed from it?
questions.answerHtml:
Breeding would mix the transgenic goat's alleles with a mate's, so only some offspring — about half, if the goat has one copy of the gene — would inherit the new gene, and it takes a generation to find out which.

Every clone is genetically identical to the transgenic goat, so every one carries the gene and makes the protein. The herd grows faster and reliably.
